March 20, 2026
To the Attention of; Hydro 2000 Inc and its Shareholders
Subject: Acquisition of 440 St. Philippe Street – Regulatory and Financial Assessment
At the request of Hydro 2000 Inc. (the “Hydro 2000”), Tandem Energy Services Inc.
(“TESI”), in its role as regulatory advisor, has reviewed the proposed acquisition of the
property located at 440 St. Philippe Street in Alfred, Ontario, including the associated
financing structure, planned capital improvements, and regulatory treatment.
Based on our review, it is our opinion that the proposed acquisition represents a
prudent and reasonable investment for Hydro 2000, both from a financial and
regulatory perspective.
Regulatory Considerations
Hydro 2000 operates within a cost-of-service regulatory framework under the Ontario
Energy Board. In practical terms, this means Hydro 2000 recovers its costs and earns
a regulated return through rates.
Only the portion of the building used for Hydro 2000 operations would be included in
rate base, (meaning the value of assets on which Hydro 2000 is permitted to earn that
regulated return). The residential leased portions of the building are considered non-
Hydro 2000 in nature and would be excluded.
Rental income generated from those non-Hydro 2000 portions would be recorded as
Other Revenue and applied as a revenue offset, reducing the overall revenue
requirement, or the amount Hydro 2000 needs to recover from customers through
rates.
This structure ensures that:
 ratepayers are not funding non-Hydro 2000 activities
 any benefit from those activities flows back to customers through lower rates.
Financial and Strategic Assessment
From a financial perspective, this is a straightforward shift from leasing to ownership.
Hydro 2000 is replacing an ongoing lease expense with control of a core operational
asset. The short-term financial impact is modest and can be absorbed within the
existing framework, particularly when considering the contribution of rental income,
which helps offset carrying costs and reduce pressure on rates.
Over time, Hydro 2000-use portion of the building can be incorporated into rate base,
supporting long-term financial stability. The additional rental unit further strengthens
the overall position, but the acquisition itself does not depend on it.
Shareholder Considerations
As the sole shareholder, the Municipality benefits through its ownership of Hydro 2000.
While the building is owned by Hydro 2000, it strengthens Hydro 2000 as a whole.
Hydro 2000 is effectively the entity that holds and manages the assets required to
deliver service. Adding a permanent operational facility, along with stable non-
regulated income, improves financial resilience, borrowing capacity, and overall
flexibility.
In practical terms:
 ratepayers benefit through reduced revenue requirements
 the Municipality benefits through a stronger, more valuable Hydro 2000.
Risk Considerations
TESI has considered the primary risks associated with the transaction. These are not
unusual for this type of investment and are well understood.
The key considerations are:
 Construction cost risk: The estimated $65,000 renovation cost is based on
current information and defined scope. As with any project, there is potential for
cost overruns; however, the magnitude is limited and can be absorbed within
Hydro 2000’s existing financial capacity.
 Rental risk: Rental income assumptions reflect current market conditions. There
is some exposure to vacancies or variability in rental rates over time, although
this risk is considered moderate and manageable.
2
 Regulatory treatment and allocation: This is not a risk to the viability of the
project, but it does require clear and consistent tracking. Hydro 2000 will need
to maintain appropriate allocation between Hydro 2000 and non-Hydro 2000
portions of the building to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements.
 Timing of rate recovery: The portion of the building attributable to Hydro 2000’s
operations will not be included in rate base, and therefore will not be reflected
in rates, until the next Cost of Service application (currently expected in 2030).
As a result, Hydro 2000 must absorb the carrying costs in the interim period.
In our view, these considerations are limited, well understood, and manageable. Hydro
2000 has sufficient financial capacity to absorb potential variability, and the proposed
structure appropriately addresses regulatory requirements. Importantly, the underlying
business case remains sound even without reliance on additional rental income.
Conclusion
In TESI’s opinion, the proposed acquisition of 440 St. Philippe Street is financially
sound, regulatorily compliant, and aligned with Hydro 2000’s obligation to manage its
assets in a prudent and cost-effective manner.
The transaction secures a critical operational asset, maintains rate stability in the near
term, and supports both long-term Hydro 2000 value and ratepayer benefit.
This approach is also consistent with a more conservative application of regulatory
principles than is sometimes observed in similar circumstances. By not seeking
immediate rate recovery and by ensuring that non-utility benefits flow through to
reduce the revenue requirement, Hydro 2000 has structured the transaction in a
manner that prioritizes ratepayer impact and minimizes regulatory risk.
Yours truly,
Manuela Ris, Regulatory Consultant
Tandem Energy Services Inc.
416-562-9295

 Potential Municipal Equipment Operator Course
Recommended Motion:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Whereas municipal public works departments from across the Province of Ontario provide invaluable services to our communities ensuring the health and safety of all residents;
And Whereas if it was not for our municipal public works employees from across the Province of Ontario maintaining our public roads systems, our communities would not be able to function as emergency personnel could not respond to calls, school buses could not get our children to school, residents would not be able to get to work, school or appointments and many more basic functions would not be able to happen;
And Whereas municipal public works departments are already feeling the impacts of a labour shortage, which will only be exasperated over the next three to five years, which will cause levels of service municipalities are able to provide to ensure the health and safety of our residents to decrease;
And Whereas there is currently no provincial-wide course that properly trains potential municipal public works employees, specifically relating to municipal heavy equipment.
Therefore It Be Resolved that the Township of Amaranth supports the work of the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors to develop a Municipal Equipment Operator Course to address this issue;
And That the Township of Amaranth calls on the Province of Ontario’s Ministry of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades to fully fund the Municipal Equipment Operator Course in 2024 through the Skills Development Fund;
And That a copy of this resolution be sent to the Minister of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades David Piccinni, the Township of Amaranth’s Member of Provincial Parliament Sylvia Jones and the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors.

SOUTH GRENVILLE O.P.P DETACHMENT BOARD
REPORT
From: Lindsey Veltkamp, Clerk
Subject: Staff Report 05-2026 - Board Appointments 2026-2030
RECOMMENDATION
THAT the South Grenville OPP Detachment Board receive Staff Report 05-2026 –
Board Appointments for the 2026-2030 Term, for information.
BACKGROUND
The upcoming municipal election and commencement of the 2026–2030 term of council
will require the appointment of new municipal and Public Members to the Grenville
O.P.P. Detachment Board.
Section 67 of the Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019, provides that for each
detachment of the Ontario Provincial Police providing policing in a municipality there
shall be an O.P.P. Detachment Board. As such, the Grenville O.P.P. Detachment Board
was established, composed of representation from the Township of Augusta, Township
of Edwardsburgh Cardinal, and the Town of Prescott.
O.Reg. 135/24 specifies that the Board shall be composed of:
• one (1) member appointed by each municipality, who is a member of the council
of the municipality, for a total of three (3) members
• one member shall be appointed by each of the municipalities, who is neither a
member of the council of, nor an employee of, the municipality, for a total three
(3) members
• two (2) members shall be appointed by the Minister.
The appointed members to the Grenville O.P.P Detachment Board included the
following individuals:
• Mayor Jeff Shaver, Township of Augusta
• Mayor Tory Deschamps, Township of Edwardsburg Cardinal
• Mayor Gauri Shankar, Town of Prescott
• Brian Purcell, Township of Augusta, Public Member
• Marina Laker, Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal, Public Member
• Rob Samojllo, Town of Prescott, Public Member
• Minister Appointments (2) - Vacant
Additionally, O.Reg 135/24 states that the term of office for a member of an O.P.P.
detachment board appointed by a municipality shall not exceed the term of office of the
council of the municipality that appointed the member.
DISCUSSION OPTIONS
The 2022-2026 term of council is scheduled to come to an end on November 14, 2026,
following the municipal election on October 26, 2026. In preparation for the upcoming
new term of council beginning on November 15, 2026, staff at the municipalities of
Augusta Township, the Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal, and Town of Prescott will
be issuing a call for applications for Public Member positions on the Grenville O.P.P
Detachment Board.
Following the inaugural meeting of each municipal council, Council appointments will be
made to the Grenville O.P.P. Detachment Board. Each municipality will receive their
individual applications for Public Member representation and appoint them locally. It is
noted that each municipality may establish its own selection process for the
appointment of its Public Member.
Staff are suggesting starting a call for applications mid-September to allow sufficient
time to advertise the positions, receive and review applications and prepare for
appointments following November 15, 2026. There are no provisions in O.Reg. 135/24
that prohibit a member from being appointed to the Board for consecutive terms.
Accordingly, current Public Members may apply for reappointment should they wish to
continue serving on the Board.
Due to the anticipated timelines for the municipal election, Council appointments, Public
Member selection, and required training for newly appointed members, Staff are
recommending that no Board meeting be scheduled for December 2026. This will
provide the new Board with an opportunity to complete the appointment and onboarding
process and will also account for the holiday period.
O.Reg 135/24 provides for continuity during the transition period. A member appointed
by a municipality may continue to sit on the Board until the earlier of:
a. Six months after the expiry of their term of office or;
b. The day the member’s successor is appointed by the municipality
This provision will assist in ensuring that the Board can continue to function while the
municipalities complete their respective appointment processes.
Staff will coordinate with the Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal and Town of Prescott
to establish a consistent timeline for the recruitment and appointment process. Subject
to Council appointments, following the 2026 municipal election, each municipality will
proceed with its own process for selecting and appointing a Public Member to the
Grenville O.P.P. Detachment Board.
Once the municipal and Public Member appointments have been completed, Staff will
coordinate the orientation and required training of the new Board members and
establish the Board meeting schedule for 2027.
Current Board members will be notified if they are to be re-appointed (should they re-
apply) or that their appointment has ended with the appointment of a new member once
the municipal appointment processes have been completed.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
There are no significant financial implications associated with receiving this report for
information. Any costs associated with advertising, training, or Board operations will be
accommodated through the approved operating budget of the O.P.P. Detachment
Board, as applicable.

SOUTH GRENVILLE O.P.P DETACHMENT BOARD
REPORT
From: Shannon Geraghty, Chief Administrative Officer
Subject: Staff Report 04-2026 – Grenville County O.P.P Detachment Annual
Report – June 30,2026
RECOMMENDATION
THAT the Grenville County O.P.P. Detachment Board receive and accept the 2025
Grenville County O.P.P Detachment Annual Report as attached to Staff Report 04-
2026.
BACKGROUND
In 2019, the Province announced that significant changes would be made to policing
services with the passage of Bill 68, the Community Safety and Policing Act (CSPA).
The CSPA came into force and effect on April 1st, 2024, and replaced the Police
Services Act (PSA). The new Community Safety and Policing Act is seen as an
opportunity to modernize policing and enhance community safety in Ontario. Under the
new Act is the creation of O.P.P Detachment Boards, which were required to be
established for each detachment of the Ontario Provincial Police. The South Grenville
O.P.P Detachment Board services the Township of Augusta, Township of
Edwardsburgh Cardinal, and Town of Prescott.
The South Grenville O.P.P Detachment Board is comprised of eight (8) members as
follows:
 Three (3) Council Member Representatives (one from each municipality)
 Three (3) Community Representatives (one from each municipality)
 Two (2) Provincial Representatives (to be appointed by the province)
Under the Community Safety and Policing Act, the key roles and responsibilities of the
newly formed South Grenville O.P.P Detachment Board are to:
 consult with the Commissioner regarding the selection of a Detachment
Commander and otherwise participate, in accordance with the regulations made
by the Minister, in the selection of the Detachment Commander;
 determine objectives and priorities for the detachment, consistent with the
Strategic Plan prepared by the Minister, after consultation with the Detachment
Commander or his or her designate;
 advise the Detachment Commander with respect to policing provided by the
detachment;
 monitor the performance of the Detachment Commander;
 review the reports from the Detachment Commander regarding policing provided
by the detachment; and
 on or before June 30 in each year, provide an annual report to the municipalities
and band councils regarding the policing provided by the detachment in their
municipalities or First Nation reserves.
DISCUSSION OPTIONS
Reporting Requirements as provided in Section 68 (1) of the CPSA outlines annual
reporting requirements and states the O.P.P detachment board shall: “On or before
June 30 in each year, provide an annual report to the municipalities and band councils
regarding the policing provided by the detachment in their municipalities or First Nation
reserves.”
To ensure compliance with the reporting requirements, Staff at the Township of
Augusta, the Township Edwardsburgh Cardinal, and the Town of Prescott, agreed to
bring the report directly to each municipal Council rather than waiting for the next South
Grenville O.P.P Detachment Board meeting scheduled for September 10, 2026.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
An amount of $10,000 each has been allocated from each of the respective
municipalities that form the South Grenville O.P.P Detachment Police Board including
the Township of Augusta, the Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal, and the Town of
Prescott. These funds are utilized to cover costs such as bursaries, training,
memberships, and per diems in accordance with the Terms of Reference.
These funds will be reviewed annually to ensure the appropriate balances are sufficient
to cover the costs and other initiatives that the Board wants to undertake with the
assistance of the Detachment Commander and O.P.P.

Foreword
We are pleased to present Belleville’s Community Safety and Well-Being (CSWB) plan, as approved
by City Council.
CSWB plans are both a legislative requirement and an important opportunity to strengthen safety
and well-being across the community. Input from service providers, community organizations, and
residents has helped identify key priorities and practical approaches to addressing them.
This plan focuses on three priority areas—housing and homelessness, mental health and addiction,
and access to services and supports. Through collaboration, partners have identified shared risks
and opportunities to better coordinate efforts in support of those most in need.
Through a collaborative approach, this plan is intended to support ongoing efforts to strengthen
community safety and well-being. Over the next four years, it will help guide coordinated action that
considers the social determinants of health and supports improved access to housing, shelter,
mental health and addiction services and other services and supports that Belleville residents need.
We are grateful to the many agencies, organizations, and individuals who contributed their time,
expertise, and perspectives. Their continued collaboration will be essential to moving this work
forward.
Together, this plan reflects a shared commitment to working across sectors to support a safer,
healthier, and more connected community.

Introduction
This is the City of Belleville’s Community Safety
and Well-Being (CSWB) Plan for 2026 through
2030.
CSWB plans aim to enhance the safety, health,
and well-being of communities by addressing
the root causes of crime, disorder, and poor
health outcomes. They bring together partners
across sectors to identify key risks and
coordinate actions that support prevention,
early intervention, and improved outcomes for
residents.
CSWB plans are mandated under Part XVI of the
Community Safety and Policing Act, 2019 (CSPA),
which requires municipalities to develop and
review their plans every four years. This plan will
guide local CSWB efforts in Belleville over the
2026–2030 period.
This work is grounded in collaboration. Input
from service providers, community
organizations, and residents helped identify the
most significant risks facing the community and
the areas where coordinated action can have the
greatest impact.
This plan focuses on three priority areas:
• Housing and Homelessness
• Mental Health and Addiction
• Access to Services and Supports
While no single plan can address all community
challenges, it provides a framework for
coordinated, sustainable action. The strategies
outlined in this document are intended to
support ongoing efforts, strengthen
partnerships, and contribute to improved
community safety and well-being over time.
7
Plan at a Glance
The City of Belleville’s 2026–2030 Community Safety and Well-Being (CSWB) plan outlines a
coordinated, collaborative approach to addressing key factors that influence the safety and well-
being of residents, aligned with Ontario’s Community Safety and Well-Being Planning Framework.
This plan reflects input from residents, service providers, and community partners, and builds on
existing strategies and initiatives. It focuses on shared priorities and opportunities where
coordinated action can help strengthen outcomes and support a safer, healthier, and more
connected community.
While a range of ideas and priorities were identified through engagement, this plan focuses on three
aligned strategies, detailed in the sections that follow.
This plan reflects input from residents, service providers, and community partners, supported by
local data and reports.
• 190 Resident Survey responses
• 20 provider interviews
• 22 providers participated in a strategy-setting session
• Review of local reports and data
Together, these inputs helped identify shared priorities and opportunities for coordinated action.
Implementation is supported through a shared leadership approach. Strategy leads help advance
each priority in collaboration with partners, while the Advisory Committee provides subject matter
expertise and supports alignment across initiatives. A Governance Committee provides oversight
and serves as a link to Council, which remains ultimately accountable. Progress is monitored over
time through regular updates, shared learning, and ongoing use of data to support coordination and
continuous improvement.

Understanding Our Community
To understand what is shaping safety and well-being
in Belleville, this plan brings together local
information, including from the Belleville Police
Service and community data sources. Taken together,
the voices and the data help tell a shared story about
who we are, what is changing, and where partners can
focus to reduce harm and strengthen well-being.
Belleville is a growing community. According to the
2021 Statistics Canada Census, Belleville’s population
was 55,071—up 8.6% from 2016.i As the city grows and
changes, CSWB planning helps local partners
anticipate pressures and strengthen the supports that
help people stay housed, well, and connected to
services.
Some community characteristics are best understood
across the wider Belleville–Quinte West area (the
census metropolitan area), which reflects where many
people live, work, and access services.
Across the Belleville–Quinte West area, people bring a
range of cultures, identities, and lived experiences to
community life. In the 2021 Census, 5.2% of residents
identified as First Nations, Métis, or Inuit, higher than
Ontario overall (2.8%). The immigrant population was
8.3% (lower than Ontario at 29.1%), and 4.1% of
residents identified as part of a racialized group (lower
than Ontario at 29.3%). These differences are
important to consider through a CSWB lens: they
remind local partners to design supports that are
welcoming and culturally safe, and to work with
Indigenous partners and diverse communities so
services are accessible, respectful, and responsive.
11
Education and employment are
important protective factors that
support stability, connection, and
opportunity. Among residents aged
25–64, 79.3% completed some form
of postsecondary education, which is
lower than Ontario overall (84.0%).
Economic conditions also shape day-
to-day well-being. Median after-tax
household income in Belleville–
Quinte West (2020) was $69,500,
which is lower than Ontario
($79,500). The unemployment rate
was 6.7%, slightly lower than Ontario
(7.4%). Through a CSWB lens, this
combination can mean that many
people are working, but some
households may still have limited
financial flexibility when faced with
rising costs, health challenges, or
housing instability. Locally, the
Hastings County Point-in-Time
Countii (October 2024) identified 210
people experiencing homelessness
county-wide, including 125 in
Belleville, reinforcing why
coordinated action on housing and
homelessness, mental health and
addiction, and access to services and
supports is central to this plan.
12
The Story in the Voices and the Data
This plan is grounded in both quantitative and qualitative evidence. Local and regional data sources
were reviewed, and input was gathered directly from residents and community partners, to better
understand community needs and priorities in Belleville, and where a more coordinated response
could add the most value.
Together, these voices and data point to four interconnected areas of focus: housing and
homelessness; mental health and addiction (including growing pressures for children and youth);
access to services and supports; and the need for a stronger, shared approach to data.

 Recommendation:
WHEREAS transparency, fiscal accountability, and long-term financial sustainability are core pillars of municipal governance within the Township of Blandford-Blenheim;
AND WHEREAS Council benefits from consistent and standardized reporting practices to support informed decision-making and effective stewardship of municipal assets and resources;
AND WHEREAS the Township's Procedural By-law establishes the framework through which information is presented to Council and decisions are made;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff to prepare an amendment to the Township's Procedural By-law to incorporate the following reporting requirements:
1. Major Capital Project Completion Reporting
A requirement that designated municipal capital and infrastructure projects, based on criteria to be established within the Procurement By-law, be subject to a mandatory Project Close-Out Report, to be presented to Council within sixty (60) days of substantial completion and to include, at minimum:
a) A comparison of final project expenditures against the approved project budget;
b) A summary and explanation of any significant financial, scope, material, schedule, or timeline variances;
c) Identification of any unresolved deficiencies, warranty matters, or outstanding items; and
d) Key lessons learned, operational considerations, and recommendations intended to improve future capital project delivery, budgeting, procurement practices, and project management.
2. Service Level Enhancement Lifecycle Analysis
A requirement that any staff report recommending the introduction of a new municipal service, or the enhancement or expansion of an existing service level, include an analysis of:
a) Anticipated lifecycle costs associated with the proposal;
b) Expected operating and maintenance impacts;
c) Future capital replacement and renewal obligations;
d) Asset management implications; and
e) Any impacts on the Township's long-term financial planning assumptions and Asset Management Plan.
The intent of this analysis is to support informed decision-making and ensure that municipal asset management information remains current, relevant, and reflective of Council's strategic priorities and service delivery objectives.

Recommendation:
WHEREAS transparency, fiscal accountability, and long-term financial sustainability
are core pillars of municipal governance within the Township of Blandford-Blenheim;
AND WHEREAS Council benefits from consistent and standardized reporting
practices to support informed decision-making and effective stewardship of
municipal assets and resources;
AND WHEREAS the Township's Procedural By-law establishes the framework
through which information is presented to Council and decisions are made;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council direct staff to prepare an
amendment to the Township's Procedural By-law to incorporate the following
reporting requirements:
1. Major Capital Project Completion Reporting
A requirement that designated municipal capital and infrastructure projects, based
on criteria to be established within the Procurement By-law, be subject to a
mandatory Project Close-Out Report, to be presented to Council within sixty (60)
days of substantial completion and to include, at minimum:
a) A comparison of final project expenditures against the approved project budget;
b) A summary and explanation of any significant financial, scope, material,
schedule, or timeline variances;
c) Identification of any unresolved deficiencies, warranty matters, or outstanding
items; and
d) Key lessons learned, operational considerations, and recommendations intended
to improve future capital project delivery, budgeting, procurement practices, and
project management.
2. Service Level Enhancement Lifecycle Analysis
A requirement that any staff report recommending the introduction of a new
municipal service, or the enhancement or expansion of an existing service level,
include an analysis of:
a) Anticipated lifecycle costs associated with the proposal;
b) Expected operating and maintenance impacts;
c) Future capital replacement and renewal obligations;
d) Asset management implications; and
e) Any impacts on the Township's long-term financial planning assumptions and
Asset Management Plan.
The intent of this analysis is to support informed decision-making and ensure that
municipal asset management information remains current, relevant, and reflective of
Council's strategic priorities and service delivery objectives.

Recommendations
1. That the report prepared by Amit Gupta, Senior Manager, Revenue Services, Finance,
to the Special City Council Meeting of August 31, 2026, re: Amendment to the 2024
Development Charges (DC) by-laws, be received;
2. That the City’s 2024 Development Charge (DC) By-laws be amended to reduce
residential development charge rates by 50% for all residential development types,
and by 65% for both large and small condominium apartments in buildings of at least
five storeys. These reductions shall take effect on March 31, 2026, and be maintained
in accordance with the terms and conditions of the Development Charge Reduction
Program (DCRP) Transfer Payment Agreement for a period of three years, ending
March 30, 2029;
3. That the expiry date of the City’s Purpose-Built Rental (PBR) Development Charge
Incentive Program be extended from November 14, 2026, to March 30, 2029, to align
with the implementation period of the Development Charge Reduction Program;
4. That staff be authorized to implement occupancy requirements for developments
benefiting from DCRP reductions, similar to the City's PBR Development Charges
Incentive Program, requiring occupancy within 30 months of Building Permit issuance,
with authority delegated to the Commissioner, Planning, Building and Growth
Management, in consultation with the CAO, to grant extensions to 36 months and up
to an additional 6 months for an eligible development dependent on construction
progress reports and project scale and timelines, and subject to consistency with the
terms and conditions of the Transfer Payment Agreement, and such building permit
has not been revoked by the City’s Chief Building Official;
5. That Council approve the amendment to the City’s 2024 DC By-laws, attached to this
report as Appendix II, to implement a 50% reduction in residential development charge
rates for all residential development types and a 65% reduction for both large and
small condominium apartments in buildings of at least five storeys, effective March 31,
2
2026, in accordance with the requirements of the Development Charge Reduction
Program (DCRP) and the Transfer Payment Agreement; and
6. That Council approve the extension of the City’s Purpose-Built Rental (PBR)
Development Charge Incentive Program from November 14, 2026, to March 30,
2029, and the associated by-law amendments attached to this report as Appendix
III.
Report Summary
On August 18, 2026, the Mayor issued a Decision, as outlined in Appendix I, directing
staff to submit an application under the Development Charges Reduction Program
(DCRP) to the Province, seeking funding to support a reduction in residential
development charge rates. The Directive instructed a 50% reduction in residential
development charge rates for all residential development types, increased to 65% for
both large and small condominium apartments in buildings of at least five storeys, and
the extension of the City's Purpose-Built Rental (PBR) Development Charge Incentive
Program, subject to the execution of a satisfactory Transfer Payment Agreement.
Pursuant to the Transfer Payment Agreement, the City is required to amend its
Development Charges By-laws to implement and maintain a 50% reduction in
residential development charge rates for all residential development types, and a 65%
reduction for both large and small condominium apartments in buildings of at least five
storeys, for a three-year period from March 31, 2026, to March 30, 2029.
This report recommends the required Development Charges By-law amendments, the
extension of the City's PBR Development Charges Incentive Program to March 30,
2029, and the implementation of occupancy requirements for developments benefiting
from DCRP reductions.
Background
On March 30, 2026, the Government of Canada and Province of Ontario announced the
Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build which identified a total of $8.8 billion available for
infrastructure investments, including a portion intended to reduce municipal
development charges.
On June 1, 2026, the Ministry of Municipal Affairs and Housing (MMAH), Ontario
opened applications for the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP),
providing up to $8.8 billion over 10 years for housing-enabling infrastructure, with
priority given to municipalities that reduce development charges for residential
development by 30% to 50% or more for a minimum of three years.
3
Prior to the launch of the DCRP, Council approved the Purpose-Built Rental (PBR)
Development Charges Incentive Program on September 10, 2025 to encourage the
construction of purpose-built rental housing in Brampton. Under the PBR Program,
approved developments have received effective development charge reductions
ranging from approximately 50% to 100%, depending on the development type, unit
mix, and number of bedrooms. The DCRP provides an opportunity to further support
housing supply by reducing development charges across all residential development
types.
Current Situation
On June 10, 2026, Council considered staff's report regarding participation in the
Development Charges Reduction Program (DCRP) and approved staff's
recommendations, subject to the execution of a satisfactory Transfer Payment
Agreement. Subsequently, on August 18, 2026, the Mayor issued a Directive, as
outlined in Appendix I, directing staff to re-submit an application under the DCRP to the
Province and pursue a 50% reduction in residential development charge rates for all
residential development types, increased to 65% for both large and small condominium
apartments in buildings of at least five storeys, together with an extension of the City's
Purpose-Built Rental (PBR) Development Charge Incentive Program, subject to the
execution of a satisfactory Transfer Payment Agreement.
Pursuant to the Transfer Payment Agreement, the City is required to amend its
Development Charges By-laws to implement and maintain these reductions for a three-
year period from March 31, 2026, to March 30, 2029.The proposed by-law amendments
are attached as Appendix II.
The City's existing PBR Development Charges Incentive Program provides
development charge reductions that exceed the minimum residential development
charge reduction required under the DCRP. To date, approved PBR applications have
received effective DC reductions between 50% to 100%, depending on the specific
development type, unit mix, and bedroom composition.
Staff are recommending that the City's PBR Development Charges Incentive Program
be extended from its current expiry date of November 14, 2026 to March 30, 2029 to
align with the DCRP implementation period. The proposed program amendments are
included in Appendix III.
Consistent with the City's PBR Development Charges Incentive Program, staff further
recommend establishing occupancy requirements for developments benefiting from
DCRP reductions. Eligible developments would be required to achieve occupancy within
30 months of Building Permit issuance, with authority delegated to the Commissioner,
Planning, Building and Growth Management, in consultation with the CAO, to extend
the occupancy requirement to 36 months and up to an additional 6 months for an
eligible development dependent on construction progress reports and project scale and
4
timelines, and subject to consistency with the terms and conditions of the Transfer
Payment Agreement, and such building permit has not been revoked by the City’s Chief
Building Official.
Financial Implications
The City will be required to implement the approved residential development charge
reductions effective March 31, 2026, resulting in foregone residential development
charge revenues over the three-year program period ending March 30, 2029. DCRP
funding will be received in accordance with the Transfer Payment Agreement and
eligible project milestones. However, timing differences between development charge
reductions, infrastructure expenditures, and funding reimbursements may require
interim financing from development charge reserves, reserve funds, or other approved
funding sources. These timing differences may also result in a temporary reduction in
reserve fund balances and associated investment income earnings.
Conclusion
The City's participation in the Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) is
conditional upon meeting program requirements and entering into a Transfer Payment
Agreement with the Province. The City is amending its Development Charges By-laws
to implement and maintain a 50% reduction in residential development charge rates for
all residential development types and a 65% reduction for both large and small
condominium apartments in buildings of at least five storeys from March 31, 2026, to
March 30, 2029.
The recommendations in this report provide for the required by-law amendments, the
extension of the City’s Purpose-Built Rental (PBR) Development Charge Incentive
Program to March 30, 2029, and the implementation of occupancy requirements for
developments receiving DCRP reductions in accordance with program requirements.

Amendment to Noise By-law - Councillor Caputo
 WHEREAS excessive noise has the effect of interfering with the use and enjoyment of an individual’s property; and
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, 2001 authorizes municipalities to pass by laws regulating noise and other related nuisances in order to protect the health, safety, and well-being of persons, and the quiet enjoyment of property; and
WHEREAS residents are increasingly entertaining at home, including hosting backyard gatherings and outdoor social events, resulting in growing concerns regarding late-evening noise impacts on surrounding neighbourhoods; and
WHEREAS City events including live band concerts and sports events with loudspeakers, result in noise disturbance; and
WHEREAS the City seeks to balance reasonable residential enjoyment with the need to protect adjacent property owners from undue noise disturbances.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Staff BE DIRECTED to prepare an amendment to the Noise By-law to establish a maximum permitted noise level of less than 50 decibels after 11:00 p.m., applicable to all residential properties, including but not limited to noise generated from outdoor entertainment, backyard events, concerts, sporting events, amplified sound, musical instruments, or other sound-producing devices; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to conduct a review of noise by-laws and decibel limits in other Ontario municipalities, including but not limited to comparable urban and suburban cities, and report back on best practices, enforcement models, and recommended alignment opportunities; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to place the proposed Noise By-law amendment on a future Council agenda for consideration, accompanied by a report summarizing findings from the municipal comparator review and outlining any operational or enforcement implications.

WHEREAS women and children experiencing intimate partner violence rely on emergency
shelters as a critical component of their safety, recovery, and transition to stable housing;
WHEREAS adequate lengths of stay in emergency shelters are often necessary to support
safety planning, access to social services, legal supports, mental health resources, and
housing stabilization;
WHEREAS funding formulas and service benchmarks directly influence shelter capacity,
operations, and the ability of service providers to meet community needs;
Whereas The City of Mississauga declared Intimate Partner Violence an epidemic on
September 13th 2023;
WHEREAS municipalities across Ontario utilize varying approaches to shelter funding and
length-of-stay expectations, providing opportunities for benchmarking and best-practice
review;
WHEREAS any reductions to funding based on the formulas may have unintended
consequences on service levels and the availability of supports for individuals fleeing
intimate partner violence;
THEREFORE BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the Mayor, on behalf of Council, write to
the Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Children, Community and Social Services, the
Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, and the local Members of Provincial Parliament
requesting a provincial review of benchmarking, funding formulas, and length-of-stay
standards for emergency shelters serving women and children experiencing intimate
partner violence, with a view to ensuring adequate shelter stays and preventing reductions
in funding that could negatively impact service delivery and client outcomes;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT a copy of this resolution be forwarded to the
Premier of Ontario, the Minister of Children, Community and Social Services, the Minister of
Municipal Affairs and Housing, local MPPs, the Association of Municipalities of Ontario
(AMO), and all Ontario municipalities for their information and consideration.

Speak at a Meeting
Menu
The City of Burlington relies on our residents to make sure we're representing the interests of the community. Speaking at a Standing Committee or Council meeting is a great way to keep us informed and accountable to your needs.
Register to speak at a meeting
Register to speak at a meeting
You can register to speak at a meeting by completing our delegation registration form
Registration deadline - You must register by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, you must register by noon on the Friday before the meeting. At the meeting, delegations are heard in the order that we receive them.
If you do not wish to speak, but would like to submit your comments in writing, please email your comments to Legislative Services. Written correspondence will be circulated to Committee members prior to the meeting.
Presentations and handouts
PowerPoint presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon on the Friday before the meeting. 
Presentation tips
Here are some helpful tips on how you can prepare for your presentation.
Make notes or write out the text of your presentation. Written material will help you to keep focused and stay within the presentation time limit
Larger groups should select a spokesperson to make their presentation. If you are appearing on behalf of a larger group, such as a neighbourhood group, let the clerk know in advance
Meeting process
This is how meetings typically run and what you can expect:
Delegations are heard shortly after the start of the meeting. The committee Chair or Mayor at Council will call out your name and identify the subject matter that you will be speaking about. You will also be reminded of the delegation speaking time limit of 10 minutes at committee and five minutes at council. Please address your remarks to the Chair and Members of the Committee, or if you are at Council, to the Mayor and Members of Council
After you are done speaking, the Chair or the Mayor at Council will ask members of Council if they have any questions for you
Once all questions have been asked, the Chair or Mayor at Council will thank you for your remarks and will not entertain any more comments from your delegation
Once all delegations have been heard, the committee will discuss each agenda item in the order of the approved agenda. Committee members will discuss and debate each item and form a recommendation, which will be forwarded to Council for final approval. In-person delegates may remain in the Council Chambers or leave to watch a livestream of the meeting online.
If you have delegated at Committee and want to speak at Council as a delegation, you must only present new information. All seven Council members are members of the standing committees, so they will have heard your delegation at committee. If the matter you want to speak to is on the Council agenda, you may register as a delegation up to noon the day before the Council meeting
For information on the rules and order of delegations at standing committee and Council meetings, please refer to our Consolidated Procedure Bylaw (059-2024).
Give us your feedback
After speaking at a committee or Council meeting, please take a few minutes to give us your feedback  on the process of registering and delegating.

Register to speak at a meeting
Register to speak at a meeting
You can register to speak at a meeting by completing our delegation registration form
Registration deadline - You must register by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, you must register by noon on the Friday before the meeting. At the meeting, delegations are heard in the order that we receive them.
If you do not wish to speak, but would like to submit your comments in writing, please email your comments to Legislative Services. Written correspondence will be circulated to Committee members prior to the meeting.
Presentations and handouts
PowerPoint presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon the business day before the meeting. If the meeting is on a Monday, presentations and handouts must be submitted by noon on the Friday before the meeting. 
Presentation tips
Here are some helpful tips on how you can prepare for your presentation.
Make notes or write out the text of your presentation. Written material will help you to keep focused and stay within the presentation time limit
Larger groups should select a spokesperson to make their presentation. If you are appearing on behalf of a larger group, such as a neighbourhood group, let the clerk know in advance
Meeting process
This is how meetings typically run and what you can expect:
Delegations are heard shortly after the start of the meeting. The committee Chair or Mayor at Council will call out your name and identify the subject matter that you will be speaking about. You will also be reminded of the delegation speaking time limit of 10 minutes at committee and five minutes at council. Please address your remarks to the Chair and Members of the Committee, or if you are at Council, to the Mayor and Members of Council
After you are done speaking, the Chair or the Mayor at Council will ask members of Council if they have any questions for you
Once all questions have been asked, the Chair or Mayor at Council will thank you for your remarks and will not entertain any more comments from your delegation
Once all delegations have been heard, the committee will discuss each agenda item in the order of the approved agenda. Committee members will discuss and debate each item and form a recommendation, which will be forwarded to Council for final approval. In-person delegates may remain in the Council Chambers or leave to watch a livestream of the meeting online.
If you have delegated at Committee and want to speak at Council as a delegation, you must only present new information. All seven Council members are members of the standing committees, so they will have heard your delegation at committee. If the matter you want to speak to is on the Council agenda, you may register as a delegation up to noon the day before the Council meeting
For information on the rules and order of delegations at standing committee and Council meetings, please refer to our Consolidated Procedure Bylaw (059-2024).

Topic: Hot (Therapeutic) Pool Basin Failure and Other Recent Issues
SUMMARY
The purpose of this report is to request funds for the supply and installation of a new
Diamond Brite plaster surface and to complete other repairs for the hot (therapeutic)
pool at Carambeck due to failure and age of the plaster basin.
BACKGROUND
On November 5, 2025, Pool staff notified the Property Management Division that the hot
pool basin plaster floor surface had lifted in areas down to the concrete substrate. The
issue was investigated by staff and a temporary solution to keep the pool open for the
day was made.
Property Management began to investigate options to complete the repair and notified
the Manager of Recreation and Culture that the pool would be required to be shut down
for a period. Staff then notified Council by email of the shut down.
The initial repair was completed and the hot pool reopened November 15, 2025.
Unfortunately, the initial repair did not hold, and arrangements were made to shut down
the pool for an extended period to complete the proper repair. The pool was again shut
down on November 24, 2025 where the initial failed areas were repaired along with
other areas that had lifted. Council was notified by staff of the shutdown. The repairs
were completed and the pool reopened on December 12, 2025.
On April 1, 2026, Property Management was informed that more areas of the plaster
basin had delaminated, and the floor was becoming rough. There are concerns that the
plaster surface would continue to fail. Staff contacted the original vendor (Benson pools)
that supplied and installed the Diamond Brite plaster in 2015 for them to complete an
assessment. The vendor indicated that they were unable to meet until April 28, 2026 –
this was deemed by staff to be an unacceptable wait to address the situation. Another
commercial pool vendor, from Ottawa, GBI Pools, was contacted for an assessment,
and a site meeting was held on April 15, 2026. GBI Pools indicated that the product life
expectancy is 10 years; the surface is now 11 years old – past its expected lifecycle
date.
GBI Pools have provided an option to repair the basin with no warranty as it may
continue to fail and an option to replace the basin by removing the Diamond Brite
plaster down to the concrete substrate and install a new Diamond Brite plaster surface
that will last for approximately 10 years.
Staff met onsite with Benson Pools on April 28, 2026 to have them complete the
assessment. They recommended that the basin not be repaired and recommended that
it be replaced with the same process and product as identified by GBI Pools.
Both GBI Pools and Benson Pools provided quotes for the replacement.
COMMENTS
The Recreation and Culture Division has identified time in August that could be made
available to complete the repair or replacement of the Diamond Brite plaster.
The quotes obtained were as follows:

COMMUNICATION 137059
Received from Ross Rankin, Property and Project Manager
Addressed to Council
Date June 25, 2026
Topic Procurement Strategy for New Recreation Facility
SUMMARY
Following discussion of the New Recreation Facility report, Staff are presenting options
for the procurement strategy of the pool project. A design-build procurement strategy is
recommended for its efficiencies with respect to schedule and overall project cost.
BACKGROUND
The Town’s Strategic Plan 2023-2026 included the priority to develop a “Multi-Use
Recreation Facility Concept Plan”. The Parks, Recreation and Culture Master Plan
(PRCMP) priority 53 discussed that current needs with respect to an aquatic facility, are
being met based on the current population. Priority 53 then recommends an additional
pool to meet the needs of a growing community but not until 2038. Priority 55 of the
PRCMP recommends a new recreation facility south of Highway 7 that would include
meeting rooms and a gymnasium at a minimum which also speaks to the need for a
facility of this type.
Staff began to prepare an overall schedule to move forward with the project design.
Summary timeline:
 On March 11, 2025 – Council gave approval to staff to develop a plan to replace
the Town’s aging indoor pool.
 A session in June 2025 led by +VG Architects presented conceptual designs for
an addition onto the Carleton Place Arena. The scope for this included an
elevated walking track, pool, gymnasium and auditorium. Staff returned to
Council in June 2025 to present these conceptual designs for information.
 In January 2026, staff presented a business plan to assess the feasibility of a
steel-walled pool system within a Sprung structure for consideration. At this
meeting, council emphasized community consultation.
 In April 21, 2026, staff returned to Council with a report on the Recreation
Concept Plan and next steps. Council decided to not move forward with public
consultation and directed staff to consult the Working Group on next steps.
 The Recreation Concept Plan Working Group met on May 28, 2026 to discuss
options for next steps on the new recreation facility. One of the outcomes of this
meeting was to develop the procurement strategy for the new facility to Council at
a special meeting in June. This report addresses this direction.
A detailed project timeline can be found in the New Recreation Facility Way Forward
report
DISCUSSION
The options are as follows:
 Non-competitive process
 Traditional Design-Bid-Build process
 Design-Build process
Staff are aware of other options for the procurement of such a facility however, only the
relevant strategies for this context are discussed in this report.
Non-Competitive Procurements
A non-competitive procurement approach has been identified as a potential option for
Council’s consideration, based on the availability of a qualified proponent with
demonstrated experience in delivering comparable aquatic and recreation facilities.
This option has been previously presented to Committee of the Whole to provide
context on alternative delivery methods.
While a non-competitive approach can offer benefits such as reduced procurement
timelines and access to specialized expertise, without the benefit of competitive bidding,
the municipality may be perceived as having limited its ability to test market pricing,
innovation, and quality benchmarks. This may raise concerns about the project with
respect to transparency, fairness, and value for taxpayers.
A key disadvantage of a non-competitive procurement approach is the heightened
reputational and governance risk to the municipality if the project is not delivered to the
expected quality, performance, or value standards. Additionally, schedule or budget
slippages will face additional scrutiny under this approach. Resident confidence in
Council’s decision‑making may also be adversely impacted.
Additionally, the Town may face increased project criticism from residents, the media,
and oversight bodies (i.e. funders). These reputational risks are amplified for complex,
high‑profile recreation facility projects such as this. Service expectations are high
among residents; this project has already gained significant traction and interest with
community members. Project outcomes are highly visible, underscoring the importance
of a competitive process and robust justification if a non‑competitive procurement
method is to be considered.
Staff are not recommending this approach as it does not meet the parameters within the
Town’s Procurement By-law for non-competitive procurement and are presenting this
option for information purposes only.
Traditional Design-Bid-Build Process
Staff would retain a consultant team to fully design the facility. The project would then be
tendered, and construction would be awarded to the lowest bidder who meets the
requirements of the procurement document.
Under the traditional design‑bid‑build procurement strategy, the municipality retains a
consulting team to complete the full design of the aquatic facility, including pool
systems, mechanical and electrical infrastructure, structural elements, and gymnasium
spaces, prior to tendering construction.
Once detailed drawings and specifications are complete, the project is competitively
tendered, and a separate construction contract is awarded to the lowest compliant
bidder, consistent with Ontario municipal procurement requirements for transparency,
fairness, and open competition.
This approach provides the municipality with a high level of control over the design and
allows Council, staff, and stakeholders to review and approve detailed plans for
specialized spaces such as pools, change rooms, and gymnasium areas before
construction pricing is established.

BY-LAW NUMBER 2019-XXX
BEING A BY-LAW TO AUTHORIZE BORROWING FROM TIME TO TIME TO MEET
CURRENT EXPENDITURES DURING THE FISCAL YEAR ENDING DECEMBER 31,
2019.
WHEREAS, the Municipal Act, 2001, S.0. 2001, Chapter 25, Section 407 (1),
provides authority for a Council by by-law to authorize the Head of Council and
the Treasurer to borrow from time to time, by way of promissory note, such
sums as the Council considers necessary to meet, until taxes are collected, the
current expenditures of the Corporation for the year; and
WHEREAS, the total amount which may be borrowed from all sources at any
one time to meet the current expenditures of the Corporation, except with the
approval of the municipal Board, is limited by section 407 (2) of the Ontario
Municipal Act; and
WHEREAS, if the Council borrows any larger amount than is permitted, every
member of the Council who knowingly votes therefore is disqualified from
holding any municipal office for two years, section 423 (1) of the Ontario
Municipal Act.
NOW THEREFORE THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION OF THE
VILLAGE OF CASSELMAN ENACTS AS FOLLOWS:
1. The Head of Council and the Treasurer are hereby authorized to borrow
from time to time by way of promissory note during the year 2019
(hereinafter referred to as the current year) such sums as the Council
considers necessary to meet, until the taxes are collected, the current
expenditures of the Corporation and the other amounts that are set out in
subsection 407 (1) of the Municipal Act.
2. The amounts may be borrowed under this by-law and the lender shall be
as determined from time to time by resolution of the Council.
3. The total amount which may be borrowed at any one time under this by-
law, together with the total of any similar borrowing that have not been
repaid shall not, except for the approval of OMB exceed from January 1st
to September 30th of the year, 50% of the total, and from October 1st to
December 31st, 25% of the total of the estimated revenues of the
Corporation as set forth in the estimates adopted for the current year.

THE MUNICIPALITY OF CASSELMAN
BY-LAW No. 2019-XXX
To amend By-law No. 2019-026 being a by-law
to Govern the Proceedings of the Council
of the Municipality of Casselman
WHEREAS The Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, authorizes the Council of every municipality
to pass by-laws for governing the proceedings of its Council, the conduct of its members
and the calling of meetings; and
WHEREAS Section 238 (2) further indicates that every municipality and local board shall
pass a procedure by-law for governing the calling, place and proceedings of meetings;
WHEREAS The Council shall also follow the regulations as set out within the Municipal
Conflict of Interest Act; and the parliamentary authority of Roberts Rules of Order;
AND WHEREAS following report GR-030-2019, the Council of the Municipality of
Casselman deems it advisable to amend By-Law No. 2019-026 as hereinafter set forth;
NOW THEREFORE the Council of the Municipality of Casselman enacts as follows:
1. That the following provision of sections of By-law No. 2019-026 are hereby amended
and reads as follows:
Section 4.1 Inaugural – time – place - held:
“The Inaugural Meeting of the Council, following a regular election, shall be
considered the Councils First meeting and shall be held on the First Tuesday in
December, of an election year, beginning at 6:00 p.m. in accordance to the
Municipal Elections Act Sec.16. ”
Section 4.2 Regular – Schedule – designated - time:
“The next and each succeeding regular meeting shall be held on the second and
fourth Tuesdays of each month, commencing at 6:00 p.m. At such place within
the Municipality of Casselman designated for such purpose by the Council and
shall be held in accordance with the schedule of meetings of Council and the
Committees of Council prepared by the Clerk.”
Section 4.2.1 Alteration of the date of a Council meeting:
“Council may alter the date and/or time of a Council meeting provided that a notice
of 48 hours (calculated on open days) is posted on the municipal Web site. A
Council meeting may also be canceled within 24 hours in case of an
emergency.”
Section 4.4 Exception to meetings:
“Notwithstanding the provisions of Section 4.2 and 4.3 of this By-law, there shall
be: one meeting of Council in the month of February, which shall be held on the
second Tuesday of the month; no meetings during the March break, one
meeting of Council in the month of July, which shall be held on the second Tuesday
of the month; one meeting of Council in the month of August, which shall be held
on the fourth Tuesday of the month and one meeting of Council in the month of
December, which shall be held on the second Tuesday of the month. Should the
meeting fall on a public or civic holiday, the Council shall meet at the same hour
on the next following day, which is not a public or civic holiday.”
Section 4.11 In Camera Meeting – closed to public - Time:
“In Camera meetings, shall commence at a time prescribed by the City Clerk
and/or Chief Administrative Officer upon consultation with the Mayor and the
meetings shall be adjourned no later than 5:55 p.m. if occurring before the
public meeting”. An in camera meeting can also occur after the public
meeting”.
Section 33.6 Meeting – continuation – 9:00 p.m.:
“No item of business other than the Confirmatory By-law shall be considered at a
meeting of the Council after the hour of 9:00 p.m. local time, unless otherwise
decided by a two-thirds (2/3) vote of the Members present. The duration of a
Council meeting shall not exceed a total of 3 hours (including in camera
meeting), unless otherwise decided by a two-thirds (2/3) vote a of the
Members present.”
Section 21.13 Committee meetings:
“No meeting shall be scheduled between the second Tuesday of the month
of July and the 4th Tuesday of August.”
2. That all other provisions of By-law No. 2019-026 will continue to be in force.
3. That this by-law shall come into effect on the passing thereof.

Types of Council Meetings
SECTION MENU
Cobourg Municipal Council conducts its business through Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Standing Committee Meetings
Standing Committees are affiliated with municipal divisions and overall priorities and policy decisions. Cobourg will now have three Standing Committees consisting of:
Community Services, Protection and Economic Development Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 9:30 a.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Adam Bureau (Chair), Councillor Aaron Burchat, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Public Works, Development Division Standing Committee
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Brian Darling (Chair), Councillor Miriam Mutton, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Corporate, Finance, and Legislative Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Thursday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Deputy Mayor Nicole Beatty (Chair), Councillor Randy Barber, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Other Members of Council can attend standing committees of which they are not members to ask questions and hear information to prepare for Regular Council Meetings. Standing Committee members discuss items on the agenda and make a recommendation to Council for the action to be taken on the matter.
Regular Council Meetings
Following the Standing Committee meetings the recommendations of the Committees will be presented at a Regular Council meeting where a final decision will be made and published in the meeting minutes. See the calendar below for meeting information including dates and times, and to access Agendas, Minutes, and videos. Unless otherwise noted, meetings are open to the general public. 
Other Types of Council Meetings
The following meeting types are held by the Town of Cobourg Council:
Standing Committee
Regular Council
Public Council
Special Council
Emergency Council
Advisory Committees and Local Boards, and
Closed Council
The public may attend any of these meetings, except Closed Council meetings. Closed meetings are held in accordance with section 239 of the Municipal Act, 2001. 
See above for information on Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Public Meetings
Public Council meetings are held to provide an opportunity for Council to receive comments from the public to assist Council in making a final decision. Public meetings are generally held on the third Wednesday of the month at 5 p.m.
Public meetings are held when changes to the following are being considered:
Certain by-laws (ie. Zoning By-law);
Licensing and Fees;
Master Plans (Parks, Waterfront, Parking, Transportation);
Official Plans; and
Other matters requiring public input.
Closed Meeting Investigator
Any person can request an investigation to see if Council has met in Closed Session for a valid, legal reason.
The Town of Cobourg has an Integrity Commissioner, Closed Meeting Investigator and Ombudsman. Fill in the Request Form for Closed Meeting Investigation and send it to the Legislative Services Department with the $25 fee.

SECTION MENU
Regular Open Council meetings commence at 7:00 p.m. on the second and fourth Mondays of the month. These meetings are open to the public. Planning and Special meetings are scheduled as required and public notice is provided per the legislation.
Closed Council meetings commence at 6:00 p.m., prior to the open sessions at 7:00 p.m.  Closed sessions are not open to the public in accordance with Section 239 of the Municipal Act. 
Agendas and Minutes
Agendas and Minutes of Open Council meetings will be published on the City's website on the Friday before the regularly scheduled meetings. This includes agendas and minutes for Open Council, Special, and Public meetings, as well as meetings of City of Dryden boards and committees.
To access these documents online, please see below:

Meeting Live Streaming and Video
To watch City of Dryden Council and OPP Detachment Board meetings live, please access the Council and OPP Detachment Board Meeting Calendar and open the agenda for the meeting you wish to watch.  The video will stream live on the agenda page in the top left corner or cursor down on the calendar to view the table and click on the video icon for the meeting you wish to watch. Following the live stream of the meeting, the video icon will disappear. Once the video has been time stamped, it will be posted again for viewing by the public usually within a day of the meeting.
  To Speak Before Council
Delegations
When a member of the community wants to speak to Council during an Open Meeting, it is called a delegation. In order to do this, you must fill out a delegation request. This can be done online here, or you can complete a hard copy at the Clerk's Office located at 30 Van Horne Avenue. 
  Closed Meeting Investigator
Municipal Councils must conduct business only at meetings that are open to the public but there are some exceptions where we have closed meetings. Members of the public have the right to submit a complaint if they feel the Municipality held a closed meeting that did not follow the rules/exemptions listed in the Municipal Act, 2001, Section 239.2 (1).
The Closed Meeting Investigator's role is to conduct investigations upon receipt of a complaint in respect of meetings or part of meetings that are closed to the public to determine compliance with the Act or the Municipality's Procedural By-law and to report the results of such investigations to Council.
Our Municipality has appointed Ombudsman Ontario to investigate any complaints made to them by the public about closed meetings. 
Their duties include:
Conducting an investigation when they receive a complaint about a meeting or part of a meeting that is closed to the public
Determining whether the meeting complied with the Municipal Act and Municipal Procedural By-law
Reporting the results of the investigation

1. Does the application maintain the general intent and purpose of the Official Plan?
The subject property is designated as Agricultural Resource Policy Area in the

The subject property is an existing 0.8 hectare parcel of land which is developed with

to protect prime agricultural lands however it also recognizes existing residential
development and the continued use and accessory uses associated with residential
uses. The proposed detached garage will not result in the removal of agricultural
lands which is currently in production and will provide the homeowner with secure
parking which is in keeping with rural residential development.
The detached garage will not result in the need for a minimum distance separation
calculation as no new residential dwelling is proposed.

system operating authorities are required to maintain accreditation to the DWQMS. As
part of this legislative requirement, operating authorities undergo an external re-
accreditation audit every three years to verify continued conformance with the DWQMS.
In preparation for the re-accreditation audit, a desktop audit review was completed by
NSF International on June 4th. The audit identified three minor Corrective Action
Requests (CARs) related to procedural documentation within the Township's Quality
Management System. Environmental Services staff reviewed the findings, updated the
applicable procedures, and submitted corrective actions to the auditor. All corrective
actions were subsequently reviewed and approved.
The subsequent on-site re-accreditation audit on July 9th confirmed that all previous
corrective actions had been effectively addressed and recommended continued
accreditation of the Township's Drinking Water Quality Management System. The audit
resulted in no non-conformances and identified six Opportunities for Improvement
(OFIs). These OFIs are recommendations to further improve the Township's Quality
Management System and do not affect the Township's accreditation status. Staff will
incorporate the recommendations into the Township's continual improvement process.

Council Meetings
Town of Georgina Council meets throughout the year to make decisions on municipal matters, from passing bylaws to adopting committee recommendations.
Council meetings are open to public and held at the Civic Centre in the Council Chambers. The meetings are a hybrid model, providing staff, Council members and the public the option of participating either in person or virtually. In addition, Council meetings are live streamed  on the Town of Georgina Agendas, Minutes and Meetings page. Should you be unable to attend the meetings, you are welcome to listen through the Live/Archived Broadcasts webpage.
The Council meeting scheduled for Sept. 23, 2026 has been cancelled. 
Council Meetings
Hybrid Council meetings 
Council meetings are in-person hybrid model at the Replacement Civic Centre. 
To view or listen to meetings only, access the relevant live stream on the Agendas, Minutes and Meetings page. Members of the public can watch live during the time of the meeting or view a recording later.
To participate in a Council meeting, the appropriate form must be submitted to the Clerks’ Division within the prescribed timeframe. Learn more in the “Speak at Council or committee meetings” section below.
Contact clerks@georgina.ca(link sends email) with any questions regarding attending or participating in Council meetings.
Speak at Council or committee meetings
Public consultation is an important part of the Council and committee process. If you wish to speak at Council or committee meetings – either in-person or virtually - you must first complete one of the following forms:
Delegation Request Form – Complete this form if you wish to speak or make a presentation regarding an item that is not listed on a Council agenda. Delegations are limited to five minutes. A five-minute extension to speak may be decided by a majority vote of Council. Regardless of participation method, Delegation Request Forms must be received no later than 10 a.m. on the Monday 10 days prior to the Wednesday meeting to pre-register.
Request to Speak Form - Complete this form to request to speak at a Council meeting on an agenda item. Speakers may speak once for up to five minutes. Virtual requests to speak must be submitted by noon the day before the meeting. In‑person requests to speak are encouraged to be submitted in advance and may also be submitted prior to the start of the meeting.
Committee of Adjustment Request to Speak Form
Be advised, the name and address of anyone submitting comments will appear in the public record and will be posted online following the meeting.

Re: Support Resolution Regarding a Feasibility Study for Highway 407
Please be advised that the Council of The Corporation of the Town of Orangeville, at its
Regular Council Meeting held on February 10, 2025, approved the following resolution:
Whereas road safety has been identified as a priority for Town of
Orangeville Council, staff, and residents; and
Whereas significant increases in truck traffic on Highway 10 have led to
safety concerns along the entire corridor from Melancthon down to the
southern point of Caledon; and
Whereas trucking companies avoid Highway 407 due to its tolls, leading
to higher volumes of traffic on other roads and highways; and
Whereas a pilot project to subsidize truck lanes on Highway 407 would
provide valuable insights into the economic and road safety impact of
diverting truck traffic to the 407; and
Therefore be it resolved that the Town of Orangeville support the City of
Vaughan's recent resolution to request that the Province of Ontario
implement a one-year pilot program that will subsidize or eliminate tolls
for dedicated truck lanes on Highway 407, evaluating the impact on
overall transportation efficiency and road safety; and
Be it further resolved that a copy of this motion be circulated to Premier
Doug Ford, Hon. Sylvia Jones, Deputy Premier and Dufferin-Caledon
MPP, Hon. Prabmeet Sarkaria, Minister of Transportation, Steven Del
Duca, Mayor of the City of Vaughan and all Dufferin municipalities.
Carried Unanimously
Yours truly,
Raylene Martell

Public Participation at Town of Gravenhurst Meetings
POLICY STATEMENT:
It is the policy of the Corporation of the Town of Gravenhurst to permit electronic participation from
members of the public during Council, Boards and SubCommittee meetings.
PURPOSE
To provide processes and a framework for electronic participation at meetings.
APPLICATION
This Policy applies to all members of the public who chose to participate in a meeting electronically.
PROCEDURE & GUIDELINES
A. General
The Town of Gravenhurst uses the MVI EasyConf Connect Conference system to facilitate electronic
audio-visual participation in Council and Committee meetings. Members of the public who have
access to a reliable internet connection, a camera and microphone may participate in a meeting
electronically versus exclusively in-person.
Members of the public wishing to participate electronically are encouraged to download the EasyConf
Connect application on their computers or smart devices. Web browsers can be used; however,
functionality may differ.
Electronic participants will receive an email before the meeting with a private link to access the
meeting. Depending on the meeting type, the participant may remain within a waiting room until their
item is on the agenda. All are encouraged to follow along through the livestream on the Town’s
YouTube channel. Note that the livestream may be 15 to 30 seconds delayed depending on the
connection.
B. Connectivity
Members of the public participating in a meeting electronically are responsible for ensuring the
reliability of their connection for the duration of their allotted time at the meeting. If a participant loses
connectivity during the meeting for more than 2 consecutive minutes, they will be deemed to have left
the meeting.
Technical support is not available during a live meeting.
While electronic participation is available for the public, the meeting’s primary location is in-person
inside the Council Chambers. The meeting will continue regardless of the participant’s ability to
connect or maintain a connection electronically.
C. Deputations
Deputations are presentations of up to 10 minutes made at Committee of the Whole, Planning
Council or Subcommittee meetings from an individual or group of persons. Additional information
regarding deputations is included within the Procedural By-law.
Deputation requests are required to be submitted in writing through the online deputation request
form. Deputations may be permitted in-person in the Council Chambers or electronically.
Those requesting an electronic deputation may do so by selecting electronic participation on their
form. Multiple accounts are permitted for deputations and must be clearly identified including
complete email addresses.
Visual presentations (PowerPoint, pdf, video etc.) are permitted during deputations. Those presenting
in-person shall submit the materials by noon the day prior to the meeting allowing the materials to be
pre-loaded into the audio-visual system. Electronic participants will be able to share their screens
directly within the audio-visual system. Please note, however, that screen sharing is not supported on
mobile devices. If your deputation includes a visual presentation, you will need to connect via a
computer.
Presentations not provided in advance may be displayed if the participant brings their own laptop with
a HDMI port.
Phones and tablets are not compatible with the audio-visual equipment.
D. Public Meetings
Public Meetings are public hearings hosted in accordance with the Planning Act to obtain public input
on Development Services matters. They generally occur during Planning Council and Committee of
Adjustment meetings.
Public participants may include the applicant, agent for the applicant, associations and general
members of the public.
Those requesting to provide verbal comments regarding an application are encouraged to attend the
meeting in-person to ensure their comments are delivered during the public meeting.
Members of the public may provide verbal comments through electronic participation. Registration,
using an Electronic Public Meeting registration form, is required by noon the day prior to the meeting.
During public meetings, members of the public wishing to make comments will be called forward by
the Chair in the following order:
1. Registered electronic participants, in order of receipt of written requests
2. Members of the public in-person
E. Additional Presenters
Additional presenters may be asked to attend a meeting – consultants, vendors, legal counsel etc.
These individuals will be able to attend electronically.
Presenters will be able to share their screens directly within the audio-visual system.

OFFICE CONSOLIDATION
Being A By-law to Govern the Proceedings of Council
and Committee Meetings of The Corporation of the
Municipality of Grey Highlands
As amended by By-law 2025-102
Whereas, Section 238 of the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25,
provides that every municipality shall pass a procedure by-law for
governing the calling, place and proceedings of meetings, for public
notice of meetings, and for electronic participation in meetings; and
Whereas, Council has reviewed By-law # 2018-009, as amended and
now deems it expedient to establish new provisions that reflect current
legislative requirements and best practices; now
Now Therefore the Council of the Municipality of Grey Highlands
hereby enacts as follows:
1. This By-law, other than in this By-law itself, shall be referred to as
the “Procedure By-law”.
2. By-law # 2018-009 and all previous by-laws related to meeting
