1. Application and Interpretation
1.1. This By-law establishes the rules of order for meetings of Council and
Committee of the Whole.
1.2. A word in this By-law expressed in the singular has a corresponding meaning
when used in the plural.
1.3. Any future amendment(s) to the Municipal Act, 2001 or other legislation as
noted in this By-law may alter the provisions of the legislation referenced but
shall not affect the validity of this By-law or any part thereof.
1.4. In an event of conflict between this By-law and any superior legislation, the
provisions of the superior legislation prevail.
1.5. A specific statement or rule in this By-law has greater authority than a general
statement or rule.
1.6. Any reference to a provision of this By-law may be referred to as “Section”
notwithstanding that it may be a section, subsection, clause, or paragraph.
1.7. If there is a conflict between two or more rules in this By-law, or if there is no
specific rule on a matter, the Chair will rule and, in making a ruling, the Chair
may consult the Clerk, rely on previous rulings and practices, or refer to
Robert’s Rules of Order.
1.8. Any use of the male or female pronouns in this By-law, shall have no
significance in the interpretation and application of the terms, provisions, and
conditions of this By-law, such use is solely for the sake of convenience.
2. Principles of this By-law
The principles of parliamentary law governing Meetings includes:
2.1. The majority of Members have the right to decide.
2.2. The minority of Members have the right to be heard.
2.3. All Members have the right to information to help make decisions, unless
otherwise prevented by law.
2.4. All Members have the right to an efficient meeting.

with respect and courtesy.
2.6. All Members have equal rights, privileges, and obligations.

Background
Hamilton Renewable Power Inc. (HRP Inc.) is a wholly owned municipal corporation of
the City of Hamilton responsible for converting biogas generated at two City facilities—
the Woodward Wastewater Treatment Plant and the Glanbrook Landfill—into renewable
energy.
On June 4, 2026, the HRP Inc. Board of Directors approved a comprehensive transition
strategy for the Corporation through Reports HRP26002, HRP26003, and HRP26004.
The approved direction includes advancing the preferred Renewable Natural Gas
(RNG) strategy for the Woodward Wastewater Treatment Plant to the next phase of
design and cost development, approving the planned transition of operations at the
Glanbrook Landfill Gas-to-Energy Facility, and directing HRP Inc. to seek Sole
Shareholder approval for a forgivable loan from the City of Hamilton to support the
Corporation's transitional operations.
The Board also authorized the retention of an external tax consultant to assess the tax
implications associated with the transfer of assets from HRP Inc. to the City of Hamilton

and to provide advice on the most appropriate corporate structure to support

Since the Board's approval, HRP Inc. has commenced implementation of the approved
transition strategy, including advancing the next phase of the Woodward biogas
feasibility study and progressing transition planning for the Glanbrook facility. During
this period, HRP Inc. continues to operate both the Woodward cogeneration facility and
the Glanbrook Landfill Gas-to-Energy Facility while meeting its contractual, operational,
and regulatory obligations.
This report has been prepared to seek Sole Shareholder authorization to enter into a
forgivable loan agreement with the City of Hamilton in an amount not to exceed
$1,500,000 to provide the financial resources necessary to support the Corporation's
operations and implementation of the Board-approved transition strategy.
Analysis
Transition Strategy
Hamilton Renewable Power Inc. (HRP Inc.) is currently implementing the transition
strategy approved by the Board of Directors on June 4, 2026. The approved direction
provides a long-term pathway for both of the Corporation's operating facilities while
recognizing that implementation will occur over a number of years.
At the Woodward Wastewater Treatment Plant, the Board approved the 100%
Renewable Natural Gas (RNG) scenario as the preferred long-term biogas utilization
strategy and authorized GHD Limited to advance the project to the next phase of design
and cost development. The existing Combined Heat and Power (CHP) facility continues
to operate during this period to maintain renewable electricity generation, utilize
available biogas, and meet operational requirements while planning and evaluation of
the preferred RNG option continues.

At the Glanbrook Landfill Gas-to-Energy Facility, the Board approved a planned and
orderly transition of operations while directing that the facility continue operating during
the transition period to allow HRP Inc. to fulfill its contractual obligations and support the
development of a business case for the City to assume responsibility for landfill gas
management.
As these initiatives progress, HRP Inc. continues to operate both facilities and remains
responsible for contractual commitments, maintenance activities, regulatory compliance,
consultant services, and overall project management associated with implementation of
the Board-approved transition strategy.
Financial Need for Transitional Funding
HRP Inc. continues to experience operating losses as it advances the transition strategy
approved by the Board of Directors. Historical financial results demonstrate that the
Corporation's current business model is no longer financially sustainable due to
declining landfill gas production at Glanbrook, aging infrastructure, increased
maintenance requirements, and reduced electricity generation.
While the Board has established the long-term direction for both facilities,
implementation of that direction will require time to complete engineering, regulatory
approvals, procurement activities, corporate reviews, and transition planning. During
this period, HRP Inc. must continue to meet its operational, contractual, and regulatory
obligations while funding the activities necessary to implement the approved transition
strategy.
The proposed forgivable loan will provide the financial resources necessary for HRP
Inc. to continue operating during this transition period without creating a long-term
repayment obligation that cannot reasonably be supported by the Corporation's current
financial position.

M O T I O N
Planning Committee: September 1, 2026
MOVED BY COUNCILLOR M. TADESON …………………………………..

Review of By-law No. 19-114 Respecting the Discharge of Firearms and
Bows
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 regulates the discharge of firearms and bows within the
City of Hamilton for the purpose of public safety;
WHEREAS, Schedule “A” of By-law No. 19-114 identifies lands within rural settlement
areas that are shown as “Firearms & Bows Prohibited” on the maps forming part of the by-
law;
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 also prohibits the discharge of firearms and bows in other
identified areas, including lands within the urban boundary, lands zoned residential, parks,
public centers, and public trails;
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 includes setback requirements for the discharge of
firearms and bows from prohibited areas and from occupied dwellings, buildings, or
structures, subject to the provisions of the by-law;
WHEREAS, certain rural and rural-settlement areas within Glanbrook have experienced
growth, changing land use patterns, increased residential presence, and increased activity
along local road corridors;
WHEREAS, concerns related to public safety, proximity to dwellings, and increased traffic
along key corridors have been raised within parts of Glanbrook, including areas along
Westbrook Road, Silver Street, and the Binbrook Road corridor;
WHEREAS, there may be locations where current permitted discharge areas no longer
align with surrounding residential, public, commercial, agricultural, transportation, or
community uses; and
WHEREAS, Council may wish to consider whether additional prohibited areas, expanded
setback distances, updated mapping, or other amendments to By-law No. 19-114 are
appropriate to address public safety concerns while maintaining lawful and appropriate
rural, agricultural, conservation, hunting, sporting, and regulated range activities.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED:
(a) That staff from the Planning and Economic Development Department, including
Licensing and By-law Services, in consultation with Legal Services, Hamilton Police
Service, and any other appropriate departments or agencies, be directed to review
By-law No. 19-114 and assess potential amendments related to the discharge of
firearms and bows within the City of Hamilton, such review to include but not be
limited to:
(i) the feasibility of the expansion of the “Firearms and Bows Prohibited” areas
identified in Schedule “A” of By-law No. 19-114 within Glanbrook, and
whether additional lands, corridors, rural settlement areas, or clusters of
residential or public use should be considered for inclusion;
(ii) the feasibility of the establishment of additional criteria for identifying
prohibited areas where population, land use, public access, or proximity to
dwellings and public uses may create public safety concerns;
(iii) review whether the existing setback distances for the discharge of firearms
and bows remain appropriate; and
(iv) review of enforcement and regulatory considerations related to recreational
discharge activity in proximity to residential dwellings, or public uses,
including whether the current by-law provides sufficient tools to address
associated public safety and nuisance concerns; and
(v) the following Glanbrook areas:
(1) Westbrook Road and surrounding lands;
(2) Silver Street and adjacent areas;
(3) the Binbrook Road corridor; and
(4) any other nearby areas identified by staff as requiring review based
on land use, residential proximity, public safety, or enforcement
considerations; and
(b) That staff report back to the Planning Committee in Q4 2027 with findings and,
where appropriate, recommendations for amendments to By-law No. 19-114.

strategy for the Corporation through Reports HRP26002, HRP26003, and HRP26004.
The approved direction includes advancing the preferred Renewable Natural Gas

At the Woodward Wastewater Treatment Plant, the Board approved the 100%
Renewable Natural Gas (RNG) scenario as the preferred long-term biogas utilization
strategy and authorized GHD Limited to advance the project to the next phase of design

CITY OF HAMILTON
M O T I O N
Planning Committee: September 1, 2026
MOVED BY COUNCILLOR M. TADESON …………………………………..
SECONDED BY COUNCILLOR .………………..………………………………
Review of By-law No. 19-114 Respecting the Discharge of Firearms and
Bows
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 regulates the discharge of firearms and bows within the
City of Hamilton for the purpose of public safety;
WHEREAS, Schedule “A” of By-law No. 19-114 identifies lands within rural settlement
areas that are shown as “Firearms & Bows Prohibited” on the maps forming part of the by-
law;
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 also prohibits the discharge of firearms and bows in other
identified areas, including lands within the urban boundary, lands zoned residential, parks,
public centers, and public trails;
WHEREAS, By-law No. 19-114 includes setback requirements for the discharge of
firearms and bows from prohibited areas and from occupied dwellings, buildings, or
structures, subject to the provisions of the by-law;
WHEREAS, certain rural and rural-settlement areas within Glanbrook have experienced
growth, changing land use patterns, increased residential presence, and increased activity
along local road corridors;
WHEREAS, concerns related to public safety, proximity to dwellings, and increased traffic
along key corridors have been raised within parts of Glanbrook, including areas along
Westbrook Road, Silver Street, and the Binbrook Road corridor;
WHEREAS, there may be locations where current permitted discharge areas no longer
align with surrounding residential, public, commercial, agricultural, transportation, or
community uses; and
WHEREAS, Council may wish to consider whether additional prohibited areas, expanded
setback distances, updated mapping, or other amendments to By-law No. 19-114 are
appropriate to address public safety concerns while maintaining lawful and appropriate
rural, agricultural, conservation, hunting, sporting, and regulated range activities.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED:
(a) That staff from the Planning and Economic Development Department, including
Licensing and By-law Services, in consultation with Legal Services, Hamilton Police
Service, and any other appropriate departments or agencies, be directed to review
By-law No. 19-114 and assess potential amendments related to the discharge of
firearms and bows within the City of Hamilton, such review to include but not be
limited to:
(i) the feasibility of the expansion of the “Firearms and Bows Prohibited” areas
identified in Schedule “A” of By-law No. 19-114 within Glanbrook, and
whether additional lands, corridors, rural settlement areas, or clusters of
residential or public use should be considered for inclusion;
(ii) the feasibility of the establishment of additional criteria for identifying
prohibited areas where population, land use, public access, or proximity to
dwellings and public uses may create public safety concerns;
(iii) review whether the existing setback distances for the discharge of firearms
and bows remain appropriate; and
(iv) review of enforcement and regulatory considerations related to recreational
discharge activity in proximity to residential dwellings, or public uses,
including whether the current by-law provides sufficient tools to address
associated public safety and nuisance concerns; and
(v) the following Glanbrook areas:
(1) Westbrook Road and surrounding lands;
(2) Silver Street and adjacent areas;
(3) the Binbrook Road corridor; and
(4) any other nearby areas identified by staff as requiring review based
on land use, residential proximity, public safety, or enforcement
considerations; and
(b) That staff report back to the Planning Committee in Q4 2027 with findings and,
where appropriate, recommendations for amendments to By-law No. 19-114.

Mandate / Purpose
The Indigenous Community Liaison Group (CLG) is intended to act as
an engagement focus group and provide input to the Indigenous
Relations Division and other City teams, as necessary. Indigenous CLG
members are encouraged to bring varied opinions and perspectives to
meetings. This group is not a decision-making body, rather it is an
engagement body that is representative of the local community.
The Indigenous Community Liaison Group will work to:
 assist the City of Hamilton to honour and engage its Indigenous
citizens in the pursuit of the City’s vision by providing advice and/or
recommendations, through the Indigenous Relations Division, that
enhance the wellbeing of Indigenous people and/or resolve
municipal issues
 align its work to the City of Hamilton’s Urban Indigenous Strategy
to support the successful and meaningful implementation of the
Strategic Actions
 envision a future where Hamilton is an inclusive and culturally-
aware community, where issues of importance to Indigenous
peoples living here are addressed proactively, effectively and
respectfully on the municipal agenda

 to assist the City in achieving and demonstrating progress or positive
change in support of the equitable economic, social, health and overall
wellbeing of Indigenous citizens;

consultation between and among Indigenous leaders and other
stakeholders, acting as a catalyst for the development of positive

Composition and Selection
The Indigenous Community Liaison Group will be comprised of seven (7)

From: Jamie McCarthy, Manager of Public Works and Projects

Subject Hanover Cemetery By-Law Amendment
Recommendation
That Report PW-17-26 Hanover Cemetery By-Law Amendment be received; and
That council approves the update as presented in By-Law Amendment 3411-26 to
Cemetery By-Law No. 3265-23.
Background
On May 5, 2026, the Town of Hanover (Town) officially expanded its boundaries, and
1,600 hectares of land are now part of the Town. The new lands were of mixed use with
one of the parcels being a pioneer inactive cemetery, St. George’s Cemetery maintained
by the Municipality of West Grey (West Grey).
St. George’s Cemetery located at 401317 Grey Road 4 is now within Town boundaries
and is legally described as PT Lot 16, Concession 1. Signage found at the cemetery show
that it was active from 1847 to 1968. West Grey has formally transferred the cemetery to
the Town, and all documents have been processed by the Bereavement Authority of
Ontario (BAO) to have St. George’s under the Town cemetery license.
Discussion
Currently, the cemetery by-law for the Town does not reflect inactive cemeteries and
therefore the following amendment is required to ensure protection, and that required
policies apply to active, inactive and memorial cairn site(s).
Staff worked with the BAO Licensing department and have confirmed that the suggested
changes are minor in nature, do not change the overall intent of the Cemetery By-Law
No. 3265-23, and the Notice of Filing Requirements have been waived by the licensing
officer.
Financial Implications
There are no major financial implications stemming from the recommendation of this
report.
A sign to indicate ownership, license number and contact information for the Town will be
ordered and installed and the cost of $50.00 will be able to be covered by current budget
allocation.

Staff Report To Council

Subject 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal
Recommendation
That Report HR-05-26 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal be received; and
That council accept the 2026 Group Benefit Plan Renewal as presented.
Background
Each year our brokers from People Corporation work with Canada Life (CL) to evaluate
the adequacy of the Town’s group benefit plan premiums in relation to the claims paid
and expenses required to operate the program. People Corporation acts on behalf of
the Town to negotiate annual benefit plan renewals, which take effect July 1st of each
year.
Extended Health and Dental benefit rates are set at a level that supports anticipated
claims and expenses for the upcoming year following an analysis of items including the
previous year’s premiums versus claims, administration costs, inflation, and trends.
Basic Life and Long-Term Disability benefits are insured and pooled. Rates are set based
on a blend of the carrier’s ‘manual’ rates, interest rate assumptions, and Town plan
member demographics, including gender, occupation, age, and amount of coverage.
Discussion
Compared to the prior period, the rate of health and vision claims increased by 14.2%
and dental claims increased by 2.0%. Massage, chiropractor, and physiotherapy remain
the top three paramedical services used in the current experience period. The top
medications claimed through the plan provide care for arthritis, glaucoma, and skin
disorders.
To help safeguard against extreme cost increases, once the total health claim amount for
an individual reaches $15,000, the remainder is removed from the Town’s claim
experience and is pooled. Drug claims are most typical of those resulting in pooling. A
total of $42,082 in claims were pooled in the current period which has protected the Town
from larger premium increases.

Subject Revision of Part Lot Control Exemption By-law for 546 and 548 9th Avenue
Recommendation
That Report PB-13-26 Revision of Part Lot Control Exemption By-law for 546 and 548 9th
Avenue be received; and
That council pass By-law No. 3407-26 to remove Part-lot Control from Lot 47, Plan 701,
as described in Parts 1 & 2 on Reference Plan 16R-9761 and Parts 3 & 4 on Reference
Plan 16R-10062, for the purpose of creating two freehold parcels corresponding to the
existing semi-detached dwellings at 546 and 548 9th Avenue; and
That council repeal By-law 3364-25, as the legal description has been updated and
superseded by the current application.
Background
On November 26, 2025, the Town received an application for Part Lot Control under
Section 50(7) of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1990, for the semi-detached dwellings located
at 546 and 548 9th Avenue. The original application referenced Parts 1 and 2 on
Reference Plan 16R-9761, consistent with the 2025 report and By-law 3364-25.
Subsequent review by the applicant’s surveyor and the Town identified that the correct
legal description for the intended freehold parcels also includes Parts 3 and 4 on
Reference Plan 16R-10062. As a result, the original by-law requires replacement to
ensure the proper parts are released from Part Lot Control.
Discussion
The purpose of this Part Lot Control application is to formally separate the two
semi-detached dwelling units at 546 and 548 9th Avenue so that each unit may be
conveyed and owned as an individual freehold parcel. The request does not involve any
construction, redevelopment, or changes to the existing buildings or services. It is a step
to ensure the legal boundaries match the established dividing wall between the two units.
During the review of the original 2025 application, it was determined that the legal
description needed to be updated. The earlier by-law referenced only Parts 1 and 2 on
Reference Plan 16R-9761. Updated survey information confirmed that the correct
description also includes Parts 3 and 4 on Reference Plan 16R-10062. The new By-law
3407-26 incorporates all four parts to reflect the complete and accurate legal description
for registration and future conveyance.
As required by the Planning Act, The by-law will also expire two years after its approval.
Because the updated description replaces the earlier version, By-law 3364-25 is repealed
in its entirety and replaced with the new By-law 3407-26.

The Town of Hanover (Town) owns and operates the water system which provides safe
and reliable drinking water to residents and businesses in Hanover. To accurately monitor
and bill for water, a water meter is installed at each customer location. The primary
function of a water meter is to measure the amount of water consumed by customers and
to facilitate fair and accurate billing of water and wastewater services. Additionally, these
meters are relied upon to ensure that appropriate revenues are collected to fund water
and wastewater operations and related capital replacement projects.
As council is aware, the water system runs as a self-sufficient utility with the expenses of
running the system, including capital projects, entirely funded by the customers of the
system, and it is therefore vital that the water meters are reading true values. As water
meters age, the potential for inaccurate readings increases. The industry standard for
replacement of water meters is recommended to be between 20 and 25 years.
Currently the Town has a backlog of aged meters which are identified as needing
replacement. In addition, the software that is used to read the meters and create utility
bills will become obsolete in the next three (3) years. As technology has advanced in the
water meter industry, the system that the Town uses has limited capacity and will no
longer be updated. Operational and administrative issues are being realized due to the
aging meters and software.
Staff have investigated potential proactive solutions and those associated costs to deal
with the above-mentioned issues and are seeking direction for this project.
Discussion
The Town initially installed water meters from 1991 to 1993 and tracking
shows there may have been some partial upgrades or replacements completed
throughout the years when some of the original meters stopped working. At this time
many of the meters have reached the end of their useful life span and need replacement.
Development and Infrastructure staff participated in demonstrations to obtain a better
understanding of options available for replacement. New technologies have emerged to
provide the system with several options. These include a complete cellular system, radio
read systems where staff would have to drive past each home to collect data, or the
possibility of installing radio frequency equipment on existing standpipes or high
elevations for data to be collected and populated through an office system. In addition,
these systems have varying degrees of user interface. Ratepayers could sign up for
things as detailed as a leak in their home, or interruptions associated with flushing, water
main breaks, to simpler issues that just inform staff of possible leaks within dwellings.
Currently 2,185 or 70% of the Town’s water meters are 25 years or older and need
replacement independent of implementing any type of advance metering technology. As
mechanical meters become older the parts may wear down, the meter may become less
accurate. This accuracy degradation varies across the flow range of the meter and is
caused by factors such as water velocity through the meter, water quality (i.e. limescale),
and age.
The Town owns and maintains 3,139 domestic water meters ranging in size from 15mm
(5/8”) to 150mm (6”).
The number of meters by size is provided below:
 Residential and Small Commercial meters sized 15mm (5/8”), 19mm (3/4”) and
25mm (1”) account for 3,060 of the Town’s total water meters. This comprises
97% of all meters
 Intermediate meters range in size from 38mm (1.5”) and 50mm (2”) and account
for 2% of the Town’s total water meters; and
 Large Commercial meters ranging in size from 75mm (3”) to 150mm (6”) are less
than 1 % of the total water meters
Meter reading technology has greatly improved and there are two main technologies that
enable the water department to perform remote reading of water meters. Advanced
Metering Infrastructure (AMI) which provides a two-way communication system that
supports near-real-time data transfer and AMR (Automated Meter Reading) which
provides a one-way communication system that enables remote collection of water usage
data. AMI uses a fixed network to regularly collect water consumption data from all water
meters in the service area. AMR uses mobile data collection devices that are affixed to
vehicles or carried as handheld devices for the same purpose. Both technologies require
the installation of data transmitters on all meters and implementation of Meter Data
Management (MDM) software. The distinct difference between the two technologies is
that AMI reads consumption data from all meters through near-continuous contact without
assistance from a worker. AMR requires a worker to physically pass a data collection
device within a short distance of each data transmitter (i.e. 50 metres). Removing the
need for a water treatment operator to drive or walk by homes would assist in saving
Report PW-13-26 | Page 2
hours spent that should be allocated to other water and wastewater operations. At this
time water operators and the utility clerk spend time troubleshooting and dealing with
software issues each month.
AMI networks deliver dedicated, town-owned infrastructure that support higher levels of
customization, reliability, and security allowing for tailored data collection, firmware
updates, and seamless integration with other municipal systems. As a result, a
standalone AMI network is being recommended for its ability to provide a secure, reliable,
and predictable data communication infrastructure.

obstruct the view of oncoming traffic at any access to a public thoroughfare, or
obstruct the view of any official traffic sign or signal.

permitted within 5 m of any building used solely for residential purposes.

located closer than 15 m to a building used solely for residential purposes shall be
designed and constructed so that their illumination is concealed from the residential
use.

development signs shall be permitted within 60 m of a building used solely for
residential purposes, except where the construction of the building or structure upon

solely for residential purposes.

development signs faster than three second intervals is permitted.

message changes, except where located closer than 60 m to the nearest traffic
signal of a signalized intersection, provided that any rotating portion does not
exceed ten revolutions per minute or any changing message is changed at not less
than three second intervals or is a continuous moving message.

Background Information:
Add No Parking Tow Away Zone - Homestake Rd
The City’s Roads Department has identified safety concerns along a section of Homestake
Road near the Treaty Three Police Service facility located at 22 Homestake Road. Vehicles
are regularly being parked along the north side of the road, creating hazardous conditions
when two vehicles meet and attempt to pass and this is also impeding winter maintenance
operations. Plow trucks and graders are forced to plow around these parked vehicles during
winter snow removal. To address these ongoing concerns, the Roads Department is
requesting no parking on both the North and South sides of the road in this area to alleviate
the ongoing issues.

Add No Parking Tow Away Zone - Boatlift Road
At the start of the 2025 summer season, a paid parking kiosk was introduced at the Boatlift
Road Boat Launch to bring this public launch in line with all other paid City boat launches.
This change prompted a noticeable shift in parking behaviour, leading to an increase in
bylaw complaints about parking congestion in the surrounding area, specifically along
Boatlift Road between the launch parking lot and the CPR tracks at the Portage Bay Bridge.
Vehicles with and without trailers have been observed parking overnight and for extended
periods of time along the sides of Boatlift Road, which is outside the established paid area
while also avoiding the “no overnight parking” restriction associated with the launch’s
parking lot. Overflow parking from Two Bears Marina customers has further compounded
the issue. With the Portage Bay Bridge closure there were times last year that the overflow
parking from the dock rentals were parked right to the bridge and entirely in front of the
jersey barriers currently blocking traffic from going onto the closed bridge. New clear
signage is being erected to help alleviate this congestion on City right-of-way close to the
bridge. Establishing a no parking zone and signage on both sides of Boatlift Road will correct
the undesired parking patterns, easing congestion and supporting safe and unobstructed
emergency vehicle access.

The City’s Director of Infrastructure and Operations received a request from a resident on
Guelph Street in Lakeside, for the City to accommodate more on street parking in this
residential area for residents, guests and service vehicles. The City had approved an
amendment November 2024 upon another resident’s request to remove the no parking zone
on Robertson Street from Seventh Street South to Guelph Street for the same reasons and
there have been no issues noted with these changes. Therefore, it was recommended
internally to accommodate the concerns by removing another related section of no parking
on Roberston Street from Guelph Street to the laneway between Guelph Street and Ninth
Street South. The parking restrictions on Robertson Street were historically in place due to
the close proximity of the Ministry building, which was previously accessed by members of
the public for various Provincial government services. This Ministry building is no longer a
service location for the public and hasn’t had full capacity of on-site staff since pre-Covid.

restriction, and the section of the street is wide enough to accommodate parked vehicles

Background Information:
New One-Way Traffic Erie Street & Eighth Street (St. Louis School)
During 2025 the Kenora Catholic District School Board reached out to the City with concerns
about traffic flow and safety at St. Louis School, requesting support towards a solution. The
school board expressed ongoing issues with vehicle congestion, traffic flow, parking and
pedestrian safety, specifically during school pick up and drop off times.
The City’s Infrastructure and Engineering division internally reviewed the concerns brought
forward by the school board. An on-site traffic study was conducted over a period of a week
during pick up and drop off times to complete traffic counts and observe traffic flow.
Following observation, it was determined that the potential solution of a one-way street
might help alleviate the ongoing issues.
A section of Erie Street at St. Louis School in Keewatin, including a section of Eighth Street
was trialed as a one-way street beginning December 29, 2025 when the signage was
installed. New signs now inform motorists that traffic passing by St. Louis School will flow
from River Street, East onto Erie St, continuing North onto Eighth Street, then exiting onto
Superior Street. Signage was also installed indicating traffic is not permitted to turn left
onto Eighth Street from Superior Street.
The new traffic regulation has been in place now for several months during the school season
and the trial has proven successful. The improvement has reduced congestion, improved
traffic flow, addressed parking and enhanced pedestrian safety for students, staff, and
community members. An amendment to the City’s Traffic and Parking bylaw is now required
to make the change permanent.

Terms of Reference
Heritage Advisory Committee
A. Mission Statement
The Meaford Heritage Advisory Committee is established by Council for the
purpose of making recommendations to Council on the identification,
conservation and preservation of buildings and landscapes of cultural
heritage value or interest, pursuant to the Ontario Heritage Act.
A. Objectives
Recognizing that heritage is an important part of the fabric of the
Municipality of Meaford, the objectives of the Meaford Heritage Advisory
Committee include the following:
• To foster community pride within the Municipality
• To attract tourism to the Municipality
• To support economic growth through the preservation of Meaford’s
Heritage District
B. General
1. The Meaford Heritage Advisory Committee (HAC) shall be created by
Council By-law which will include these Terms of Reference (TOR).
2. The HAC shall consist of up to seven voting members appointed by
Resolution of Council.
3. The membership shall contain at least one member of Council, who
shall serve as the committee chair, and may contain two members
at the discretion of Council.
4. Where possible, a youth representative may be appointed.
Page 1 of 8
Heritage Advisory Committee Terms of Reference
5. The members of the HAC shall be appointed in accordance with the
Municipality’s Appointments Policy.
6. Members of the HAC will be selected based on a demonstrated
interest in heritage, local knowledge and/or relevant expertise. The
selection process will be open and merit-based, with consideration
given to ensuring diversity and inclusion.
7. No public member of HAC shall be a member of another municipal
committee or Board.
8. The Mayor shall be an ex-officio member of the HAC.
9. The term of office of the members of the HAC shall expire as of
January 31 immediately following each regular municipal election.
C. Definitions
1. “Chair” means the person chairing any meeting of the HAC.
2. “Committee” means the Municipality of Meaford Heritage Advisory
Committee (HAC).
3. “Council” means the Mayor and Council of the Municipality of
Meaford.
4. “Deputation” means a verbal presentation about a subject that is on
the published HAC agenda for that meeting.
5. “ex-officio” means a member that may fully participate in HAC
discussions but cannot vote.
6. “Majority” shall mean more than half of the Members present and
voting on an issue. The count shall include only those present,
including the Chair of the Meeting.
7. “Member” shall mean a person appointed by Municipal Council
Resolution to the HAC and does not include an ex-officio member.
8. “Municipality” shall mean the Municipality of Meaford.
9. “Non-statutory Role” shall mean activities the members of the
Heritage Committee engage in which are not set out in the Ontario
Page 2 of 8

Heritage Act, and may include performing research and advising on
by-laws, programs and policies related to heritage matters.
10. “Presentation” means the verbal and/or visual provision of
information to Council by an individual, community group or
organization.
11. “Procedural By-Law” shall mean the most current By-Law concerning
the Proceedings of Council and its Committees as adopted by
Council.
12. “Public Works” encompass engineering, construction and related
activities carried out by government for the benefit of citizens, and
include the acquisition, leasing, maintenance and disposal of
immovable assets held by the municipality.
13. “Quorum” shall be the number equal to a majority of members of
the whole Committee. (i.e. a quorum is 4 in the case of a 7-member
HAC).
14. “Statutory Role” shall mean the work of the Committee in advising
Council on Heritage matters as set out in the Ontario Heritage Act.
15. “Vice-Chair” shall mean the person who has been selected to the
position by a majority of the HAC and shall have all the powers of
the Chair in the absence of the Chair. The Vice-Chair shall be elected
from among the members at the inaugural meeting of the HAC then
at the first meeting of each year thereafter.
D. Mandate
The Heritage Advisory Committee has a Statutory Role under the Ontario
Heritage Act, 1990, to provide advice and recommendations to Council. The
Heritage Advisory Committee may also perform a Non-statutory Role, under
the direction of Council.
Statutory Role of the Committee
The Ontario Heritage Act (s. 28) defines the committee's statutory role is
to:
Page 3 of 8
Heritage Advisory Committee Terms of Reference
• Advise and assist the council on all matters relating to the
designation of individual properties under Part IV or heritage
conservation districts under Part V
• Make recommendations on applications to alter, erect, demolish or
remove any buildings or structures on designated properties
• Advise Council on applications to repeal by-laws which designate
individual properties as heritage properties
• Make recommendations to Council whether to enter into heritage
conservation easement agreements or covenants, and
• Advise and assist Council on other heritage matters as Council may
deem appropriate by by-law.
Non-statutory Role
The Heritage Advisory Committee may engage in non-statutory activities
with the aim of heritage preservation, public engagement and awareness
and heritage recognition in the community, including:
• Researching, identifying and evaluating all the properties and areas
that may deserve protection by maintaining an inventory of listed
heritage properties (structures)
• Identifying issues related to designated or listed properties under
the Ontario Heritage Act
• Promoting heritage conservation as well as advising property owners
on appropriate conservation and maintenance practices
• The development of community recognition for architectural
preservation through commemorative initiatives such as plaque
programs, awards for restoration and sympathetic infill development
• Advising Council of new heritage legislation and funding initiatives
• Advising Council on changes to by-laws and policies which may
impact Heritage matters, such as Official Plan policy, Zoning By-law
amendments, Property Standards By-laws and so on.

E. Meetings
1. Frequency: Scheduled meetings will be held six times per year, with
additional meetings called as necessary by the Chair and CAO acting
collaboratively.
2. Quorum: At least 50% plus one (1) of the appointed members must
be present to constitute a quorum.
3. Agendas: Shall be prepared and published by municipal staff. A
meeting between a member of the Legislative Services division, the
staff subject matter expert, committee Chair and a rotating member
of the committee shall take place a week prior to agenda
publication.
4. Minutes: To be taken at each meeting and a draft will be circulated
to members within a week after the meeting.
F. Administration
1. Members of the HAC shall sign the Municipality’s Advisory
Committee & Volunteer Code of Conduct and are subject to
investigation by the Municipality’s Integrity Commissioner following
alleged breaches of the Code, or the Municipal Conflict of Interest
Act.
2. In the case of a disagreement between these Terms of Reference
and the Municipality’s Procedural By-Law, the Procedural By-Law
shall govern.
3. Council, on the recommendation of the HAC, may declare vacant,
the seat of any HAC member missing from three consecutive regular
meetings without a valid reason.
4. All meetings of the HAC, whether Regular or Special, shall be open
to the public, and shall be live-streamed.

committee shall provide the Committee Coordinator or

d. Conduct research on request and report back to the

e. Be familiar with municipal, provincial and federal legislation

f. Publicly support the recommendations of the HAC.

government information and new legislation pertaining to the

b. Facilitate the recommendations of the HAC to Council through

a. Develop an annual calendar of meetings.
b. Develop committee agendas in consultation with the Chair and

c. Publish and distribute committee agendas, including

d. Take minutes at committee meetings.
e. Publish and distribute minutes following committee meetings.
5. Additional municipal staff shall be in attendance at HAC meetings as

What is a Closed Session?
In Ontario, Councils of a municipality can convene in closed sessions (private meetings) for specific reasons outlined in Section 239 of the Municipal Act, 2001. These reasons typically include:

- Personal matters
- Litigation or potential litigation
- Advice subject to solicitor-client privilege
- Negotiations
- Matters that could reveal confidential information

The purpose of closed sessions is to allow Councils to discuss sensitive matters that require privacy and confidentiality while still ensuring transparency and accountability in the decision-making process. Council typically cannot vote within a closed session unless to direct Staff. Any motions discussed in a closed session are forwarded and voted on in an open session.

Deliberations within closed sessions must remain on-topic and cannot be shared outside the meeting. Closed sessions are only convened as allowed by the Municipal Act.

reducing infrastructure expansions to service future development in comparison to other proposed areas.
As noted above, the subject lands are located at the southern edge of the existing Waterford Urban Area with

inclusion of the entirety of the subject lands would result in the orderly and logical extension of the existing residential
uses, with the proposed extension of Jong Street, creating pedestrian connections between existing and future
communities. It would also provide an opportunity to improve the existing park fronting onto County Road 24.

Bernard’s School, Waterford District High School) and recreational uses (i.e. Yins Park, Tricenturena). More

walking distance, therefore any proposed development of the subject lands will have an opportunity to expand the
commercial presence along County Road 24, while increasing customers to the commercial area and reducing the
dependency on automobile uses, while promoting active transportation for day-to-day tasks. Currently, there are no
existing sidewalks along County Road 24, however connections to existing sidewalks for safe pedestrian movement
can be provided through the proposed Jong Street Extension. Additionally, an existing walkway from Yu Boulevard
to the commercial uses on County Road 24 is located within 500 metres from the proposed Jong Street Extension,
which will provide accessible access to nearby commercial services.

to a wider range of demographics and socio-economic characteristics. This would meet the proposed mix within the
preferred Growth Strategy and assist with meeting some of the priorities of the County’s Housing and Homelessness
Plan. Precedent images of the proposed medium density housing forms have been included as Appendix A to this
letter.
Location wise, the subject lands provide an ideal opportunity to create a gateway feature, which will frame a key
transportation corridor. Through built form and/or signage, the proposed gateway would provide for a visually
attractive and welcoming feature for visitors entering the community of Waterford.

9. NEW BUSINESS
Support for Local Governance of Conservation Authorities
Moved By: Jamie MacDonald
Seconded By: Carma Williams
Proposed Amendments to the Conservation Authorities Act and ERO #025-1257
WHEREAS the Conservation Authorities Act (1946) enables municipalities to establish
Conservation Authorities and appoint locally elected representatives to their Boards, ensuring
direct municipal oversight and accountability for programs funded by municipal taxpayers;
AND WHEREAS the municipalities within the South Nation River watershed established South
Nation Conservation (SNC) in 1947 to protect people, property, farmland, water resources, and
natural systems through a watershed-based model that reflects local geographic, hydrologic, and
community needs;
AND WHEREAS municipalities within the SNC jurisdiction currently provide between 25% and
50% of total funding for conservation authority operations, while provincial funding has
declined to approximately 3% in recent years;
AND WHEREAS SNC delivers essential services that support municipal responsibilities,
including:
● natural hazard identification and permitting;
● watershed planning and development review;
● flood forecasting, emergency management, and low water response;
● drinking water source protection;
● watershed monitoring, reporting, and technical studies;
● sustainable forestry, agricultural stewardship, and restoration programs;
● management of over 13,000 acres of conservation lands, including lands donated by
residents and managed through municipal service agreements;
AND WHEREAS on November 7, 2025, the Ministry of the Environment, Conservation and Parks
posted ERO #025-1257 proposing to consolidate Ontario’s 36 Conservation Authorities into
seven regional conservation authorities and to establish a new Ontario Provincial Conservation
Agency, with limited consultation and without accompanying cost-benefit analysis or evidence
demonstrating the need for this restructuring;
AND WHEREAS Schedule 3 of Bill 68 enables the Province to assume governance authority over
regional conservation authorities, raising concerns regarding diminished municipal
representation, loss of local decision-making, and centralization of watershed management;
AND WHEREAS municipalities in Eastern Ontario have expressed concern, including the United
Counties of Stormont, Dundas and Glengarry, that restructuring may:
● increase red tape and administrative burden;
● impose significant transition costs for HR, IT, land transfers, and governance realignment;
● dilute rural voices within large regional agencies dominated by major urban centres;
● erode donor confidence and affect the stewardship of thousands of acres of locally
donated lands;
● disrupt bilingual service delivery in designated municipalities governed by the French
Language Services Act;
AND WHEREAS Conservation Authorities—including SNC—already collaborate regionally
through successful shared-service models, joint watershed studies, coordinated flood
forecasting, agricultural stewardship partnerships, digital permitting, and harmonized technical
reviews, demonstrating that modernization and efficiency can be achieved without dismantling
local governance structures;
AND WHEREAS municipalities rely on SNC’s field-based expertise, rapid on-site support,
landowner relationships, and local knowledge—services that risk being weakened under a
large, centralized regional structure;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Council of Township of North Glengarry urges the
Government of Ontario to maintain local, municipally governed, watershed-based Conservation
Authorities, including South Nation Conservation, to ensure effective natural resource and
natural hazard management, transparent local services, and accountability for municipal levy
dollars;
AND FURTHER THAT this Council does not support the proposed consolidation boundaries
presented in ERO #025-1257 or the creation of a new provincial Conservation Agency without
evidence-based analysis, transparent consultation, and clear articulation of impacts to
municipal budgets, local service delivery, donor lands, and bilingual obligations;
AND FURTHER THAT this Council encourages the Province to work collaboratively with
municipalities and Conservation Authorities to identify opportunities for improved consistency,
modernization, and shared-service approaches within the existing watershed governance
model;
AND FURTHER THAT a copy of this resolution be sent to:
● the Minister of the Environment, Conservation and Parks;
● local MPPs and MPs;
● all municipalities within the South Nation Watershed;
● the Association of Municipalities of Ontario;
● the Rural Ontario Municipal Association;
● Conservation Ontario; and
● all Conservation Authorities in Ontario.
Deferred

Executive Summary
Purpose
 To provide North Grenville’s Council with an update on the United Counties of
Leeds and Grenville’s Growth Management Strategy and pass along any
comments that Council may have related to the Study on to the United Counties.
Key Findings
 The United Counties is undertaking a Growth Management Strategy to update
the Counties Growth projections and policies as part of their upcoming Official
Plan Update.
 North Grenville undertook their own Growth Management Forecast in 2023,
which projected that the Municipality requires more land to be added into the
urban settlement area to accommodate future growth. The Counties Growth
Management Strategy and the Municipality’s Growth Forecast are closely
aligned in regards to the amount of land required to support projected growth.
 The Growth Management Strategy includes policy recommendations for the
Counties consideration. Staff have provided comments for Council’s
consideration should they wish to submit comments to the Counties on the
Growth Management Strategy.
Financial Implications
 Staffing implications, as they relate to implementing Council’s decision on this
matter, are limited to the existing staff complement and applicable administrative
policies as approved by Council.
Background/Analysis
The United Counties of Leeds and Grenville are undertaking a Growth Management
Strategy (GMS) to update growth forecasts and review growth related policies ahead of
the Counties Official Plan update. The GMS implicates all lower tier municipalities and
provides an analysis of historical growth as well as projections for future growth. The
study analyzed growth needs against available lands within existing settlement
boundaries to support future growth. North Grenville was identified as not having
sufficient land to support the long-term growth needs of the Municipality over the 25-
year horizon.
North Grenville also undertook our own Growth Management Forecast with KPMG in
2023 to understand the Municipality’s growth needs. Based on the forecast prepared by
KPMG, North Grenville needs approximately 189 hectares of developable land by 2046,
with 112 hectares being required by 2036.
The United Counties GMS identified a need of approximately 182 hectares by 2051 to
accommodate the Municipality’s growth.
Employment Lands
The GMS also considered employment lands and projections for employment related
growth. North Grenville continues to be a driver for employment growth. Over the 2051
planning horizon North Grenville accounts for 41% of the employment growth in the
County.
The Counties GMS identifies collectively that the County needs 245 gross hectares to
support future employment growth. There is an existing supply of 307 gross hectares
across the county, creating a surplus of 61 gross hectares.
For North Grenville, over the 2051 planning horizon, 13.1 gross hectares of land is
needed to accommodate employment growth. The Municipality currently has 16.4
hectares of land designated for employment. This indicates that over the next 25 years
the Municipality has sufficient designated land to accommodate employment related
growth, with a surplus of just over 3 gross hectares. No changes are recommended to
the employment area designation or the Counties Regionally Significant Economic
Lands designation at this time.

Urban Settlement Area Policies
North Grenville’s Official Plan encompasses many of the policies identified in this
section of the GMS. Municipal Staff are supportive of expanding North Grenville’s Urban
Settlement Area, being Kemptville, to identify opportunities to support growth over the
2051 planning horizon, as recognized in the GMS and the Municipality’s own growth
forecast.
The Municipal Official Plan update considers updating policy language to speak to
complete communities, as introduced in the 2024 Provincial Planning Statement.
Comments for Consideration:
At this time Staff have prepared a recommendation for Council’s consideration that
directs Municipal Planning Staff to work with County Planning Staff on reviewing areas

by the Planning Advisory Committee at the United Counties of Leeds and Grenville.
Settlement Area Boundary Expansion/Reallocation Policy Recommendations
The GMS recommends policy considerations around the topic of boundary expansion
and reallocation.
It is important to note that in 2024 the Province of Ontario changed the policies within
the Provincial Planning Statement that changed the criteria for consideration of a
settlement boundary expansion. Prior to this change, Municipalities had to undertake an
intensive study and review to amend or expand their boundaries.
The policies of the Provincial Planning Statement establish minimum criteria to be
considered including as per Section 2.3.2:
In identifying a new settlement area or allowing a settlement area boundary expansion,
planning authorities shall consider the following:
a) the need to designate and plan for additional land to accommodate an appropriate
range and mix of land uses;
b) if there is sufficient capacity in existing or planned infrastructure and public service
facilities;
c) whether the applicable lands comprise specialty crop areas;
d) the evaluation of alternative locations which avoid prime agricultural areas and,
where avoidance is not possible, consider reasonable alternatives on lower priority
agricultural lands in prime agricultural areas;
e) whether the new or expanded settlement area complies with the minimum distance
separation formulae;
f) whether impacts on the agricultural system are avoided, or where avoidance is not
possible, minimized and mitigated to the extent feasible as determined through an
agricultural impact assessment or equivalent analysis, based on provincial guidance;
and
g) the new or expanded settlement area provides for the phased progression of urban
development.
The GMS builds upon these policies and recommends that the Counties develop an
additional requirement for a Land Needs Assessment for privately initiated applications
seeking to expand a settlement area to add in lands. This would ensure that both
Counties and Local Official Plan growth considerations are taken into consideration, and
that meets the intent of the 2024 Planning Statement.
Staff are supportive of this policy directive. This ensures that any privately initiated
request for a settlement boundary expansion takes into consideration the need to add in
these lands, among other requirements, such as serviceability.
Staff are also supportive of the recommendation for coordination between both tiers of
government. This is indicate in the proposed resolution for Council’s consideration for
both planning departments to work together to identify opportunities for growth.

Under Section 78 of the Drainage Act, Council may undertake and complete the
maintenance or repair of any drainage works constructed under a bylaw passed under this
Act or its predecessor. Section 78 is to be used where it is considered expedient to change
the course of the drainage works, or to make a new outlet for the whole or any part of the
drainage works, or to construct a tile drain under the bed of the whole or any part of the
drainage works as ancillary thereto, or to construct, reconstruct or extend embankments,
walls, dykes, dams, reservoirs, bridges, pumping stations, or other protective works as
ancillary to the drainage works, or to otherwise improve, extend to an outlet or alter the
drainage works or to cover the whole or any part of it, or to consolidate two or more
drainage works, the Council whose duty it is to maintain and repair the drainage works or
any part thereof may, without a petition required under Section 4 but on the report of an
Engineer appointed by it, undertake and complete the drainage works as set forth in such
report.
Existing Conditions
The Brown-Rose Drain (Main Drain) is an open channel for approximately 160m west (all
directions relative to drawing north) of Petty Street in Lot 12, Concession 5. The open
channel continues in an easterly direction to the east side of Petty Street. From there the
drain continues as a twin tile drain of varying sizes in a generally north easterly direction to
-2-
a basin approximately 130m west of Argyle Street. A single tile drain continues easterly to
the Concession 1 and 2 line in Lot 13. There are 3 existing branch drains. Branch “A” is
located in Lot 13, Concession 3, Branch “B” in Lot 13 and 14, Concession 3 and Lot 14,
Concession 2, and Branch “C” in Lot 13, Concession 2.
Background
Under an Engineer’s report dated January 2, 1969 the Brown-Rose Drain, including the
branches, were constructed.
Under an Engineer’s Report dated June 4, 1980 the open channel was improved and the
open channel from Petty Street to Branch “B” was enclosed with a twin tile drain.
Under an Engineer’s Report dated February 11, 2020 Branch “A” was replaced and Branch
“B” was replaced from the Main Drain to the east side of Argyle Street. The drains were
sized to accommodate 38mm/24hrs.
Drain Classification
The open channel portion of the Brown-Rose Drain is currently classified a Class “F” drain
according to the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) classification as presented by
the Ontario Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Agribusiness Agricultural Information
Atlas.
Approvals
The drain will require approval from the Ausable Bayfield Conservation Authority and the
Department of Fisheries and Oceans. Construction cannot commence without necessary
approvals.

DEI Priorities – Workplan Development (2024-2026)
Below is a summary of the key priorities/issues and related action items identified by the North Perth DEI Advisory Committee as part of the
prioritization brainstorming exercise undertaken at the November 2024 and January 2025 committee meetings. Full notes from this exercise
are also available following the summarization to provide additional context. As the next step in this process, the DEI Advisory Committee
will identify the issues/actions items they would like to address in the short term. Once those items are complete, the Committee will re-
visit this priority list for future actions to tackle.
Summary of Key Priorities, Issues, and Action Items by Topic
Indigenous Peoples
• Key Issues: Higher rates of unemployment, substance use, mental health issues; lower education levels; lack of clarity about treaty
obligations.
• Action Items: Advocate for Truth and Reconciliation, promote culturally appropriate services, build relationships with Indigenous
organizations, and educate on myths and facts about Indigenous issues.
2SLGBTQI+
• Key Issues: Hate speech, lack of inclusive spaces, and limited events for the community.
• Action Items: Offer public education on inclusivity, promote gender-neutral spaces, and support social connection events.
Newcomers and New Canadians
• Key Issues: Language barriers, social isolation, and difficulty navigating services.
• Action Items: Implement multilingual tools, community tours, and accessible service registration; promote settlement workers and
ESL programs; provide culturally relevant education.
Persons Living with Low Income
• Key Issues: Affordable housing, food security, and healthcare access.
• Action Items: Advocate for anti-poverty strategies, educate the public about housing issues, and explore home-sharing platforms.
4
Persons with Disabilities
• Key Issues: Lack of affordable housing, digital literacy challenges, and limited accessibility.
• Action Items: Improve accessibility, communicate in-person service options, and address programming shortages.
Racialized People
• Key Issues: Ignorance, cultural assumptions, and limited understanding of diversity.
• Action Items: Promote cultural events and understanding through local media, host inclusive programs, and investigate holiday
policy flexibility.
People Over 55
• Key Issues: Social isolation, scams, and healthcare accessibility.
• Action Items: Educate on scams, expand programs like "Lonely No More," and promote fitness opportunities.
Women
• Key Issues: Barriers due to childcare, domestic violence, and social isolation.
• Action Items: Include childcare in programs and support EarlyON and home daycare initiatives.
Youth
• Key Issues: Mental health stigma, substance use, and technology overuse.
• Action Items: Provide counseling, free youth programming, safe spaces, and internet safety education.
General DEI / Community Inclusivity
• Key Issues: Lack of understanding of inclusion and privilege, and awareness of services.
• Action Items: Host educational programs like the "Human Library," movie nights, and self-reflection workshops; enhance
communication through local media.
5
Overall Themes Across Topics
1. Education and Awareness: Emphasis on addressing misinformation, cultural awareness, and inclusivity education.
2. Accessibility: Ensuring physical, digital, and financial access to services and programs.
3. Community Connection: Creating spaces and events to foster relationships and understanding.
4. Advocacy and Support: Promoting systemic changes and supporting marginalized groups.
5. Local Partnerships: Collaborating with organizations and leveraging local media for outreach.
This approach reflects a holistic commitment to diversity, equity, and inclusion in North Perth.

By-Law No. 2022-83
Being a by-law to appoint an Integrity Commissioner for the Corporation of
Northern Bruce Peninsula
WHEREAS section 223.2 of the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, as amended,
requires that each municipality in the Province of Ontario establish codes of conduct
for members of its Council and local boards;
AND WHEREAS section 223.3 of the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, as
amended, requires that each municipality in the Province of Ontario appoint an
Integrity Commissioner, who shall be responsible for performing in an independent
manner the functions assigned by the municipality with respect to any of the matters
referenced in that section
NOW THEREFORE the Council of the Corporation of the Municipality of Northern
Bruce Peninsula enacts as follows:
1. THAT Aird & Berlis LLP is hereby appointed as the Integrity Commissioner for
the Corporation of the Municipality of Northern Bruce Peninsula.
2. THAT the Integrity Commissioner is hereby assigned the functions
assigned by the municipality with respect to the following:
a. The application of the code of conduct for members of council and the code
of conduct for members of local boards;
b. The application of any procedures, rules and policies of the municipality and
local boards governing the ethical behaviour of members of council and of
local boards;
c. The application of sections 5, 5.1 and 5.2 of the Municipal Conflict of
Interest Act to members of council and of local boards;
d. Requests from members of council and of local boards for advice
respecting their obligations under the code of conduct applicable to the
member;
e. Requests from members of council and of local boards for advice
respecting their obligations under a procedure, rule or policy of the
municipality or of the local board, as the case may be, governing the ethical
behaviour of members;
f. Requests from members of council and of local boards for advice
respecting their obligations under the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act, and
g. The provision of educational information to members of council, members of
local boards, the municipality and the public about the municipality's codes
of conduct for members of council and members of local boards and about
the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act.
3. THAT the Integrity Commissioner and any person acting under the instructions
of the Integrity Commissioner is hereby indemnified and saved harmless for
costs reasonably incurred in connection with the defence of a proceeding if the
proceeding relates to an act done in good faith in the performance or intended
performance of a duty or authority under this Part or a by-law passed under it
or an alleged neglect or default in the performance in good faith of the duty or
authority.
4. That the Mayor and Clerk are hereby authorized to execute the Retainer
Agreement between the Corporation of the Municipality of Northern Bruce
Peninsula and Aird Berlis LLP for the purpose of Integrity Commissioner
5. That this By-Law shall be effective until December 31, 2023.
6. That this By-Law shall come into force and take effect immediately upon passing
and By-Law No. 2020-86 is rescinded.

lands.

The subject lands are described as Part of Lot 6, Concession 3 (North Norwich), in the Township
of Norwich. The subject lands are located on the east side of Slant Road lying between Quaker
Street and Evergreen Street and are municipally known as 793424 Slant Road.

COUNTY OF OXFORD OFFICIAL PLAN:
Schedule ‘N-1’ Township of Norwich Land Use Plan Agricultural Reserve

(a) Purpose of the Application:
The applicants are proposing relief from the above-noted provisions of the Township Zoning By-
law to recognize a recently constructed accessory building (approximately 167.2 m2 (1,800 ft2) in
size) and an existing barn that is used for storage (approximately 72.8 m2 (784 ft2) in size). The
total gross floor area of all accessory structures is approximately 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) in size,

prefer to maintain both structures for personal storage and it was noted that the subject minor
variance would be required.

240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) and the report will recommend this amended relief to align with the applicants’

Oxford Natural Heritage Systems Study (ONHSS); however, the recently constructed accessory
building is already located within this area and was situated in a way that there was little impact

a single detached dwelling with attached garage, the existing barn and the recently constructed
accessory building.

accessory structure on the subject lands, as well as their setbacks and dimensions.

The Township of Norwich Fire Department and County of Oxford Public Works have indicated
that they have no objections to the proposal.
Township of Norwich Building Department confirmed that the location of the new accessory
building was located the required distance from the municipal drain as per the zoning by-law and
was inspected at time of footing installation.

The subject property is located within the Agricultural Reserve designation according to the
Official Plan, which supports a wide range of agricultural type land uses. The Official Plan also
recognizes existing non-farm rural residential uses, together with their accessory buildings on
lands designated as Agricultural Reserve and it is the intent of the Official Plan to ensure that
non-farm rural residential uses shall not hinder surrounding agricultural operations.
Planning staff are generally satisfied that the development of a residential accessory structure will
have minimal impact on surrounding agricultural land uses. As such, staff are of the opinion that
the requested variances are in-keeping with the intent of the Official Plan.

The subject property is zoned ‘Residential Existing Lot Zone (RE)’, which permits single detached
dwellings and accessory structures thereto.
Accessory structures are permitted on parcels zoned ‘RE’ to a maximum lot coverage of
170 m2 (1,830 ft²) of gross floor area or 10% of the lot area, whichever is lesser. This provision
is intended to ensure such structures remain clearly secondary and ancillary to the main use of
the property and limit impacts on neighbouring properties. This provision also assists to ensure
sufficient space is maintained on the property to accommodate private services, grading/drainage
and amenity space.
In this case, the applicants have recently constructed a new accessory building being
approximately 167.2 m2 (1,800 ft2) but also want to maintain an existing barn structure being
approximately 72.8 m2 (784 ft2), that is being used for personal storage as well. The applicants
had indicated that they would demolish the barn structure after the new building was constructed,
however, the applicants have now submitted the subject application in order to keep both
structures with an increased total lot coverage for all accessory buildings.
Planning staff are satisfied that the subject lands are of sufficient size to provide adequate space
to accommodate the recently constructed accessory structure and existing barn, and given the
proposed location, being setback sufficiently from Slant Road, as well as being located within the
rear yard on the property, staff are satisfied that the proposed accessory structure will remain
secondary and ancillary to the main residential use of the property, provide for all other applicable
setbacks required by the zoning by-law, and provide for amenity space and adequate area for the
provision of private services.

accessory structure and an existing barn structure which results in a cumulative overall gross floor
area of 240.6 m2 (2,590 ft2) for all accessory structures whereas the Zoning By-law permits 170 m2
(1,830 ft2).

width from 1.5 m (4.9 ft) to 0.94 m (3.11 ft) to recognize an existing deficient side yard
width to facilitate the construction of a two-storey dwelling.
LOCATION:
The subject lands are described as Lot 11, North side of Main Street, Plan 43, in the Township of
Norwich. The lands are located on the north side of Main Street lying between Grove Street and
Maple Street and are municipally known as 276 Main Street West, Village of Otterville.

COUNTY OF OXFORD OFFICIAL PLAN:
Schedule “C-3” County of Oxford Settlement Strategy Plan Village

Surrounding land uses include low density residential type housing in the village of Otterville. Otter
Creek is located to the east, and the Otter Creek golf course is located to the south of the subject

(a) Purpose of the Application:
The applicant is seeking relief from the Township Zoning By-law in order to recognize an existing
legal non-conforming interior side yard width of 0.94 m (3.11 ft). The subject lands previously
contained a one storey dwelling which benefitted from a lesser interior side yard based on the
zoning provisions of previous versions of the zoning by-law. The previous dwelling was recently
razed by fire and the applicants are proposing to replace the dwelling, on the same foundation,
with a two storey dwelling.
Section 5.19.6 of the Zoning By-law does recognize the ability for additions to non-conforming
buildings, provided that the addition does not contravene any other zoning provisions. In this
instance, the addition will contravene the interior side yard setback provisions and therefore the
variance is required to recognize the deficiency.
The subject lands are approximately 1,057.68 m2 (11,386.7 ft2) in area, are currently vacant aside
from the foundation of the previous dwelling. A two storey dwelling is proposed and a detached
garage.
Plate 1, Location Map with Existing Zoning, shows the location of the subject lands and the current
zoning in the immediate vicinity.
Plate 2, Aerial Map (2020), shows the location of the subject lands and surrounding properties,
and the location of the existing bunker silos.

(b) Agency Comments
Township of Norwich Fire Department and Oxford County Public Works indicated no concerns
with the subject application.
Township of Norwich Building Department noted that a Real Property Report will be required to
confirm that setback and location of the foundation as it exists.

The application was circulated on September 25, 2025, in accordance with the requirements of
the Planning Act. To date, no concerns or objections with the application have been raised.

The subject property is located within the Village of Otterville, which is designated ‘Village’
according to the Settlement Strategy Plan for the County of Oxford, and ‘Settlement’ according to

permitted, with the exception of multiple unit residential development involving more than two
units.

(e) Intent and Purpose of the Zoning By-law:
The subject lands are currently zoned ‘Residential Type 1 Zone (R1)’, according to the Township
of Norwich Zoning By-law. Permitted uses within the R1 zone include a single detached dwelling,
home occupation, a group home, and accessory buildings/structures.
The provisions of the R1 zone require a minimum lot area of 2,800 m2 (30,140 ft2) where sanitary
sewers are not available, minimum lot depth of 50 m (164 ft), front yard depth of 7.5 m (24.6 ft),
rear yard depth of 7.5 m (24.6 ft), exterior side yard width of 7.5 m (24.6 ft) and an interior side
yard width of 1.5 m (4.9 ft). Properties within the R1 zone are permitted a maximum lot coverage
of 30%.
The existing foundation has an approximate interior side yard setback of 0.94 m (3.11 ft), the
previous version of the zoning by-law (1976) permitted an interior side yard of 1.2 m (4 ft) which
is why the foundation exists as it does. The previous one storey dwelling would have benefitted
from a legal non-conforming status when the current zoning by-law (2003) was passed. When the
existing dwelling was razed by fire, it could have been replaced by another one storey dwelling,
however, the applicants are proposing a two storey dwelling instead.
As noted, Section 5.19.6 does permit the extension or addition to a non-conforming use, building

maintenance of the property, proper drainage, and appropriate access to the remainder of the
property. The applicant is proposing a setback of 0.94 m (3.11 ft) which would recognize the

Building on the County-wide forecasts provided in Section 1.1, population, housing, and

• Supply of potential future housing stock in the development approvals process by

• Residential intensification opportunities;

• Consideration of water and wastewater servicing capacity; and
• Provincial, County, and Area Municipal policy direction regarding forecast

Demand Factors
• Historical population, housing, and employment trends based on Statistics

• A review of recent residential and non-residential building permit data by housing
structure type and employment sector by Area Municipality;
• Historical commuting trends and anticipated employment growth opportunities
within the surrounding market area;
• A review of local employment opportunities by sector and Area Municipality.
• Forecast population trends by major age group and associated household
formation trends by age of household maintainer;
• Consideration of long-term housing needs by housing tenure (i.e. ownership vs.
rental housing) and influence on housing demand by structure type; and
• Housing market demand by Area Municipality across all major demographic

accommodate the proposed development for specific blocks.

Plan of Subdivision application will divide the subject lands into blocks and create
public roads. This will allow the developer to phase their construction or sell off
parcels, while the Town acquires other blocks into public ownership. It should be
noted that once approved and conveyed, the development blocks will be subject to
Site Plan Control to review technical and functional aspects of each site.

Public Participation in Electronic Council Meetings and Planning Public Meetings/
Hearings Protocol
Please note: That, in order to reduce strain on the technology, if you only wish to listen to the
meeting please access the livestream on the Township’s YouTube Channel
Purpose:
This procedure has been created to establish a protocol for public participation in electronic
Council and Planning Public Meetings in the Township of Oro-Medonte in accordance with
Section 238 (3.3) of the Municipal Act, 2001, the Planning Act, 1990, c.P.13. and the
Emergency Management and Civil Protection Act. This procedure also outlines the public
responsibility in order to participate in an electronic meeting via telephone or video.
Scope:
The procedure applies to all members of the public, applicants, consultants and delegates
wishing to participate in an electronic Council or Planning Public Meeting, either via video or
telephone. Nevertheless, this policy is subject to rules of procedure as stated in the
Procedural By-law and other Provincial legislation.
Definitions:
Electronic Meeting – a meeting hosted through telephone conference call or video platform
Video Conferencing Solutions – an electronic meeting platform
Chair – Mayor or Designate
Members – Members of Council
Clerk/Designate – means the Clerk of the Township of Oro-Medonte, or Deputy Clerk, acting
in the capacity of the Clerk in his/her absence, or a person who the Clerk has delegated
authority to in accordance with Section 228(4) of the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended.
IT – Information Technology Division
Share Screen Viewing – two or more applications visible on screen at once (eg. Power Point
Presentation and participating Members)
Waiting Room – a virtual room where attendees wait to join the meeting or are placed in, in
the event of a pecuniary interest
