Procedure:
Open Forum
Public attendance to Electronic Meetings during the course of an Emergency may be
restricted to electronic means and will be indicated on the meeting agenda.
There are two ways you can participate in Open Forum during a Council Meeting - by
Electronic Participation or Written Submissions.
Electronic Participation (speaking during Open Forum using ZOOM):
• If you wish to make an oral statement during the Open Forum portion of a Council
Meeting on an agenda item, please submit a completed Request for Public
Participation Form, found on the Township website, prior to noon on Monday before the
meeting to register or call 705-487-2171.
• Ensure you have a device with internet access to participate electronically as an
‘Attendee’ to make your oral statement during the meeting. Please refer to following
tutorial for ZOOM details: https://support.zoom.us/hc/en-us/categories/200101697
• While computer attendance is encouraged, if you do not have the necessary
technology to participate by computer, you may use a telephone and call in to make
your Open Forum comments. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person; registration
is still required to present Open Forum comments.
• If you are participating by telephone, you will not have the option to type in your name.
We will ask for the phone number you will be using to participate in the meeting. This
information will let us associate the correct name with your phone number. Please
note, that depending on the volume of speakers, telephone numbers may be visible to
the public; however, every effort will be made to change prior to attendees being
promoted to panelists.
• Once you have completed the Request for Public Participation Form regarding a
Council meeting agenda item and the webinar registration is closed, all applicants are
uploaded to ZOOM. Meeting invites are then sent by Zoom to the e-mail you provided
in the registration form.
• Please note this link is unique to you and should not be shared with others. Only those
whose registration form was received will be permitted attendance.
On the day of the meeting, we ask that you join the meeting fifteen to twenty (15-20)
minutes before your scheduled time to speak. When joining via ZOOM, please type in
your name so we know who you are. You will be granted the ability to unmute your
microphone when it is your time to speak. Please wait for the Chair to request you to
speak. You will be able to hear and view the meeting in progress. You will not be able
to see other attendees nor will you appear on video

• When you have finished speaking, unless you anticipate making further comments, we
ask that you leave the Zoom Meeting. If you wish to follow the meeting, please watch
it on the Township’s YouTube Channel. If you do not leave the meeting and have to
be removed by the host, you will not be able to return to the meeting.
• Please do not watch the livestream on YouTube while you are using the ZOOM
technology as this can distort the sound.
Written submissions submitted by email
• Depending on circumstances, an Electronic Meeting may not permit an in-person
Open Forum, but will permit electronic submissions received in advance of the
meeting.
• Agenda Comment input shall be submitted through an email containing your name,
address and your comments regarding the agenda item to agendacomment@oro-
medonte.ca by 3:00 p.m. the day prior to the start of the Electronic Meeting, or as
otherwise noted on the agenda. Your correspondence will be directed in accordance
with the amended procedural by-law and filed with the Township as part of the public
record.
As noted above, your comments must relate to an item on the agenda. Please note you are
free to contact any member of Council directly with other matters or questions at
council@oro-medonte.ca or via telephone at the following link Contact Us.
For all meetings, the Clerk/designate will authorize all requests to ensure they are related to
agenda items for the meeting.
The Corporate Services Division will ensure that information on how the public may access
and provide input during the meeting is provided on the meeting agenda and on the
Township website.
Deputations and Presentations
• Submit a completed Request for Public Participation Form found on the Township
website, including preferred meeting date.
• Ensure any presentation material you wish to share during your deputation is received
by the Clerk by 9:00 a.m. 10 calendar days prior to the preferred meeting.
• All presentation material must include page numbers for ease of reference during
the meeting.
• If attending electronically, ensure you have a computer with internet access to enable
you to participate electronically as an ‘Attendee’ to make your deputation/presentation
during the meeting. Please refer to following tutorial for ZOOM details:
https://support.zoom.us/hc/en-us/categories/200101697

telephone and call in to participate and make your deputation.
• If you are participating by telephone, you will not have the option to type in your name.
We will ask for the phone number you will be using to participate in the meeting. This
information will let us associate the correct name with your phone number. Please
note, that depending on volume, telephone numbers may be visible to the public;
however, every effort will be made to change prior to attendees being promoted to
panelist. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person to present a deputation.
• Once you have completed the Request for Public Participation Form for your

Meeting invites are then sent by Zoom to the e-mail you provided in the registration
form.
• Please note this link is unique to you and should not be shared with others. Only those
whose registration form was received will be permitted attendance.
On the day of the meeting, we ask that you join the meeting fifteen to twenty (15 to 20)
minutes before your scheduled time. When joining, please type in your name so we
know who you are. You will be granted the ability to unmute your microphone when it
is your time to speak. Please wait for the Chair to request you to speak. You will be

All comments or questions on planning applications should be submitted in writing as noted in
the Notice of Application and/or Notice of Public Meetings/Public Hearings.
• If you wish to make an oral statement during the Planning Public Meeting, please
submit a Request for Public Participation Form, found on the Township website, prior
to noon on Monday before the meeting to register or call 705-487-2171.
• While computer attendance is encouraged, if you do not have the necessary
technology to participate by computer, you may use a telephone and call in to make
your comments. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person.
• Ensure you have a computer with internet access to enable you to participate
electronically to make your comment during the meeting. Please refer to following
tutorial for ZOOM details: https://support.zoom.us/hc/en-us/categories/200101697
• If you are participating by telephone, you will not have the option to type in your name.
We will ask for the phone number you will be using to participate in the meeting. This
information will let us associate the correct name with your phone number. Please
note, that depending on the number of speakers, telephone numbers may be visible to
the public; however, every effort will be made to change the phone number prior to
attendees being promoted to panelists. Alternatively, you may also attend in-person to
present verbal comments.

closed, all applicants are uploaded to ZOOM. Meeting invites are then sent by Zoom
to the e-mail you provided in the registration form.
• Please note this link is unique to you and should not be shared with others. Only those
whose registration form was received will be permitted attendance.

on the Township’s YouTube Channel. If you do not leave the meeting and have to be
removed by the host, you will not be unable to return to the meeting.
• Please do not watch the livestream on YouTube while you are using the ZOOM
technology as this can distort the sound.
Participation as an Applicant or Applicant’s Agent
Page 5 of 6
If you are the applicant or applicant’s agent and plan to make a presentation to the
Development Services Committee or Council, please send an email to planning@oro-
medonte.ca by noon on the Monday prior to the meeting to submit your digital presentation
materials (i.e. PowerPoint presentation, etc.). Digital presentations will be recorded as part of
the electronic meeting and uploaded to the Meeting Agenda. You will be provided further
instructions on how you will connect to the virtual meeting. Presentations received after the
above noted timing will not be accommodated.
To reduce strain on the technology and keep public meetings-hearings streamlined, the
Township requests that at this time only one (1) representative of the owner/applicant
participate per application as the spokesperson for the application.
All oral statements will be recorded as part of the electronic meeting, uploaded to the Meeting
Agenda, and will be posted for public viewing on the Township of Oro-Medonte YouTube
channel.
Any questions with respect to this Protocol may be directed to the Clerk at yaubichon@oro-
medonte.ca.
Please note that the Township shall not be held responsible for issues related to
technological failure that may impede a member of the public from participating
electronically in a meeting.

CO-25-19 - Request from Region of Durham for On-Street Parking Permits (Ward 4)
 Recommendation
Whereas the Region of Durham has requested dedicated parking permits for the on-street parking spaces on Centre Street North and Richmond Street West, in front of and adjacent to the Durham Regional Police Services (D.R.P.S.) station (see Attachment 1); and,
Whereas the D.R.P.S. station, located at 77 Centre Street North, is bordered by a total of nine (9) on-street parking spaces, including four (4) located on Centre Street North and five (5) located on Richmond Street West; and,
Whereas the D.R.P.S. station is situated adjacent to a grocery store and an apartment building, both of which have dedicated private parking lots; and,
Whereas the hourly rate for on-street parking is $1.25/hr, with a maximum time limit of two (2) hours; and,
Whereas nine (9) on-street parking permits would generate approximately $657 per month; and,
Whereas licencing nine (9) on-street parking spaces will increase the forecasted long-term utilization percentage for on-street parking as reported in CO-24-60 dated December 4, 2024, from 49% to 50%,
Therefore be it resolved that based on Item CO-25-19 dated May 12, 2025:
That the request from the Region of Durham dated April 10, 2025, to permanently licence nine (9) on-street parking spaces bordering the D.R.P.S. station be approved, increasing the forecasted 2034 utilization of 49% to 50% of the 85% critical threshold; and,
That the City of Oshawa enter into an agreement with the Region of Durham to licence up to nine (9) on-street parking spaces bordering the D.R.P.S. station at the monthly rate applicable for the spaces in accordance with the City’s Fees and Charges By-law 109-2024, as amended; and,
That the Commissioner, Community and Operations Services Department, be authorized to execute the licence agreement in a final form and content satisfactory to the Commissioner, Community and Operations Services Department, the Commissioner, Corporate and Finance Services Department and the City Solicitor.
CO-25-20 - Request to License up to 60 Parking Spaces for 78 Richmond Street West (Ward 4)
 Recommendation
Whereas, Farhi Holdings Corporation has requested to licence up to sixty (60) parking spaces at the McMillan Parking Garage for prospective tenants and current professional tenants at 78 Richmond Street West (see Attachment 1); and,
Whereas, 78 Richmond Street West has a private parking lot with approximately forty-nine (49) parking spaces; and,
Whereas, the City operates three (3) Municipal Parking Public Garages within walking distance of 78 Richmond Street West; and,
Whereas, the licencing of sixty (60) parking permits would generate approximately $4,437 per month; and,
Whereas, the forecasted long-term utilization percentage for off-street parking as reported in Report CO-24-60 dated December 4, 2024 was 52%; and,
Whereas, previous requests for new and amending agreements decreases the long-term utilization percentage of 52% to 51%; and,
Whereas, licencing sixty (60) parking spaces in the City’s Municipal Parking Lots will increase the forecasted long-term utilization percentage from 51% to 54%,
Therefore be it resolved that based on Item CO-25-20 dated May 12, 2025:
That the request from Farhi Holdings Corporation dated April 15, 2025, to license up to sixty (60) parking spaces within the City’s Municipal Parking System be approved, increasing the forecasted 2034 utilization of 51% to 54% of the 85% critical threshold; and,
That the City of Oshawa enter into an agreement for a period of five (5) years with Farhi Holding Corporation to licence up to sixty (60) parking spaces in the City’s Municipal Parking System at the monthly rate applicable for the spaces in accordance with the City’s Fees and Charges By-law 109-2024, as amended; and,
That the Commissioner, Community and Operations Services Department, be authorized to execute the licence agreement in a final form and content satisfactory to the Commissioner, Community and Operations Services Department, the Commissioner, Corporate and Finance Services Department and the City Solicitor.
CO-25-21 - Technical Amendment to Skateboard and Bicycle By-law 78-91 (All Wards)
 Recommendation
Whereas the Skateboards and Bicycles By-law 78-91, as amended ("Skateboard and Bicycle By-law") regulates the use of skateboards, bicycles, and similar devices including e-scooters within the City of Oshawa ("City") to ensure public safety and proper usage; and,
Whereas on June 20, 2022, City Council considered Report DS-22-163 dated June 8, 2022, authorizing the City’s participation in the Province of Ontario’s an E-scooter Pilot Program and the implementation of a shared micromobility pilot program (“Shared E-mobility Program”); and,
Whereas on January 27, 2025, in accordance with Report ED-25-14 dated January 8, 2025, City Council approved the extension of the Shared E-mobility Program for a further thirty (30) months, or until June 30, 2027; and,
Whereas Report ED-25-14 identified enhancements to the Shared E-mobility Program in order to improve e-mobility devices service providers’ accountability which included the ability to charge fees and/or fine those service providers for improperly parked e-mobility devices; and,
Whereas to ensure that an Administrative Monetary Penalty (“A.M.P.”) can be issued against Micromobility Service Providers of the City’s Shared E-mobility Program for the improper parking of “Electric Kick Scooters” on the sidewalk, an amending by-law to the Skateboard and Bicycle By-law 78-91 is required to include the definition of a "Person" (see Attachment 1);
Therefore be it resolved that based on Item CO-25-21 dated May 7, 2025, City Council pass an amending by-law to the Skateboard and Bicycle By-law 78-91, as amended to add the definition of a “Person” in a final form and content satisfactory to the Commissioner, Community and Operations Services, Commissioner, Safety and Facilities Services Departments and the City Solicitor as generally set out in Attachment 1 to said Item.

CO-25-23 - Review and Update of the Community Legend Award and the E.P. Taylor Windfields Farm Champion Award Process (All Wards)

 Recommendation
Whereas the City of Oshawa is proud to celebrate the individuals, collectives and organizations that contribute to making Oshawa a great place to live, work and play; and,
Whereas the City of Oshawa has two award programs that are administered by Recreation Services; the Community Legend Award and the E.P. Taylor Windfields Farm Champion Award; and,
Whereas the Community Legend Award recognizes individuals and organizations whose everyday actions make a positive impact on Oshawa and is awarded on an annual basis; and,
Whereas the E.P. Taylor Windfields Farm Champion Award celebrates someone who exemplifies innovation and has overcome adversity and is awarded every four years; and,
Whereas each award has specific eligibility criteria that must be met by the individuals being nominated; and,
Whereas the general eligibility criteria for both awards do not indicate whether self-nominations are permitted, and the criteria for the Community Legend Award does not indicate whether posthumous nominations are permitted;
Therefore be it resolved that staff be directed to undertake a review and update of the Community Legend Award and the E.P. Taylor Windfields Farm Champion Award process to clarify the eligibility criteria to include exclusions regarding self-nominations and posthumous nominations.  
CO-25-24 - Community Care Durham Mobile Food Market (All Wards) 
 Recommendation
Whereas Community Care Durham is a multi-service registered charitable organization providing a broad range of support services for individuals over the age of 16 and their caregivers; and,
Whereas in 2023, Community Care Durham piloted a Mobile Food Market in partnership with Durham College that provides fruits and vegetables sourced from a variety of local partners in Durham Region including The Barrett Centre of Innovation in Sustainable Urban Agriculture, the W. Galen Weston Center for Food, Common Ground Food Share, Pingles Farm, Algoma Orchards and The Veggie Shack to address the rising rate of Food Insecurity across Durham Region; and,
Whereas the 2023 Mobile Food Market pilot occurred in the Town of Ajax at Ajax Community Centre; and,
Whereas in 2024, the Mobile Food Market was expanded to include a location in Whitby at   Whitby 55+ Recreation Centre on Brock Street South; and,
Whereas Community Care Durham would like to expand in 2025 to include a location in Oshawa in the parking lot of North Oshawa Park near where many individuals reside whom already receive services offered by Community Care Durham such as Meals on Wheels and the Community Food Box; and,
Whereas the footprint of the Mobile Food Market will require the use of a total of six (6) parking spaces on Wednesdays from 1:30 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. from June to October 2025; and,
Whereas the Fees and Charges By-law 109-2024 has a user fee for the facility rental of a Parking Lot of $300 per day and does not contain a user fee for the facility rental of a limited area of a Parking Lot; and,

Motion for Which Notice was Previously Given by Councillor Farmer at the April 15, 2024 Regular Council meeting Re: Social Assistance Rates and Guaranteed Livable Income Program
This item has Video
 "WHEREAS the rising cost of living and rapid inflation are putting significant financial pressure on individuals and families, especially those living in poverty;

AND WHEREAS residents on programs such as Ontario Works receive maximum fixed monthly incomes of $733, and ODSP recipients receive $1,376;

AND WHEREAS people living with low income are more likely to be renters and the Community Foundation Focus on Housing report found that in 2021 more than 40% of homes in Owen Sound are rented;

AND WHEREAS rent is considered affordable when it is no more than 30% of gross annual income and the 2021 census reports that 38.3% of tenant households in Owen Sound are spending more than 30% of their income on housing;

AND WHEREAS as of March 31, 2024, there 1,650 Grey County households on the Community Housing Waitlist including only those who presently reside in the area;

AND WHEREAS the 2023 Grey County Housing Action Plan identified the need to advocate to the Provincial and Federal governments for housing solutions which may relate to “the ‘income’ side of the housing affordability equation, for example relating to minimum and living wages [and] social benefits (e.g., ODSP; OW)”;

AND WHEREAS poverty also increases food insecurity which negatively impacts physical and mental health especially for children and adequate income is an important social determinant of health that greatly impacts food security;

AND WHEREAS in 2023, the Salvation Army food bank use rose by 42% in Owen Sound and annual meals provided by OSHARE increased 18.6% or 23,000 meals from 2022;

AND WHEREAS in the 2024 Monitoring Food Affordability in Grey Bruce report on food insecurity, Grey Bruce Public Health calls on municipalities to “advocate for federal and provincial government policies (e.g.., increases to income tax credits for low-income households) and programs (e.g., basic income guarantee) to ensure an adequate and secure income for all in Canada”;

AND WHEREAS in February 2024 the Grey Bruce Poverty Task Force issued a call for income solutions to food insecurity;

AND WHEREAS neither municipal governments nor the non-profit sector have the resources to address the root causes of poverty on their own;

AND WHEREAS decreasing poverty levels benefits individuals and their communities by reducing reliance on food banks, social services, health care, emergency services, and other supports as well as improving quality of life and creating positive local economic impacts;

NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT City Council join other municipalities across Ontario to urge the Federal and Provincial governments to increase social assistance rates for Ontario Works and the Ontario Disability Support Program and to establish a Guaranteed Livable Income program;

AND THAT this resolution be sent to the Prime Minister, the Premier, the leaders of all parties sitting at Queen’s Park, the Minister of Children, Community and Social Services, the Minister of Health, the Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, Alex Ruff, MP for Bruce-Grey-Owen Sound, and Rick Byers, MPP for Bruce-Grey-Owen Sound requesting a response;

AND FURTHER THAT this resolution also be shared with Grey County, Bruce County, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM), the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), and the Western Ontario Wardens’ Caucus (WOWC)."

Procedural Bylaw No. 4507(2022)
Being a bylaw to govern the proceedings of the Town of Pelham Council, its Committees, the conduct of its Members and the calling of Meetings.
Procedural By-law No. 4507(2022) was adopted on January 30, 2022, repealing and replacing Bylaw No. 4107(2019), as amended.
This By-law directs regular meetings of Council to be held on the first and third Wednesday of the month, commencing at 9:00 a.m. Public Meetings under the Planning Act are to be scheduled on the second Wednesday of the month, commencing at 5:30 p.m. Dates are subject to change to accommodate various Statutory Holidays, World Religious Holidays, major conferences and other known events. Please refer to the Council Meeting Schedule for approved meeting dates.
Additional notable changes include a new curfew of 1 pm, restructuring of regular meetings of Council to include Committee within Council, hybrid meeting participation, increase of three (3) to four (4) delegations permitted with a five (5) minute time limit, re-classification of Committees to include Statutory, Advisory and Volunteer Working Groups, a delegation submission deadline of ten (10) days prior to the meeting and the requirement to post agendas to the public five (5) days prior to the date of the meeting, being the Friday.

Auto Mayors Motion
 WHEREAS the Auto Mayors work collaboratively at the provincial and federal orders of government to promote awareness, advocacy and strategic policy initiatives that strengthen the Canadian economy through advancements and investments in the automotive sector;
WHEREAS continued progress toward tariff-free access to the U.S. market and maintaining an integrated North American auto sector remain the auto sector’s top priority;
WHEREAS the Auto Mayors welcome ongoing collaboration with the Province and the Federal government on greenhouse gas regulations and electrification targets and policies that reflect current market demand, infrastructure readiness and alignment with the U.S.;
WHEREAS the Auto Mayors are ready to work with Federal partners on a coordinated approach to global competition that ensures Canada remains an attractive destination for investment;
WHEREAS strengthening domestic production requires aligning tariff remission frameworks with manufacturing levels and strengthening Buy Ontario procurement policies to ensure public sector fleet purchasing continues to support Ontario based manufacturers;
AND WHEREAS regular review and monitoring of industrial electricity rates, including how domestic rates compare to export rates, will help ensure Ontario manufacturers remain competitive and positioned for growth.
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the City of Peterborough, as a member of the Auto Mayors Caucus, support the Auto Mayors’ continued efforts to highlight the automotive sector’s local economic impact, including jobs, supply chains, and community stability, while supporting the automotive ecosystem through business retention and economic development efforts;
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT the City of Peterborough joins with the Auto Mayors to support the Federal government’s ongoing efforts in the Canada-U.S. trade negotiations to protect and secure the long-term prosperity of Canada’s automotive industry;
AND BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT this motion be shared with the Right Honourable Mark Carney, Prime Minister of Canada, the Honourable Dominic LeBlanc, President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade and One Canadian Economy, the Honourable Melanie Joly, Minister of Industry, the Honourable Anita Anand, Minister of Foreign Affairs, the Honourable Maninder Sidhu, Minister of International Trade, Parliamentary Secretary Karim Bardeesy, MP Emma Harrison, Premier Doug Ford, the Honourable Vic Fedeli, Ontario Minister of Economic Development, Job Creation and Trade, MPP Dave Smith, the Federation of Canadian Municipalities (FCM), the Association of Municipalities of Ontario (AMO), the Ontario Big City Mayors (OBCM), and key automotive industry stakeholders.

Critical Pathway for RFP-96-26 Supply, Delivery and Installation of a Miniature Train Amusement Ride
Background
Riverview Park and Zoo have done substantial work over the last several years, to maintain this miniature passenger
train. The owner, the City of Peterborough, is requesting a proposal from all feasible specialists to develop a Next Phase
Plan for our miniature passenger train amusement device, which is a vital revenue source providing key component of
financial sustainability.
The expectation would be that the proposal would entail possible solutions not just for replacing the train itself, but the
track, storage, maintenance, certification and any further considerations the specialist may offer. The City will consider all
feasible solutions including but not limited to; Updating the Train to modern mechanical standards, with electric propulsion
systems and new coaches that meet/exceed TSSA regulations. A proposal to supply and operate a Miniature Train Ride
experience. Maintain the track system, new or retrofitted to current landscape. Upgrade or completely rebuild to the asset
storage area known as the train tunnel. Submissions should offer considerations to; Accessibility for Ontarians with
Disabilities Act (“AODA”), environmental & climate, accessibility, workplace and environmental safety, longevity (Total Cost
of Ownership (TCO)), maintenance, staffing obligations, asset storage, seasonality, materials, user friendliness, growth
and development, licensing / certifications, stakeholders, cultural significance to the Peterborough, Ontario Canada and
any other information specialists would reasonably consider within the scope of this RFP.
The City is asking that proponents provide budgetary price ranges for this competitive Request for Proposals (RFP). The
City understands that these costs will be presented as estimates but could include a list of other applicable costing
considerations.
1
RFP Structure
The following components that can be bid on individually, or on multiple parts, or the whole of the project in its entirety:
A. Replace the Amusement Ride Locomotive for long-term sustainability and reduced maintenance costs:
a. Gasoline Fueled train
b. Diesel Train
c. Electric Train, complete with the charging components and upgrades to the train station and tunnel storage
B. Retrofit the existing train, ensuring all TSSA regulations are met
a. Replace the accessible coach, caboose
b. Convert the Gasoline Engine to Electric complete with the charging components and upgrades to the train
station and tunnel storage to maintain the asset
C. Track Repair and Maintenance
a. Annual Inspections
b. Seasonal repairs and start up, erosion control, safety and state of good repair inspections
D. Asset Storage
a. Upgrade or rebuild new tunnel housing for winter insulation
b. Asset protection, charging and mechanical servicing needs
E. TSSA-ADR Mechanical maintenance
a. Mechanical
b. Electric
c. Seasonal inspections and start up
F. Train Operations
a. Ensure TSSA regulation permit and license
b. Qualified train operators and ticket sales customer service representatives
c. Meet all employment and safety standards

Report regarding Retail Businesses being permitted to open on Statutory Holidays 
 Whereas the City of Peterborough has been approached by local retailers asking that they be permitted to open on statutory holidays such as Canada Day and Labour Day;
Whereas many local businesses are reporting lower sales due to the uncertainty caused by tariff wars and inflation, and assert that opening on some statutory holidays would allow them to benefit from consumer spending on those days;
Whereas The Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O., 1990, which prohibits most retail businesses from opening on statutory holidays, allows municipalities to pass a by-law to render the Act inapplicable in their jurisdiction;
Whereas City Council last considered a report on this matter in 2011;
Whereas the Government of Ontario passed legislation this year to allow retailers across the province to open on Family Day and Victoria Day;
Now therefore be it resolved that City staff be directed to bring a report to Council in the first quarter of 2027 with information on the considerations of retail businesses being permitted to open on various statutory holidays, and outlining the options and required next steps should Council wish to proceed further at that time.

Background
The Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) is intended to help municipalities
reduce development charges (DCs) and build infrastructure that supports new housing.
Through the program, municipalities will need to reduce DCs by 30% to 50% or more for
3 years. The DCRP is part of the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build with
federal funding delivered through the Build Communities Strong Fund’s Provincial and
Territorial Stream.
On June 15, 2026, City Council approved a motion to reduce DCs by 50%, effective
March 30, 2026, and will maintain this reduction for all residential development types for
3 years.
As part of the June 15, 2026, approved City Council motion, it stated:
"4. The City Treasurer and the Commissioner of Infrastructure Planning and
Growth Management are authorized and directed to determine which housing-
enabling infrastructure projects will best support the creation of new housing and
thus be prioritized and to report back to Council on the projects selected for
inclusion in the application, and the rationale for their prioritization, at the first
regular meeting of Council following submission of the application."
On June 19, 2026, the City of Peterborough submitted two applications to the DCRP.
The first application included a total of 5 different Roads and Related projects, and the
second application included a series of Water and Wastewater projects intended to
service growth in the Coldsprings Planning Area. Details of each application and related
projects are further described below.
Application Criteria and Project Selection
A strong DCRP application demonstrates a clear connection between meaningful
residential development charge relief and the timely delivery of infrastructure required to
support housing growth. Competitive applications identify projects that directly enable a
significant number of housing units, are sufficiently advanced to proceed within the
program timelines, and are supported by municipal planning, development charge and
capital plans. Applications are further strengthened by a higher municipal contribution,

and maintain the infrastructure over its lifecycle.

 A substantial, municipality-wide residential development charge reduction
maintained for three years.
 A clear and measurable housing benefit, including units receiving DC relief and
units enabled by each project.
 Priority investment in housing-enabling infrastructure such as roads, water,
wastewater, stormwater and transit.
 Strong project readiness, supported by completed planning, engineering,
approvals, land acquisition, dedicated reserves or tendering.
 Inclusion in the City’s Development Charge Background Study, capital plan and
future asset management planning.
 A clear scope, schedule, dependencies, risks and mitigation measures, with
completion by October 31, 2035.
 A credible financing plan, including the municipal contribution, upfront cash-flow
capacity and responsibility for cost overruns and lifecycle costs.

The application for Zoning By-law Amendment accompanied by a planning justification
report proposes to the zoning from I – Institutional and R4 – Fourth Density Residential

hall, apartment building and personal service business while recognizing the existing
location of the building, and allowing for a reduction in lot area per unit, minimum floor
area for a unit and parking. These changes are being sought to permit the conversion
from an institutional building into a 22-unit apartment building with a hall and office space
on the property.

COUNCIL MEETINGS
Council meetings are a key part of local government, providing residents with the opportunity to observe decision-making, stay informed, and participate in the democratic process. The Township of Schreiber is committed to open, transparent, and accessible governance.
This page outlines when Council meets, how to attend meetings, how to speak to Council, and where to find related information and records.
COUNCIL & COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE MEETING SCHEDULE
Council and Committee of the Whole meetings are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month at 6:30 p.m. in the Council Chambers at the Schreiber Municipal Office. Meeting dates may occasionally change due to statutory holidays, scheduling conflicts, or special circumstances. Residents are encouraged to review the meeting agenda in advance to confirm the meeting date, time, and location.
Members of the public are welcome to attend Council meetings to observe local decision-making and stay informed about municipal initiatives and community matters.
Visit the Agendas & Minutes page to view upcoming agendas and approved meeting minutes.

AGENDAS & MINUTES
Agendas and minutes are published to provide residents with transparent access to the decisions and discussions of Council and its Committees. Agendas are typically posted approximately one week prior to each meeting. Minutes are posted after they have been reviewed and formally approved by Council.
Residents are encouraged to review agendas to stay informed about upcoming discussions and to read approved minutes for official records of Council decisions.
COUNCIL AGENDAS
Council agendas outline the items that will be discussed at upcoming meetings of Council. These documents provide an overview of reports, presentations, bylaws, and other matters requiring Council discussion or decision.
Agendas are typically posted approximately one week before each meeting to allow residents time to review upcoming municipal business.

THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER
BYLAW 13-2019
BEING A BYLAW TO APPOINT AN INTEGRITY COMMISSIONER
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, Chapter 25, Section 223.3 (1), authorizes the
municipality to appoint an Integrity Commissioner who reports to Council and who is
responsible for performing in an independent manner the functions assigned by the
municipality with respect to,
(a) the application of the code of conduct for members of Council and the code of conduct
for members of local boards or of either of them;
(b) the application of any procedures, rules and policies of the municipality and local boards
governing the ethical behaviour of members of council and of local boards or of either of
them.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION
OF THE TOWNSHIP OF SCHREIBER ENACTS AS FOLLOWING:
1) That Expertise for Municipalities (E4m) shall be appointed and act as Integrity
Commissioner.
2) That this appointment shall be subject to the executed Letter of Engagement,
attached as Appendix “A” of this Bylaw.
3) This Bylaw shall come into force and effect upon enactment.
4) This Bylaw may be cited as “Township of Schreiber Integrity Commissioner Bylaw
13-2019”.
Read a first and second time this 26th day of March, 2019.
Read a third time and finally enacted, this 26th day of March, 2019.

The Corporation of the Township of
Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield
By-law No. 2010-045
Being a By-law to Regulate and Restrict Water Use for the Users of the
Lakefield Area Water System and for the Users of the Woodland Acres Area
Water System
Whereas the Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, Section 2, as
amended, states that municipalities are created by the Province of Ontario to be
responsible and accountable governments with respect to matters within their
jurisdiction, and as such, municipalities are given powers and duties under this
Act, and many other Acts, for the purpose of providing good government with
respect to those matters; and
Whereas the Ontario Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25, Section 5.3, as
amended, states that a municipal power shall be exercised by By-law unless the
municipality is specifically authorized to do otherwise; and
Whereas, the water systems servicing the Lakefield Area and the Woodland
Acres Area may have difficulty meeting the daily demands for water during
certain periods of the year; and
Whereas; the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield passed By-law No. 2002-
68, being a By-law to regulate and restrict the use of water supplied to the users
of the Lakefield Area water system and the Woodland Acres Area water system
and now deems it advisable to repeal stated By-law;
Now Therefore, the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Smith-
Ennismore-Lakefield hereby enacts as follows:
1. That, in the Lakefield Area, from May 15th to September 15th of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an even number be permitted to
water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an even number
between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours of 6:00
p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
2. That, in the Lakefield Area, from May 15th to September 15th of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an odd number may be permitted
to water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an odd
number between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours
of 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
3. That, in the Woodland Acres Area, from June 1st to August 31st of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an even number be permitted to
water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an even number
between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
4. That, in the Woodland Acres Area, from June 1st to August 31st of each year,
those premises with addresses ending with an odd number may be permitted
to water their lawns and gardens on calendar dates ending with an odd
number between the hours of 7:00 a.m. and 10:00 p.m.
5. Notwithstanding Section 1, 2, 3, and 4 of this By-law, watering of newly
seeded or sodded lawns shall be permitted on any day between the hours of
7:00 a.m. and 9:00 a.m. and between the hours of 6:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m.
with a hand held hose until such time as the seed or sod is established.
6. Notwithstanding Section 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of this By-law, in the event of an
emergency situation, whereby normal water volumes and pressures are
jeopardized, or where extraordinary circumstances warrant, the Chief
Administrative Officer of the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield, or
his/her designate, in consultation with the system operator, shall be
authorized and directed to take whatever steps necessary to alleviate the
problem, which may include changes to the existing water restrictions and/or
a total ban on lawn and garden watering.
7. That no other high volume uses of water shall be permitted except under the
direction and control of the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield.
8. Violation of any of the provisions of this By-law shall constitute an offence.
9. A surcharge in the amount of $50.00 shall be imposed upon the account of
any customer that is found using water in violation of any of the provisions of
this By-law.
10. That each day on which any violation described in the By-law is continued
shall constitute a separate offence and the surcharge provided for under
Section 9 will apply once for each day that such violation occurs.
11. That this By-law applies to all customers of the water systems servicing the
Lakefield Area and the Woodland Acres Area.
12. That the Township of Smith-Ennismore-Lakefield By-law No. 2002-68 is
hereby repealed in its entirety.
13. That this By-law shall come in to full force and effect on the date of passing
thereof.
Read a first, second and third time and finally passed this 15th day of June A.D.,
2010.

The Corporation of the

By-law 2022-084
Procedure By-law
Being a By-law
To Govern the Proceedings of
Council and Committees or Local Board of the
Corporation of the Township of Selwyn
Whereas pursuant to Section 238 of the Municipal Act, 2001, as amended, every
municipality and local board shall pass a procedure By-law for governing the calling, place
and proceedings of meetings;
Now Therefore the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn Enacts as
follows;
Definitions
1. In this By-law:
a) “Abstain” means a member who is lawfully entitled to vote but chooses not to
exercise their right to vote on a matter, and in such cases in abstention shall be
deemed as a negative vote (Municipal Act S. 246. (2)).
b) “Clerk” means the Clerk of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
c) “Committee” means any advisory or other Committee, subcommittee or similar
entity of which at least 50 per cent of the members are also members of one or
more councils or local boards. A local board does not include police services
boards or public library boards (Municipal Act S. 238. (1)).
d) “Council” means the Council of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
e) “Electronic Participation” includes telephone, video, audio or audio-visual conferencing,
or any other interactive method whereby Members, staff and the public are able to hear
the Member(s) participating by electronic means and the Member(s) participating by
electronic means are able to hear other Members, staff and the public.
f) “Head of Council” means the Mayor of the Corporation of the Township of Selwyn.
g) “Live streaming” is a method of providing video over the internet in real time. The
video stream can be saved and archived allowing those with internet access the
ability to view recordings at their convenience.
h) “Meeting” means any regular, special, committee or other meeting of a Council, or
of a local board or of a committee of either of them, where,
(a) a quorum of members is present, and
(b) members discuss or otherwise deal with any matter in a way that materially
advanced the business or decision-making of the Council, local board or Committee
(Municipal Act S. 238 (1).
i) “Pecuniary Interest” means a direct or indirect pecuniary interest of a member of
Council within the meaning of the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act, R.S.O. 1990, as
amended.
j) “Presiding Officer” means the member of Council who, as determined under Section
12, 13 or 17 of this By-law, is responsible to preside over or act as the Chairperson
of a meeting.

k) “Point of Order” means an issue or concern regarding conformity to this By-law
and/or the rules of order of Council, difficulty in continuation of a meeting, improper,
offensive or abusive language, notice that discussion is outside the scope of a
motion or notice of motion, or irregularities in the proceedings.
l) “Point of Privilege” means a concern about the honour, dignity, character, rights or
professionalism of the Mayor, Members of Council or members of staff.
General
2. The rules and regulations contained in this By-law shall be observed in all
proceedings of the Council and shall be the rules and regulations for the order and
dispatch of business for Council and Committees appointed by Council and in any
case which provision is not made herein, the procedure to be followed shall be, as
near as may be, that followed in the Legislative Assembly of Ontario and its
Committees.
3. Applicable meetings of Council and Committee of Adjustment will be broadcast
through live streaming in accordance with Schedule “A” attached hereto and
forming part of this By-law.
4. Members of the public or media may record the proceedings of meetings in keeping
with the Township’s live streaming policy. Should the recording of a meeting differ
from the Township live streaming policy, a Resolution of Council passed by a simple
majority will be required to authorize the recording.
Council Meetings – Start Times, Public Notice and Electronic Participation
5. Meetings of Council may be held in-person at the Council Chambers or by
Electronic Participation or by a combination of in-person and Electronic
Participation. The inaugural meeting of Council shall take place at 3:00 pm on the
1st Tuesday following November 14th in the year of a regular election. The next and
each succeeding regular meeting of Council shall generally be held on the 2nd and
4th Tuesday of each month, save and except the months of January, July, August
and December when one meeting will be held in each month. The Clerk shall
prepare a report for Council in the fourth quarter of each year identifying the
following year’s meeting dates. These meeting dates shall be adopted by a
resolution of Council.
a) Meetings - Start Time
i) Regular Council meetings shall commence at 1:00 pm
b) Meetings – Closed Session Matters – Start Time
i) 2nd Tuesday meeting – Closed session matters (Municipal Act Section
239 (2), (3) and (3.1)) will be dealt with at the end of the meeting
ii) 4th Tuesday meeting - Closed session matters (Municipal Act Section
239 (2), (3)and (3.1)) will be dealt with at the end of the meeting
c) Public Notice of Meetings
Notice of all public meetings of Council, a local Board or a Committee of either of
them shall be made by means of posting the information on the Township’s
website a minimum of twenty four (24) hours in advance. In the event of a
special meeting, the information would be placed on the Township’s website and
if deemed appropriate by the Clerk, or requested by Council, a notice will also be
placed in the local paper and/or broadcast on a local radio station. The term
Committee means any advisory or other committee, subcommittee, or similar

more Councils or local Boards.
(Municipal Act S. 238 (2.1))
d) Electronic Participation in Meeting
Members of Councils, local boards and committees who participate
electronically in open and closed meetings may be counted for purposes of
quorum.
Public or Civic Holidays
6. When the day for a regular meeting of the Council is a public or civic holiday, the
Council shall meet at the same hour on the following day, which is not a public or
civic holiday, unless an alternative day is determined by resolution of Council.
Cancelling and Rescheduling Meetings
7. Council may, by resolution passed at a regular meeting, cancel a scheduled regular
meeting or reschedule a regular meeting to another date and may hold a meeting at
another location other than the Council Chambers.
In the event of an exceptional circumstance (e.g. emergency situation, unsafe
weather or where the Clerk becomes aware that quorum will not be met) the Clerk
can cancel a scheduled meeting and seek input from the members on an alternate
date/time, if required. The Clerk shall notify Council members of the cancellation
and any other relevant parties as soon as possible and post notice of the
cancellation on the Township’s website.
Where quorum can be met, the Clerk can conduct the meeting by Electronic
Participation or a combination of in-person and Electronic Participation. In the event
that the format of the meeting is changed to Electronic Participation or a
combination of in-person and Electronic Participation, the Clerk shall notify the
members of Council of the format and any other relevant parties as soon as
possible and post the change on the Township’s website.
Special Meetings
8. The Head of Council may at any time summon a special meeting of Council on
forty-eight (48) hours notice to the members of Council, or upon receipt of the
petition of the majority of the Members of the Council, the Clerk shall summon a
special meeting for the purpose and at the time mentioned in the petition.
(Municipal Act S.240 )
9. Forty-eight (48) hours notice of all special meetings of Council shall be given to the
Members, either verbally or written, through the Clerk’s Office.
10. The only business to be dealt with at a special meeting is that which is listed in the
notice of meeting.
11. In the event of an emergency, as determined by the Head of Council, a meeting
may be called at any time.
Appointment of Acting Head of Council
12. In the case of the absence of the Mayor from the Municipality, or if the Mayor is
absent through illness, or refuses to act or that office is vacant, the Deputy Mayor
shall act from time to time in the place and stead of the Head of Council and while
so acting as the Presiding Officer shall have all the rights, powers and authority of
the Head of Council.

Presiding Officer
13. The Head of Council, except where otherwise provided, shall preside at all meetings
of Council. (Municipal Act S.241(1))
14. In the absence of the Head of Council, the Acting Head of Council shall be the
Presiding Officer.
Calling of Meeting to Order and Quorum
15. A majority of the whole number of members required to constitute a Council is
necessary to form a quorum. (Municipal Act S.237(1))
16. As soon after the hour fixed for the holding of the meeting of the Council as a
quorum is present, the Head of Council shall take the Chair and call the meeting to
order.
Absence of Presiding Officer
17. Should the Head of Council not attend within five (5) minutes after the time
appointed for a meeting of Council and the Acting Head of Council is not present to
assume the role of Presiding Officer, the Clerk shall call the members to order and a
Presiding Officer shall be appointed by resolution from among the members
present, and they shall preside until the arrival of the Head of Council or the Acting
Head of Council and while so presiding shall have all the powers of the Head of
Council. (Municipal Act S.242)
No Quorum
18. If no quorum is present fifteen (15) minutes after the time appointed for a meeting of
the Council, the Clerk shall record the names of the members present and the
meeting shall stand adjourned until the date of the next regular meeting. The
members present shall be entitled to remuneration as approved from time to time.

MEETING TYPE: Regular Council Meeting
To: Council
From: Jackie Trenholm, Deputy Clerk
Date: April 16, 2025
Subject: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
Report No.: 2025-529
TITLE: 2026 Municipal Election Matters
RECOMMENDATION:
THAT Council authorizes the passing of By-law No. 25-25, Being a By-law Relating to 2026
Municipal Election Matters (language(s) to be used for election forms/notices/information; use
of alternative voting method; use of vote-counting equipment).
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this recommendation is to enable Council to make certain decisions respecting
the 2026 Municipal Election, including the use of the "telephone/internet" voting method.
BACKGROUND:
Several items must be addressed relative to the 2026 Municipal Election, including:
1. Use of Alternative Voting Methods
2. Advance Poll
3. Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
4. Use of vote-counting equipment
5. Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
6. Payment of rebate for campaign contributions
7. Ward(s) review/changes
8. Electronic filing of financial statements
9. Submitting a By-law or question to the electors (question on the ballot)
10. Appointment of Compliance Committee
DISCUSSION:
Item No. 1: Use of Alternative Voting Methods
The Municipality had been employing the vote-by-mail (VBM) voting method for several prior
general municipal elections (2003, 2006, 2010 and 2014). This alternative voting method has
been successful, having yielded higher voter turnout rates over traditional elections in each of
the last four general elections.
While this method has increased voter turnout, compared to the traditional in-person polls, the
participation rate has decreased over the last decade-and-a-half, as follows:
• Voter turnout 2003 – 60.61%
• Voter turnout 2006 – 57.72%
• Voter turnout 2010 – 56.86%
• Voter turnout 2014 – 55.95%
Given this gradual, but steady, decline in voter participation, staff recommended the use of the
telephone/internet voting method in the 2018 general election, the 2020 by-election and the
2022 general election. Voter turnout for those elections was as follows:
• 2018 General Election – 55.21%
• 2020 By-election – 32.48%
• 2022 General Election - 33.10%
Given the trend in municipal elections, across Ontario, of having fewer voters participate in
such elections, achieving a 55.21% voter turnout in 2018 was excellent, and placed Sioux
Lookout in among the highest of voter turnout results in Ontario. By-elections typically result in
lower number of voters. The 2020 By-election turnout was approximately 2.5% higher than the
last by-election in 2015. The 2022 voter turnout was lower than the 2018 general election.
When there isn’t a mayoral race, voter turnout is typically lower.
Vote-by-Mail versus Telephone/Internet Voting – An Analysis
Election Principles
Despite which voting method is selected, it is the responsibility of the Clerk/Returning Officer
to uphold the following election principles:
• The secrecy and confidentiality of the individual votes is paramount;
• The election must be fair and non-biased;
• The election must be accessible to all voters;
• The integrity of the process must be maintained throughout the election;
• There must be certainty that the results of the election reflect the votes cast; and
• All voters and candidates must be treated fairly and consistently.
Vote by Mail – Overview
Electors receive a voting kit in the mail. They mail in their signed declaration form along with
their secrecy envelope containing their marked ballot. The declaration form is scanned prior to
voting day; the secrecy ballot is kept in a secure ballot box until the close of election. On
Election Day, Staff open the ballot boxes containing the secrecy envelopes and review each
ballot to determine if the ballot is spoiled or rejected. Staff then feed the ballots through a vote
tabulating machine or count them manually. Once all of the ballots have been fed through the
vote tabulator (or counted manually), the tabulator totals the votes and provides a printable
receipt of the results to election officials, or the totals of votes cast and counted manually are
reported to the Returning Officer.
Advantages and Disadvantages: Vote-by-mail (VBM)
Advantages:
Signed declaration – provides security against voter fraud
Improved size and efficiency. Desk top tabulators are hooked up to a PC laptop and can
scan 40 ballots per minute and results are quick. They also store the image of each
ballot for recount/audit purposes.
Longer voting period
Disadvantages:
With VBM, staff are required to facilitate vote tabulation by feeding ballots into vote
tabulators, or physically/manually examining each ballot, and must make a determination
with respect to spoiled and rejected ballots
Staff resources and time - secrecy ballot envelopes cannot be opened until close of
voting. Ballots must then be organized, reviewed, scanned, counted and then eventually
destroyed.
If not using vote-counting equipment, manual vote-counting is extremely time consuming
– unofficial results in 2014 were not available until 2:00 a.m. (6 hours after close of
voting).
Opportunity for Spoiled ballots – vote does not count (e.g. elector included ballot with
signed declaration card; no signed declaration form or no declaration form included;
marking on the ballot that does not indicate choice or there is no marking on ballot)
Spoiled ballots – the voter has no way of knowing if their ballot was spoiled. There is no
confirmation process.
Potential to receive voter kits by unintended recipient which includes the ballot
Postal service – takes five days for voter to receive vote by mail kit; takes five days for
municipal office to receive marked ballot with secrecy envelope (total 5-10 days) by mail,
unless dropped off at municipal office
Costs – more expensive voting method due to need for more staff; manual count;
training of staff, etc.
Internet/Telephone Voting - Overview
Internet Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They log onto the election server on any computer,
vote by using their keyboard in response to a virtual ballot, the vote is stored on the election
software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation number or
printable receipt. At the close of Election Day, the internet software totals the votes received
and provides a printable receipt of the results to election officials.
Telephone Voting – Electors receive a Voter Information Letter containing a Personal
Identification Number (PIN) in the mail. They call a toll-free number from a touchtone phone;
vote by pressing buttons in response to a voice recording and the vote is stored by the
election software. The elector receives confirmation of their vote by way of a confirmation
number. At the close of Election Day, the telephone voting results are combined with the
internet voting results for one total result. A printable receipt of the results is made available to
election officials.
It is recommended that both internet and telephone options be provided to electors for the
2026 municipal election.
Advantages and Disadvantages of Internet/Telephone Voting
Advantages:
Less staff and administrative resources required and less expensive overall (except in
first year of implementation, due to public education costs)
No ballot errors/spoiled ballots because the software does not permit it. There are built in
reminders or safeguards to prevent accidental voting
Voter is provided with confirmation that their vote counted by issuance or confirmation of
a receipt
Elector participation is real time and results are immediate
Ballot destruction after election is electronically completed and verified
Voter has the opportunity to review selection and make changes prior to submitting vote
Lowered carbon footprint; environmentally sustainable due to less paper required
Recounts are instantaneous and inexpensive
Most accessible form of voting. Allows persons with disabilities the opportunity to
completely mark their ballot in private without the assistance of a designated friend or
election official, therefore providing greater dignity
Disadvantages:
Not everyone has access to a computer or is computer literate; however, telephone
voting would be the alternative to those who do not have internet access or low levels of
computer literacy
Security and viruses; voter authentication - however, the preferred vendor has
implemented robust measures to mitigate such threats
Telephone voting takes time – audio ballot
Telephone voting - Voter cannot see the names of the candidates
Other Benefits of Internet/telephone Voting
• provides convenience, accommodates changing lifestyles, demanding work schedules;
• enhances accessibility for students studying away from home, those travelling, shift
workers, infirmed persons, and persons with language barriers.
• for persons with disabilities, it provides greater dignity and privacy for electors;
• engages a wider range of age demographics, provides greater accuracy and fast results, is
convenient for seasonal residents, and has the potential for increased voter turnout.
Public Education & Outreach
Public education and outreach will play a critical role in the 2026 municipal election, should the
telephone/internet voting method be adopted. Although this method has been used several
times in Sioux Lookout, to ensure that concerns and questions regarding this voting method
are adequately addressed, a prior election education campaigns will be enhanced and
administered by the Clerk.
In order to mitigate concerns regarding accessibility for senior citizens to vote, the Clerk, as in
the 2018, 2020 and 2022 elections, will arrange to attend multi-residential senior complexes
throughout the community to provide senior citizens the opportunity to vote at their residence.
Additionally, for those who are not comfortable with internet voting or telephone voting on their
own, an electronic voting station will be established at the Municipal Office, with staff on hand
to provide assistance, as requested. Furthermore, remote voting locations will be established
at the Sioux Lookout Senior’s Centre, the Sioux Lookout Meno Ya Win Health Centre, the
William George Extended Care Unit, the Nishnawbe-Gamik Friendship Centre, and in Hudson.
Accessibility for Persons with Disabilities
Internet/Telephone voting offers the most accessible form of voting. Voters are offered the
greatest secrecy and less assisted voting thereby enhancing the quality of the vote and
anonymity.
Security
Section 89 of the Municipal Elections Act provides for penalties for any contravention of the
Act, as follows:
A person is guilty of an offence if he or she,
(a) votes without being entitled to do so;
(b) votes more times than this Act allows;
(c) votes in a voting place in which he or she is not entitled to vote;
(d) induces or procures a person to vote when that person is not entitled to do so;
(e) having appointed a voting proxy that remains in force, votes otherwise than by the proxy;
(f) having been appointed a voting proxy, votes under the authority of the proxy when the
elector has cancelled the proxy, is no longer entitled to vote or has died;
(g) before or during an election, publishes a false statement of a candidate’s withdrawal;
(h) furnishes false or misleading information to a person whom this Act authorizes to obtain
information;
(i) without authority, supplies a ballot to anyone;
(j) delivers to the deputy returning officer to be placed in a ballot box a paper other than the
ballot the deputy returning officer gave him or her;
(k) takes a ballot away from the voting place;
(l) at an election, takes, opens or otherwise deals with a ballot, a ballot box, or a book or
package of ballots without having authority to do so;
(m) attempts to do something described in clauses (a) to (l)
Clearly, accountability of voting rests with the voter and there are penalties associated with
voter fraud. Unsupervised voting facilitates the potentiality of these offences. Voter
impersonation, coercion and fraud are concerns which are mitigated through the design of any
voting system, regardless of whether it is a supervised or unsupervised model.
Item No. 2: Advance Poll
The use of the vote-by-mail or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for
advance polls. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk,
via the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 3: Early Voting and/or Reduced Voting Hours
The vote-by-mail voting or telephone/internet voting methods eliminates the need for these
measures. Additionally, determination of this matter has now been delegated to the Clerk, via
the Municipal Elections Act, Council no longer makes these decisions.
Item No. 4: Use of Vote-Counting Equipment
The Municipality had used Electronic Vote Tabulators (EVTs) in the 2000, 2003, 2006 and
2010 Municipal Elections. Ballots were created and coded by Ward, School Board
candidate(s) and Municipal Council (Mayor and Councillors-at-Large) candidates and
processed by the EVT on voting day. In the past, this has resulted in election results within
minutes of the close of polls.
For the 2014 Municipal Election, the Clerk chose to use manual vote-counting procedures
given that vote-counting equipment rental had significantly increased in cost increase since
the 2010 Municipal Election. The primary impact on the election was a longer time-frame
between the close of polls and the announcement of the unofficial results – a total of six hours.
If Council chooses to use the Vote-by-Mail voting method in 2026, vote tabulators will be
required to ensure the efficient tabulation of results; this is an additional cost to using this
voting method.
Item No. 5: Language(s) in Notices/Forms/Information
Prescribed forms (those set by legislation) must be provided in English only, but may be
provided in English and French only. Other forms/notices/information can be provided in
English, French or any other language, providing Council passes a by-law permitting such.
In one previous election, prior to 2003, some of the Notices were provided in both English and
Oji-Cree. This exercise was costly and was subsequently discontinued. It should be noted that
the onus is on the elector to provide translation services when voting. In 2003, 2006 and 2010,
the Clerk recommended and Council passed a By-law to provide notices in Oji-Cree at the
discretion of the Clerk.
Staff recommends that Council permit notices to be published in Oji-Cree for the 2026
Municipal Election, at the discretion of the Clerk.

Title: Tree Canopy Assessment Update – 2019 vs 2024
Recommendation: That Council receives Report 2026-111 for information
Purpose: The purpose of this report is to present the findings of the Town’s 2024 Tree
Canopy Assessment and compare them with the revised 2019 baseline assessment to
better understand how canopy coverage changed over time.
Background: In 2021, Council adopted the Tree Canopy and Vegetation Preservation and
Enhancement Policy in recognition of the importance trees and the natural environment play
in supporting the health, character and resilience of our community. The Policy identifies
urban forests as invaluable municipal assets that provides environmental, social, economic
benefits, including stormwater management, reducing urban heat, enhancing biodiversity,
improving public spaces, and contributing to the overall quality and well-being of Smiths
Falls.
Moving towards this objective, a minimum 30% tree canopy coverage was established as a
long-term goal within the Policy. Recognizing the importance of establishing a consistent
baseline and monitoring changes over time, the Policy commits the Town to completing
periodic tree canopy assessments using a consistent methodology to identify longer-term
trends and inform future decisions related to the preservation, management and growth of
our urban tree canopy.
Using 2024 Digital Raster Acquisition Project for Eastern Ontario (DRAPE)
orthophotography, which is detailed aerial imagery, Staff completed the town's second
urban tree canopy assessment. The first assessment was completed in 2024 using the 2019
DRAPE providing the foundation for future comparisons. The assessment measures the
area covered by tree crowns through GIS analysis, providing a town-wide understanding of
our tree canopy distribution.
Staff began the update by reviewing the 2019 DRAPE urban tree canopy assessment,
including the original GIS methodology and calculation process, to confirm the approach
used and determine how it could be replicated for the 2024 assessment. The 2019
methodology was then recreated as closely as possible using the 2024 DRAPE
orthophotography to ensure consistency between the two assessment periods.
During this review, Staff identified an error in the calculation of the 2019 canopy area. While
the original methodology was intended to account for overlapping tree canopy areas only
Page 1 of 6
once, the final calculation resulted in some overlapping areas being counted multiple times.
The 2019 results were therefore recalculated using the original intended approach to
establish a corrected baseline for comparison with the 2024 assessment. The recalculation
resulted in a 2019 urban tree canopy coverage of 23.77%, compared with the previously
reported value of approximately 35%.
The revised 2019 results replace the figures presented in the draft and provide the
appropriate reference point for comparison with the completed 2024 assessment.
To better understand localized canopy conditions, the assessment was also organized by
defined Community of Interest areas, such as the Downtown Core and the Lombard Street
Corridor. These areas reflect distinct neighbourhoods, corridors, and land use contexts
within the Town. Evaluating canopy coverage by area provides a more useful understanding
of where change is occurring than a single Town-wide value alone. This approach allows
canopy conditions and changes to be considered alongside local planning objectives,
existing zoning, development pressures, and opportunities for targeted vegetation
enhancement.
For more details, see Appendix A—2024 Communities of Interest Zone Map and Table 1—
Urban Tree Canopy Coverage Distribution Chart in Appendix B—2019 and 2024 Urban
Canopy Tree Canopy Coverage.
Analysis: Overall, the change in canopy coverage between 2019 and 2024 was modest,
decreasing by 0.52 %, from 23.77% to 23.25%. This represents approximately 13 acres of
net canopy loss over the five-year period (from 600.52 acres in 2019 to 587.50 acres in
2024). The Town-wide reduction of 0.52 % provides an overall measure of canopy change;
however, it does not capture how that change occurred across the community. The mapping
identifies areas where canopy loss was more concentrated, including areas experiencing
recent development and redevelopment. Table 1 provides a breakdown of canopy coverage
within each Community of Interest in 2024.
Using the corrected methodology, Staff performed a tabletop exercise, reviewing the 2019
tree canopy dataset against the 2024 DRAPE imagery. The exercise involved removing
trees no longer present, adding newly planted trees, and updating crown diameters of
existing trees to reflect observed growth. The assessment measures only canopy coverage
and does not assess tree health, species distribution, or whether a tree is on public or private
property.
Changes in canopy coverage varied across the Town. The Southwest Residential Area
experienced the largest decrease, from 22.98% in 2019 to 17.04% in 2024, largely due to
residential development, including the Bellamy Farm and Maple Ridge subdivisions. The
Southeast Residential Area decreased from 25.56% to 23.84%, primarily reflecting canopy
removal associated with the development of the Broadview Nursing Home. The Lombard
Street Corridor decreased from 21.88% to 20.81%, reflecting new commercial development
and associated site clearing and parking areas.
The Downtown Core decreased from 10.61% to 9.48%. During the assessment period,
streetscape renewal resulted in the removal of mature trees and the planting of replacement
Page 2 of 6
trees. As newly planted trees require time to establish and develop larger crowns, their
canopy contribution is not yet fully reflected in the 2024 assessment.
In contrast, the Gallipeau Centre & Lorne Street Development Area continues to have the
Town’s highest canopy coverage, increasing from 37.29% to 38.87%. Limited development
activity and the continued growth of established trees contributed to this increase. The
Northern Mixed-Use Area also increased from 9.58% to 10.77%, while Uptown East and
Uptown West remained relatively stable.
Overall, canopy change was modest at the community-wide level but varied considerably
by area. The Town’s 2024 urban tree canopy coverage of 23.25% remains below the
minimum 30% target established in the Policy.
The results suggest that a five-year assessment period is a relatively short timeframe for
evaluating meaningful changes in the Town’s overall tree canopy coverage. The 2019 to
2024 assessment period coincided with one of the most significant periods of development
and growth in Smiths Falls in recent times.

Subject: August Concert Series Bluewater Park
Recommendation:
That Council approves $5,000 to be drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax
Reserve, Account 34012 for the purpose of a Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater
Park Bandshell for the month of August;
And further that if sponsors are confirmed for the concert series, sponsorship funds will be
allocated to the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve.
Link to Strategic Planning: Goal 4: Healthy, Vibrant and Safe Communities
4.1 Enhance facilities for healthy living and affordable and cultural opportunities.
Background:
As part of a successful grant application through the Federal Economic Development
Agency of Southern Ontario's Community Revitalization stream, the Town of South Bruce
Peninsula was awarded $375,000. These funds are designated for upgrades to Bluewater
Park, including improvements to the pier and causeway, accessibility enhancements, the
bandshell, and indigenous and marine interpretive signage.
The bandshell construction is now complete, and on July 11, 2024, the Town hosted a
grand opening event at Bluewater Park. Local musicians Midnight Blue performed at the
concert, and the event was a resounding success, attracting over 400 attendees to the
ribbon-cutting ceremony and the concert.
The long-term goal for the bandshell is to encourage rentals for regular concerts and events,
thereby attracting visitors and creating a positive economic impact on the local economy.
The rental rate for the bandshell is set at $150 for not-for-profit events and $450 for for-profit
events.
In collaboration with a local musician, staff have organized a concert series featuring various
artists on Thursday evenings from 7:30 pm to 9:00 pm during the month of August, with
performances scheduled for the 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th. This concert series aims to
showcase the new venue and generate interest in future rentals.
With the summer season well underway, staff have worked expeditiously to organize this
series in advance of the first concert date on August 8th. For future Town-run events, staff
will seek sponsorship to support these initiatives.
Staff are recommending that the total project budget of $5,000 to fund this concert series be
drawn from the Municipal Accommodation Tax working capital reserve as these events
support a tourism attraction in South Bruce Peninsula.
Staff are also seeking sponsorship for the Thursday night music series and if successful, the
initiative will be partially/fully funded via sponsorship. At the Time of writing this report,
sponsorship funding has not been secured, hence the request to utilize MAT funds. Any
sponsorship funding will be utilized to pay for the concert series and replenish MAT
reserves, if funding comes at a later date.
Options:
A $5,000 to be allocated from the Municipal Accommodation Tax Reserve for the
Thursday night concert series at the Bluewater Park Bandshell in the month of
August.
B. Provide alternate direction.

None
Inter-Departmental Impact:
The Manager of Economic Development will work with the Recreation and Parks
Department on venue booking and equipment set up. Communications of the concert series
will be through the website and social media channels.

Background: The Community Grant Program Policy (TR.18.2) was adopted by Council
in 2021 as a means to streamline the requests that Council receives from members of
the community seeking funding. The policy has undergone amendments since its initial
adoption with the last amendment being adopted in 2024. One of the requirements in
the policy is that the grant recipients are required to make a final report 90 days
following their event or by November 30, 2024, whichever is earlier.
The 2024 program application period closed on November 30, 2023 with eighteen (18)
submissions being received. Two of the applicants did not receive funding as they did not
meet the program criteria, proposing projects for Town and other Government Agency
property. Subsequent to deliberations, Council adopted resolution R-07-2024 wherein
funding awards were decided and additionally, Council decided to remove the previous
"automatically recurring" grants which staff had been including in the annual budgets. Using
the last remaining budget allocation, Council has also provided funding support to two
additional organizations since the original allocation of funding.
Staff have received the final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club which supported
the annual Canada Day event held in Bluewater Park. The grant allocation was $500.
The final report from the Wiarton District Optimist Club explains that the event had vendors,
a BBQ, a pancake breakfast and family entertainment. The Wiarton District Optimist Club
was fortunate in that they secured several local sponsors and funding through the Celebrate
Canada Grant Program. All of the funds, including those from the Town allowed them to
hold a family friendly event which they feel was a success. The Optimist Club was able to
finish the event with a surplus of $2,839.08. The Town's donation was directed toward the
Bluewater Park rental costs.
