WHEREAS the Council of the Township of Tyendinaga has previously passed
resolutions expressing concerns regarding the Alto High-Speed Rail Project and
Bill C-15;
AND WHEREAS Council has stated that it does not support the project as presented
due to its potential impacts on residents, farmland, the environment, municipal
infrastructure and property rights;
AND WHEREAS the recently announced consideration of a route serving Kingston,
including the possibility of an alignment along or near Highway 401, would not
eliminate these concerns but could create significant adverse impacts in another
area of Tyendinaga Township;
AND WHEREAS this area contains homes, productive farmland and Tyendinaga
Public School, the only public school located within the Township, serving nearly
400 students;
AND WHEREAS Tyendinaga Township is a wholly rural municipality whose
residents rely heavily on access to the urban centres of Belleville and Napanee for
employment, shopping, health care and other essential services, with three
Highway 401 interchanges and an additional overpass currently supporting that
access;
AND WHEREAS Old Highway 2, the principal alternative route to Belleville and
Napanee, is located south of Highway 401 and could also become inaccessible to
affected residents if crossings through the potential rail corridor are closed,
restricted or altered;
AND WHEREAS the resulting loss or restriction of access to Highway 401 and Old
Highway 2 could significantly affect residents, school transportation, emergency
response and access to area hospitals;
AND WHEREAS the project’s estimated cost of $60 billion to $90 billion is
preliminary and cannot be properly evaluated before the route, required
infrastructure, environmental and geological challenges, property acquisition costs
and impacts on municipal infrastructure and services are known;
AND WHEREAS proceeding with a project of this scale without a defined route,
dependable cost estimate and clear accounting of its full financial implications
presents a significant risk to Canadian taxpayers;
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT the Council of the Township of
Tyendinaga reaffirms its previous resolutions and its position that it does not
support the Alto High-Speed Rail Project as presented;
AND THAT Council confirms that a potential Highway 401 route through
Tyendinaga Township could cause unacceptable harm to residents, farmland,
Tyendinaga Public School, municipal roads and infrastructure, emergency services,
and access to Highway 401, Old Highway 2 and area hospitals;

Alto has publicly provided a defined route, a credible and independently reviewed

The Corporation of the Municipality of Tweed
Staff Report
Date: August 11, 2026 Council Meeting
Report to: Council
Report from: Cindy Chow, Manager, Community Development, Parks & Rec
Department: Community Development
Title: Backyard Hen Program - Background Report
PURPOSE:
The purpose of this report is to provide Council with background information regarding
backyard hen programs and to summarize regulations currently in effect in several
Ontario municipalities. The report is intended for Council's consideration of a potential
Backyard Hen Program within the Municipality of Tweed and to seek direction regarding
the development of a draft by-law and regulatory framework for future Council review.
BACKGROUND:
Staff have received inquiries from residents regarding the keeping of backyard hens for
personal egg production. A growing number of Ontario municipalities permit backyard
hens while establishing regulations intended to address animal welfare, public health,
biosecurity, neighbourhood compatibility, property maintenance, and enforcement
requirements.
Benefits of backyard hens:
 Supports local food production and food security.
 Provides educational opportunities for families and youth.
 Encourages self-sufficiency and sustainable living practices.
 Aligns with Tweed's rural character and agricultural heritage.
 May contribute to waste reduction through composting of approved organic
materials and responsible manure management.
Challenges of backyard hens:
 Potential noise and odour complaints.
 Attraction of pests, rodents, and predators.
 Disease and biosecurity concerns, including Avian Influenza.
 Animal welfare considerations.
 Compatibility concerns within residential neighbourhoods.
 Additional municipal administration, enforcement, and oversight requirements.
Review of municipal backyard hen programs indicates several common
regulatory provisions:
 Roosters are generally prohibited.
 Most municipalities limit the number of hens permitted.
 Backyard hens are intended for personal use only.
 Coops and runs are required to meet setback and construction standards.
 Coop size and height restrictions are commonly established.
 Manure management and sanitation requirements are required.
 Property owners are responsible for cleanliness, maintenance, and animal care.
 Building, Planning, and Municipal Law Enforcement staff typically play a role in
implementation and enforcement.
 Most municipalities utilize a complaint-based enforcement model.

POTENTIAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE MUNICIPALITY OF TWEED
Should Council direct staff to prepare a draft by-law, the following framework could be
considered:
 Maximum of six (6) hens per residential property.
 Roosters prohibited.
 Home slaughter is prohibited.
 Breeding is prohibited.
 No commercial egg production or sales.
 No commercial agricultural operation.
 No ducks, geese, turkeys, guinea fowl, peafowl, or other poultry species.
 Rear-yard coop placement only.
 Minimum setbacks from lot lines and neighbouring dwellings.
 Compliance with zoning, property standards, and animal welfare requirements.
 Secure storage of feed and bedding materials.
 Proper disposal of deceased birds in accordance with applicable regulations.
 Complaint-based enforcement model.
 Potential licensing or permit requirements subject to further review.
Zoning Considerations
Staff will review whether backyard hens should be permitted as an accessory residential
use and identify any necessary zoning restrictions, including permitted areas, minimum
lot sizes, and setback requirements for coops and runs.
Licensing Considerations
Council may wish to consider a licensing system to support education, compliance
tracking, and enforcement. Without licensing, enforcement would be primarily
complaint-driven.
Building and Coop Requirements
Staff will consult with Building Services regarding permit requirements, size and height
restrictions, construction standards, and predator protection measures for coops and
runs.
Property Standards and Nuisance Control
A backyard hen by-law should address manure management, odour, pests, waste
storage, and general property maintenance to prevent nuisance conditions.
Animal Welfare
Minimum standards should include access to food and water, adequate shelter and
ventilation, protection from predators, and appropriate coop and run sizes.
Avian Influenza and Biosecurity
Staff will review applicable biosecurity practices, disease prevention measures, and any
provincial guidance related to avian influenza.
Predator Control
Requirements may include secure feed storage, predator-resistant coops, enclosed
runs, overnight confinement of hens, and proper waste management to reduce wildlife
attraction.
Enforcement Considerations
The effectiveness of a backyard hen program depends largely on having clear,
enforceable regulations. A complaint-based enforcement model is generally appropriate
because:
 Proactive inspections are resource intensive;
 Routine inspections are generally unnecessary;
 Most complaints involve odour, sanitation, noise, rodents, predators, or excessive
numbers of hens.
Potential enforcement tools may include:
 Written warnings;
 Orders to Comply;
 Administrative Monetary Penalties, where applicable;
 Licence suspension or revocation, if licensing is implemented; and

 WHEREAS, the transportation of students to and from school is an essential public service that supports families, education, and the community; and
WHEREAS, many school bus drivers are employed on a part-time basis and are authorized by their employer to park their assigned mini or wheelchair-accessible school bus at their residence; and
WHEREAS, permitting these smaller school buses to be parked on private residential driveways can improve driver recruitment and retention, reduce unnecessary travel to and from bus yards, reduce fuel consumption and emissions, and improve operational efficiency; and
WHEREAS, mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses are generally between 19 and 25 feet in length and have a significantly smaller neighbourhood impact than full-size conventional school buses; and
WHEREAS, Section 3.9(5) of Parking By-law 89-2000 currently prohibits the parking of school buses, used as commercial vehicles and designed for carrying ten or more passengers, on private property in a residential zone, without distinguishing between mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses and full-size conventional school buses; and
WHEREAS, the proposed review seeks to balance the operational needs of school transportation providers with the preservation of the safety and character of residential neighbourhoods; and further
WHEREAS, this motion applies only to the parking of mini and wheelchair-accessible school buses on private residential driveways and does not propose permitting school buses to park on public streets.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT Council directs staff to review Section 3.9(5) of Parking By-law 89-2000 and report back with recommendations regarding an amendment to permit mini school buses and wheelchair-accessible school buses not exceeding 26 feet (7.9 metres) in length to be parked on private residential driveways only, where the vehicle is assigned to a resident by a licensed school bus operator' and further
THAT staff consult with local school bus operators as part of the review and provide recommendations respecting appropriate eligibility requirements, safety considerations, operational conditions, and any other amendments necessary to implement such an exemption.  Ref. No. 26-22

WHEREAS, individuals experiencing homelessness, mental health challenges, and addictions frequently require access to crisis stabilization, withdrawal management, complex care, recovery supports, and integrated health services; and
WHEREAS, gaps in local and regional treatment capacity contribute to increased emergency department utilization, hospital strain, EMS offload delays, and ongoing pressures on frontline services; and
WHEREAS, the Province of Ontario has identified mental health and addictions as priority areas for investment and healthcare system transformation; and
WHEREAS, the Niagara Health Welland Hospital site is currently undergoing planning and redevelopment consideration through a provincially supported planning process; and
WHEREAS, meaningful collaboration between municipalities, healthcare partners, social service agencies, and individuals with lived and living experience can strengthen long-term community outcomes.
NOW THEREFORE LET IT BE RESOLVED THAT THE COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF WELLAND formally declares homelessness, mental health, and substance use to constitute a municipal and public health emergency requiring coordinated action across all levels of government; and
THAT the City of Welland calls upon the Ontario Ministry of Health and Niagara Health to ensure the ongoing planning and future redevelopment of the Welland Hospital site includes consideration for expanded:
- mental health and addictions treatment services;
- withdrawal management and stabilization capacity;
- complex continuing care and recovery beds; 
- integrated community-based health supports; and
THAT the City of Welland requests that municipal perspectives, local service impacts, and community-based healthcare needs be incorporated into the ongoing planning and business case development process for the future of the Welland Hospital site; and further
THAT this resolution be circulated to the Minister of Health, local MPPs, Niagara Region, Niagara Health, and Niagara-area municipalities for their consideration.   Ref. No. 21-30

Dear City Clerk and Members of Council,
We, the parents and next of kin of Carrie Lynn Pinard, hereby submit this formal letter of
support and consent in accordance with the City of Welland’s Facility Naming Policy. This
submission is provided to support the naming of the Dain City new school’s dedicated
community space in honour of our daughter, Carrie Lynn Pinard, and includes background and
biographical information demonstrating her significance to the local community.
Carrie was raised in the City of Welland, specifically within the Dain City community, where
she lived, attended school, and developed strong personal and community ties. Dain City was
Carrie’s home throughout her formative years, and it remains the community most closely
connected to her life and legacy. The proposed facility is located within this same community,
establishing a clear and meaningful geographic and historical connection.
Carrie attended Bridgeview School from kindergarten through Grade 8. During her time there,
she was well known and well respected by peers, educators, and community members. She later
continued her education at the secondary level, carrying forward the values instilled through her
upbringing in Welland—kindness, generosity, and respect for others.
At the age of 18, Carrie’s life was tragically and senselessly taken as a result of gun violence
while she was in Toronto. She was an innocent victim, in the wrong place at the wrong time. Her
death had a profound impact on her family, friends, and the Welland community and extended
beyond the municipality, contributing to broader public awareness and dialogue related to gun
violence, the young offenders act and community safety. Carrie’s story became part of the
momentum supporting changes to gun legislation in Canada, reflecting the wider social
significance of her legacy.
At the time of her passing, Carrie was working part-time as a model and had just been accepted
to attend the University of Toronto. Carrie was known for her confidence, determination, and
positive spirit. She was widely regarded as kind, generous, and compassionate, with a warm
smile and genuine care for others. She was a loving and devoted sister to her two sisters and a
cherished daughter. Carrie was admired not only for her outward beauty, but for her character
and the way she treated those around her.
In recognition of Carrie’s life and the impact of her story, the recreation gym at the former
Bridgeview School, which has been leased by the City of Welland since 1994, was previously
named the Carrie Lynn Pinard Community Memorial Centre. That naming reflected the
community’s desire to acknowledge both Carrie’s connection to Welland and the lasting
significance of her legacy. The facility served as a space for recreation, inclusion, and
community gathering, and its name became associated with remembrance, safety, and collective
responsibility.
As the City undertakes the development of a new school and dedicated community space to
address the needs of Dain City’s growing population, we respectfully request that this established
recognition be carried forward. Naming the new community space in honour of Carrie Lynn
Pinard would preserve continuity, reflect the historical significance already recognized by the
City, and maintain a meaningful connection between the facility and the community it serves.
On behalf of our family and friends, we formally provide our full consent and support for the
naming of the new school’s dedicated community space in honour of Carrie Lynn Pinard. We
appreciate the City of Welland and it’s Council, their consideration of this request and its
commitment to recognizing individuals whose lives and legacies hold lasting significance within
the community.
Sincerely,
Bob and Margaret Pinard

1. To recognize the reconfigured lot area and frontage of PIN 221870105 from 0.49ha and 53.6m

boundaries, and to allow for an accessory building’s lot coverage to exceed up to 85% of the lot coverage of
the main dwelling. This application was deferred by the Committee of Adjustment at their October 1, 2025,
meeting until such time as outstanding issues regarding the proposed entrance had been resolved.
Since that time, the applicant has made slight modifications to the proposal and retained Salvini Consulting to
conduct a sight line review for an additional entrance to the properties. The sight line assessment concluded that
a second driveway to Huron Road could be located between the existing driveway and the second hydro pole to
the east and meet Transportation Association of Canada Geometric Design Guide for Canadian Roads (TAC)
intersection sight distance requirements. Further, the study concluded that vehicles leaving the property would
have visibility of oncoming traffic in both directions to safely complete turning movements. This assessment was
reviewed by corridor staff within the Township’s Infrastructure Services Department who agreed with the findings.
Ultimately, should this application proceed, the Township’s Infrastructure Services would be required to approve
an entrance permit for the installation of the second access.
In circulating the application, staff did not receive any concerns and are recommending that the application be
approved.

TOWNSHIP OF WILMOT
REPORT TO WILMOT COMMITTEE OF ADJUSTMENT
MINOR VARIANCE APPLICATION
SUBMISSION NO: A-12/26
APPLICANT: Sam Head (DSH Planning)
PROPERTY ADDRESS / LOCATION: Part of Lot 16, Concession North of Snyder’s Road
142-148 Snyder’s Road West, Baden
SUMMARY OF REQUEST: To reduce the front and side yard setback
OFFICIAL PLAN: Urban Residential
ZONING BY-LAW: Zone 3 (Residential)
Comments:
This application proposes to reduce the front yard setback from 2.25 metres to approximately 1.6 metres and to
reduce the east side yard setback of a two-storey building from 2.0 metres to approximately 1.4 metres.
The property was rezoned in 2021 allowing redevelopment of the subject lands with 18 units in the form of
single-detached, semi-detached, townhome and apartment dwellings. The previously approved application
also reduced the west side yard setback from 2.0 metres to 1.2 metres and the rear yard setback from 7.5
metres to 2.3 metres.
The applicant is currently advancing a site plan approval application for a concept showing a total of 14 units.
The current concept proposal requires a reduction to the east side yard and front yard setbacks. All other
aspects of the development comply with the property's current zoning. As it relates specifically to the front
yard setback, both buildings adjacent to the proposal do not meet the 7.6 metre front yard setback
requirement. Section 6.4.4 of the Township’s Zoning By-law states:
On any lot between two existing buildings which are not more than 60.0 metres apart and both of which are
between the street line and the front yard or exterior side yard setback established by this By-law, a building
may be erected in line with the existing building closest to the required front yard or exterior side yard
setback.
The closest building to the required front yard setback requirement is 2.25 metres from the front property
line, therefore serving as the starting point for the reduction. To facilitate a development that directs parking
to the rear and provides a street-facing façade, a reduction to the front yard setback is being proposed.
In circulating the application, staff did not receive any concerns and are recommending approval of the
application.
Recommendation:
That the Wilmot Committee of Adjustment approve Submission A-12/26, by Sam Head (DSH Planning), affecting
Part of Lot 16, Concession North of Snyder’s Road, to reduce the front yard setback from 2.25 metres to approximately
1.6 metres and to reduce the east side yard setback of a two-storey building from 2.0 metres to approximately 1.4
metres.

To obtain Council’s approval for additional funds for the Transit portion of the Fee Assistance in
Recreation (F.A.I.R) program.
BACKGROUND
In 2023, Council approved Transit to be included in the FAIR program. A total of $30,000 was
included in the 2024 and 2025 Revenue budgets for this program. The program allows qualified
individuals or households to purchase Transit passes at a 50% discount. Purchase of the
monthly passes using the FAIR program can be done at the Cowan Park Sportsplex, Southside
Aquatic Centre and Reeves Community Complex.
COMMENT
When a qualified individual applies and is approved for Transit FAIR funds, the funds necessary
for that individual to receive a year’s worth of passes is earmarked. This guarantees that the
funds are available to that individual to purchase Transit passes at the subsidized rate for the
remainder of the year. This also results in a situation where the money may not all be spent yet
but is earmarked already. This is what has happened to the fund this year. There has been
sufficient applications to the fund that all of the budgeted amount is already earmarked for the
remainder of the year. Because of this Staff have had to put on a waiting list recent applications
for the program due to unavailable funds.
To assist qualified applicants to receive funding, Staff have been reaching out to already qualified
applicants to confirm if they will be using their approved funding or not. The intent is that if they
are no longer planning on using the fund, the money earmarked for their use can be reclassified
as available so that others can use it. To date, Staff have been unable to free up sufficient funds
to help those on the waiting list.
Although Staff will continue to reach out to approved recipients of the fund, this does not address
the immediate need of other qualified applicants not being able to take advantage of this fund due
to unavailable funds. To address this issue, Staff requests that City Council approve an
additional $30,000 to account 0709-77143-0314 Transit Admin - Fee Assistance Subsidy to be
funded from the Slot Machine Reserve Fund. Approval of these funds will allow Staff to approve
access to more individuals immediately.
Staff will continue to monitor usage and release earmarked funds that will not be used. It should
be noted that the approved budget amounts may not be all spent. In 2024, $25,705.50 was
approved however a total of $8,717.25 was spent. So even though $30,000 has already been
earmarked this year, the recipients may not end up taking advantage of the full amount.
RECOMMENDATION
That Woodstock City Council approve an additional $30,000 to account 0709-77143-0314 Transit
Admin - Fee Assistance Subsidy to be funded from the Slot Machine Reserve Fund.

Background:
Ontario Regulation 191/11: Integrated Accessibility Standards 4(1) requires designated public

and meet its requirements under this Regulation.
In addition, Section 4(3) requires those same designated public sector organizations to
prepare an annual status report on the progress of measures taken to implement the
strategies of the multi-year accessibility plan and to post the status report on their website.

Accessibility Status Report
This Accessibility Status Report is the annual update on the progress of measures taken to improve
accessibility and implement the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA) and the
Integrated Accessibility Standards Regulation (IASR).
This status report includes the accessibility initiatives that were completed in 2021 to implement
the strategies outlined in Bruce County’s Multi-Year Accessibility Plan.
Bruce County’s Commitment to Accessibility
The Corporation of the County of Bruce is committed to eliminating barriers and improving
accessibility for persons with disabilities in a manner that respects dignity, independence
integration and equal opportunity.
Bruce County recognizes the diverse needs of all our residents and customers and will respond by
striving to provide services and facilities that are accessible to all. Bruce County is committed to
meeting the needs of people with disabilities in a timely manner and will do so by preventing and
removing barriers to accessibility and meeting accessibility requirements under the Accessibility for
Ontarians with Disabilities Act.
The County will promote accessibility by ensuring that compliance is met for all regulations made
under the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005. To ensure that timelines are met,
the County will establish, implement and maintain a multi-year accessibility plan. The plan will
outline the County’s strategy to prevent and remove barriers to people with disabilities.
AODA Compliance
The County completes an AODA compliance report for the Province every two years. A compliance
report was completed and submitted to the Province on December 17, 2021.
The County reported non-compliance for the Information and Communications Standard, for
accessible websites and web content. Though we are non-compliant, the County will continue to
work towards compliance with the requirements of the AODA for accessible websites and web
content.
2021 Accessibility Status Report
The 2021 Accessibility Status Report includes the County of Bruce's commitment to removing
barriers to our programs, services and facilities and the progress we have made on the actions to
meet the AODA.

The County is committed to offering excellent accessible customer service by making sure all
members of the public receive a fair customer service experience that meets their needs. Ongoing
compliance with the customer service standard includes the training of new hires as part of their
orientation and volunteers who interact with the public on the County’s behalf.
Accomplishments:
• Continued to review customer feedback and take appropriate action.
• Continued to comply with the requirements of the Customer Service Standard, including
implementing the Accessibility policy and training staff on an ongoing basis.
2. General Requirements
The County is committed to developing, implementing and maintaining policies governing how we
achieve or will achieve accessibility through meeting our requirements under the accessibility
standards referred to in the Integrated Accessibility Standards Regulation.
Accomplishments:
• Reviewed the County's Multi-Year Accessibility Plan in preparation of the Annual Status
Report which will be posted on the County’s website.
• Continued to incorporate accessibility features into our procurement or acquisition of goods,
services and facilities where applicable.

Human Rights Code (OHRC) as it pertains to people with disabilities.

requirements and establishes the County’s core accessibility principles. The Policy’s

of all people. The Policy was updated in 2017 to include revisions related to service animals

The County is committed to ensuring information and communications are available and accessible
to people with disabilities.

are created in a way that considers accessibility.

in London. As a condition of Paramedic Service’s funding agreement with the MOHLTC, Bruce
County Paramedic Service is committed to provide transfer services as directed by the ACC.
Depending on the acuity of a patient’s condition there are three modes of interfacility transfer
which can be used to facilitate their transport. Ornge could be used for patients requiring
ongoing critical care during their transportation. The Bruce County’s Paramedics supports the
needs of patients requiring the services of Primary Care Paramedics. More complex patients
can be transported by Paramedic Services if the sending hospital assigns a nurse or physician
to provide care during transport. The third would be a private transfer service which currently
is contracted by the hospitals to Voyageur.
As the MOHLTC continues to centralization of medical specialists into Centers of Excellence
there will be a continuing need to transfer patients to and from these facilities which are
outside of Bruce County. In addition, changes in the treatment protocols for conditions such
as strokes and cardiac conditions can see patients, who were treated in their local hospital
today for these conditions, required to be transferred to another facility tomorrow so they
can receive the appropriate level of care or diagnostic services. Paramedic Services is
carefully monitoring discussions surrounding these potential changes as the direct transfer of
patients to healthcare facilities outside Bruce County would place increased pressures on the
service’s current deployment plan as units may have to travel as far as London.

The Museum Director reported that as per the closed report on July 12, County

with and without the Applied Research Centre (Ontario Nuclear Innovation
Institute) on the newly acquired property at 254 High Street.
Since that time the work towards progressing the Nuclear Innovation Institute
(NII) has advanced and we continue to work with Bruce Power to further
define the physical footprint of the Museum expansion including the NII.
After several discussions with the selected architectural firm Reitch & Petch it
has become apparent that in order to accommodate the physical needs of the
space for both the Museum and the NII, benefit from the full utilization of a
shared spaces model and incorporate considerations from the public regarding
the aesthetics of the building it is clear that the original options provided have
limitations and would not allow for the vision to be accomplished.

distinct buildings allows for better utilization and flow of shared space, the
necessary square footage for the Museum expansion, as well as,
accommodating all functions for the NII (Innovation / Incubation / Skilled
Trades Secretariat); while providing seamless integration of the new
building with the existing footprint.

at the original size of 18,935 sq. ft. with the NII at 12,730 sq. ft. with access
to shared space at 2,190 sq. ft. (2 classrooms and Community Gallery) plus the
theatre. With the approach of a single build the Museum expansion still
maintains the footprint required at 18,935 sq. ft., with most of the space fully
accessible on one level which allows staff easier access of documents and
monitoring of space.

identifies the square footage gained by combining the footprint in one build.

review the conceptual drawings and recommendation for consideration.

community safety.

important to continue to build and strengthen partnerships across sectors, and we
thank our many community partners that have come together to develop this Plan.

Community Safety and Well-Being
Planning In Ontario: An Overview
In 2009, the work of community safety and well-being planning began in Ontario with a
partnership between the Ministry of the Solicitor General and the Ontario Association of
Chiefs of Police. Community safety and well-being is broader than the traditional
definition of safety (i.e. crime) and is critical to ensure that community members are
safe, have a sense of belonging, have opportunities to participate, and are able to meet
their needs for education, health care, food, housing, income, and social and cultural
expression. Ensuring this sense of safety and well-being requires a multi sector,
‐
collaborative effort.
The Police Services Act (1990) mandates every municipal council to prepare and adopt
a Community Safety and Well-Being (CSWB) Plan. Under the legislation, municipalities
have the discretion and flexibility to develop joint plans with surrounding municipalities.
The municipalities in Aylmer-Elgin-St. Thomas are working collaboratively to develop a
shared Community Safety and Well-Being Plan for all of Elgin.
As part of the legislation, the Province has mandated a number of requirements.
Municipalities must:
Prepare and adopt a Community Safety and Well-Being Plan
Work in partnership with a multi-sectoral advisory committee comprised of
representation from the police service board and other local service providers in
health/mental health, education, community/social services and children/youth
services
Conduct consultations with the advisory committee and members of the public
The Ontario Framework
The Ontario Community Safety and Well-Being Planning framework operated as a guide
in developing the Aylmer-Elgin-St. Thomas Community Safety and Well-Being Plan. This
framework focuses on collaboration, information sharing and performance
measurement, and identifies four areas in which communities can be made safer and
healthier:
1. Social Development
2. Prevention
3. Risk Intervention
4. Incident Response

The Provincial planning framework for Community Safety and Well-Being Plans
highlights a number of critical success factors of community safety and well-being
planning. These include
Strength-Based – recognize the work that’s already being
done in the community and collaborating to do more and
leverage local expertise
Risk-Focused – focus on the risk, preventing something
bad from happening rather than trying to fix it after the
fact

place to live

of sectors, agencies, organizations and groups

community safety and well-being, no single individual,
agency or organization can fully own the planning process
Evidence and Evaluation – part of the planning process
must involve gathering information and evidence to
provide a clear picture of what is happening in the
community
Cultural Responsiveness – being open to and respectful
of cultural difference
Our approach to developing the Aylmer-Elgin-St. Thomas Community Safety and

success factors.

Phase 1: Project Planning and Onboarding

Phase 2: Research and Asset Mapping
The second phase of the community safety and well-being planning process
focused on collecting local data and information about the communities in Aylmer-
Elgin-St. Thomas. This is a key component in the creation of the Community Safety
and Well-Being Plan as it provides a snapshot, that is based on data, about what is
happening in the areas of health, well-being and safety in the Elgin region.

An inventory of existing planning tables in Aylmer-Elgin-St. Thomas was also
conducted. A total of 20 planning tables were identified. This inventory highlighted:

A key aspect in the development of the Aylmer-Elgin-St. Thomas Community Safety
and Well-Being Plan is making sure the plan is evidence-informed. To ensure this,

moves into implementation. A Data Package was developed to support this process.

The third phase of the community safety and well-being planning process focused
on community engagement. Throughout this phase we engaged with residents and

COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE REPORT
REPORT NO. CW-040-2026
ACCESSIBLE PARKING SPACE DESIGNATION - COUNTY ROAD 8 (MAIN STREET),
VILLAGE OF ELGIN
ADEM ADEBAYO
MANAGER OF CAPITAL PROJECTS AND ENGINEERING
RECOMMENDATIONS
THAT the Committee of the Whole recommend that Council designate one (1)
accessible on-street parking space on County Road 8 (Main Street), in the Village of
Elgin, Township of Rideau Lakes, generally adjacent to the frontage of Elgin Pharmacy at
15 Main Street, as shown on the design drawing;
THAT the necessary by-law amendment be prepared once the Township of Rideau
Lakes has completed the works.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
The Counties will be responsible for the by-law amendment process and the supply and
installation of the regulatory accessible parking sign and post hardware, estimated at
less than $1,000.00.
The Township of Rideau Lakes has confirmed that it will be responsible for the design
and construction costs required to make the space barrier-free, including curb and
sidewalk modifications, pavement markings, and ongoing maintenance of the painted
markings.
STRATEGIC INITIATIVES
This recommendation supports the United Counties of Leeds and Grenville’s 2024-2026
Page 2
ACCESSIBLE PARKING SPACE DESIGNATION - COUNTY ROAD 8 (MAIN STREET), VILLAGE OF ELGIN
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
Strategic Initiatives Framework. It aligns with Pillar Two: Support key investments in the
well-being of our residents, by improving barrier-free access to a local pharmacy and
supporting residents, seniors and visitors with mobility challenges.
The project reflects the Framework values of being accountable, inclusive, respectful and
improvement focused through coordination with the Township of Rideau Lakes.
CLIMATE CHANGE IMPLICATIONS
There are no direct climate change implications.
ACCESSIBILITY CONSIDERATIONS
The designation will create a dedicated and enforceable accessible parking space in
front of Elgin Pharmacy, improving access to an important local service for persons with
disabilities, seniors and residents with mobility challenges.
COMMUNICATIONS CONSIDERATIONS
The Township of Rideau Lakes initiated the request and has been involved throughout
the review process.
Staff will continue to coordinate with the Township on the timing of the works and
signage installation. Once the by-law is approved, the approved works are complete,
and the regulatory signage is installed, the designation will be communicated to the
public through the posted accessible parking signage and pavement markings.
BACKGROUND
The Township of Rideau Lakes requested that the Counties designate an accessible on-
street parking space on County Road 8 (Main Street), generally in front of Elgin
Pharmacy at 15 Main Street, in the Village of Elgin.
DISCUSSION/ALTERNATIVES
Page 3
ACCESSIBLE PARKING SPACE DESIGNATION - COUNTY ROAD 8 (MAIN STREET), VILLAGE OF ELGIN
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
Counties staff advised that there was no objection in principle to the request; however,
technical review identified that the existing raised curb created a barrier between the
road and sidewalk. The Township retained Jewell Engineering to prepare a design.
Counties staff reviewed the revised drawing and confirmed that the Counties
requirements have been met, including the depressed curb/sidewalk ramp and the
International Symbol of Access pavement marking. The Township also confirmed
responsibility for the related construction costs and ongoing maintenance of the
pavement markings.
Enacting a by-law that designates an accessible parking space allows for enforcement
(by Rideau Lakes) under the Municipal Act, 2001, Section 427 and the O. Reg. 581
Accessible Parking for Persons with Disabilities, Section 11.

KATIE CLARKE
DEPUTY TREASURER
PAT HUFFMAN
TREASURER
RECOMMENDATIONS
THAT the Committee of the Whole recommends that the 2025 year-end surplus of
$43,337.57 be transferred to the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve in accordance with Policy
ADM-020.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
KPMG has completed their fieldwork for the 2025 year-end audit, however, Partner
review and sign-off is still outstanding. Based on the current results, the 2025 surplus is
$43,337.57.
Policy ADM-020, a Year-End Operating Surplus/Deficit Policy for the United Counties of
Leeds and Grenville was adopted in By-Law No. 19-64. This policy recommends the
surplus be allocated in the following order:
a) Transfer 10% to the Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve until the optimal level has
been attained;
b) Transfer 30% to the Working Fund Reserve until the optimal level has been
attained;
c) Transfer 30% to the Roads Amortization Reserve until the optimal level has been
attained;
Page 2
2025 YEAR-END BUDGET VARIANCE REPORT
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
d) Transfer 30% to the Bridges/Culverts Amortization Reserve until the optimal level
has been attained;
e) If surplus funds still remain, Council can approve transfers to additional Reserves
and/or Reserve Funds;
f) If surplus funds still remain, the amount shall be carried forward to the
subsequent year’s budget in accordance with the Municipal Act.
Staff are recommending that the full year-end surplus be allocated to the Tax Rate
Stabilization Reserve as this reserve is $758K under the optimal level and it will have
significant pressure on it in 2026 due to the delay in opening G. Tackaberry and Family
Home. Any overall deficit at December 31, 2026 will need to be funded from the Tax
Rate Stabilization Reserve. The Working Fund is at the optimal level at the end of 2025,
and both the Roads Amortization and Bridges/Culvert Amortization Reserves had
transfers of funds back into these reserves due to projects coming in under budget in
2025.
STRATEGIC INITIATIVES
The recommendation supports Section 4.2 of the Counties’ Strategic Initiatives,
maintaining the financial sustainability of the Counties, by allocating the surplus to the
Tax Rate Stabilization Reserve as this reserve will experience pressure in 2026.
CLIMATE CHANGE IMPLICATIONS
Where possible reports are provided in a digital format to reduce the Counties carbon
footprint.
ACCESSIBILITY CONSIDERATIONS

manner that is inclusive, to ensure accessibility barriers are reduced or eliminated where
possible.

OPS HARMONIZATION
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
BACKGROUND
The Ontario Ministry of Transportation (MTO) is proposing a new regulation that would,
for the first time, make provincial road construction standards mandatory for
municipalities across Ontario.
The proposed regulation would mandate the use of Ontario Provincial Standards for
Municipal Road Construction (OPSS.MUNI) in three priority areas: hot mix asphalt,
aggregates, and drainage. In addition to technical standards, all municipalities would be
required to use the OPSS.MUNI 100 General Conditions of Contract as the standard set
of terms and conditions in contracts with third-party road construction contractors.
The proposed regulation includes a process for municipalities to request an exemption
from a specific standard. Requests must be submitted to MTO with supporting
documentation, including details about the project in question and a rationale for why
an exemption is appropriate.
Municipalities would be required to submit annual reports to MTO on their application
of the mandatory standards. The Minister would have the authority to publish
information from these reports.
All municipalities must be in compliance with the mandatory standards by July 1, 2027,
which is just over a year away.
The Proposal is closed for comments in the Ontario Regulatory Registry, with the
summary available online: https://www.regulatoryregistry.gov.on.ca/proposal/53294
DISCUSSION/ALTERNATIVES
The Municipal Engineers Association (MEA, co-steward of the OPS) has recently
provided comments to the Province's plan to Harmonize the OPS. The MEA's comments
are attached to this report and were forwarded to all Ontario Clerks so that all Ontario
Municipalities be made aware of the MEA's significant concerns regarding
Harmonization of Municipal Road Construction Standards.
UCLG currently uses the OPSS-MUNI, including the General Conditions, with
modifications to develop road construction contracts. In reviewing MTO’s proposed
regulation, Counties Administration shares the concerns of the MEA, particularly relating
to the:
Page 3
OPS HARMONIZATION
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
1. Approval Process for Exemptions: UCLG typically uses special provisions to
modify the OPS to suit the needs of the project, our geography, climate,
operational constraints, and local material and labour availability. Seeking
approvals for exemptions may impact the ability of staff to deliver projects
successfully in any given budget cycle.
2. Mandatory Annual Reporting: UCLG was not clear on the purpose, or
anticipated administrative effort, of the proposed annual reporting.
Like the MEA, Counties Administration are supportive of the intent of the regulation to
promote consistency, quality, and efficiency across municipal road construction projects.
However, we agree that additional consideration be given to the time and administrative
effort associated with preparing, reviewing, and obtaining exemptions and reporting, as
well as the cumulative impacts on project delivery arising from project‑by‑project
assessments.

Governance Model.

Conference on March 31, 2026

March 29, 2026
Municipal Standards Harmonization Office (MSHO)
Subject: MEA Comments to Ontario Regulatory Registry 26-MTO003
We are writing to respond to Ontario Regulatory Registry 26-MTO003 - Harmonization of
Municipal Road Construction Standards.
Municipal engineers play a vital role in planning, maintaining, renewing, and constructing
municipal infrastructure. Their expertise spans all aspects of municipal infrastructure
services - from design and construction to project management and leadership – ensuring
the successful delivery of both small and large-scale capital infrastructure projects.
Through its membership, MEA provides specialized knowledge in all areas of municipal
engineering in Ontario. In partnership with the Ministry of Transportation Ontario (MTO),
MEA co-manages the Ontario Provincial Standards & Specifications (Municipal) and
delivers training on Ontario Provincial Standards.
While we support the intent of the regulation to promote consistency, quality, and
efficiency across municipal road construction projects, we recommend that additional
consideration be given to the time and administrative burden associated with preparing,
reviewing, and obtaining exemptions, as well as the cumulative impacts on project delivery
arising from project by project assessments.
‑ ‑
Exemption requests that require detailed technical justification across multiple evaluation
criteria can take a considerable amount of time to prepare, particularly for complex or
large scale projects. This work frequently requires the involvement of senior engineering,
technical, legal, and procurement resources, diverting limited capacity away from active
‑
project delivery. The time required to assemble a complete exemption request should
therefore be recognized as a potential schedule, cost, and resourcing risk in its own right.
Equally important is the duration and predictability of the Minister’s review and response
timelines. When exemptions are assessed on a project by project basis without defined
service standards or response timelines, projects may experience material delays while
‑ ‑
awaiting decisions. These delays can produce cascading impacts, including missed
construction windows, contractor demobilization and remobilization costs, loss of price
certainty, and increased exposure to supply chain volatility. For time sensitive or critical
‑ ‑
Office of the President
1525 Cornwall Road
Oakville ON
L6J 0B2
president@municipalengineers.on.ca
infrastructure projects, even relatively short delays in regulatory decision making can
result in disproportionate impacts to project schedules and budgets.
‑
To better reflect these realities, we recommend that the exemption framework explicitly
consider additional criteria, including:
• Administrative and decision cycle timelines, including the anticipated time required
for review and approval and the impact of uncertainty on project planning and
‑
procurement;
• Cumulative impacts across multiple projects, particularly where similar exemption
requests are repeatedly submitted for comparable project types or conditions;
• Schedule dependency and critical path impacts, including whether delays in
exemption approval would directly affect construction sequencing, seasonal work
constraints, or contractual obligations; and
• Consistency and precedent considerations, whereby prior approvals for similar
circumstances could support streamlined or standardized decision making, rather
than requiring repetitive project level analysis.
‑
‑
Incorporating these considerations would help ensure that the exemption process
supports timely and efficient project delivery while still meeting regulatory objectives.
Clear expectations regarding submission requirements and response timelines, as well as
opportunities for programmatic or category based exemptions where appropriate, would
significantly reduce risk to project schedules and budgets without compromising safety,
‑
performance, or sustainability outcomes.
Looking ahead, and assuming the Ministry is able to successfully deliver the current list of
harmonized standards within the proposed timeframe, we agree that the remaining
OPSS.MUNI standards should be prioritized for future harmonization based on where the
greatest time, cost, and administrative efficiencies can be achieved. In our view, this
would include:
• Standards with the highest frequency of use across municipalities, where
harmonization would reduce repetitive project specific reviews, municipal
deviations, and contract amendments;
‑
• Standards that routinely generate exemptions, interpretations, or disputes,
indicating inconsistency or misalignment that drives additional design effort,
approval cycles, or delays;
• Standards that significantly affect project schedules or cost certainty, including
those related to materials, construction methods, or inspection requirements that
influence procurement and delivery timelines;

alignment would enhance system coherence and reduce unintended conflicts or
inefficiencies; and
• Standards that affect regional or multi jurisdictional projects, where inconsistent
requirements currently increase coordination challenges and administrative
‑
complexity.
A transparent, phased approach, supported by demonstrated progress on the initially
harmonized standards, would help ensure that future harmonization efforts are achievable
and deliver tangible benefits. Clearly articulating how the Ministry will complete the
current scope, and how lessons learned will inform the prioritization of remaining
standards, will be essential to achieving intended efficiency gains without overextending

RECOMMENDATIONS
THAT the Committee of the Whole recommends to Council that staff communicate with
the Town of Smiths Falls and the Ministry of Economic Development, Job Creation and
Trade (MEDJCT) regarding the Small Business Enterprise Centre (SBEC) contract as
outlined in Option _______ of Report No. CW-021-2026.
FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS
The Leeds Grenville SBEC contract for 2024-2026 was $269,727 with the Town of Smiths
Falls SBEC contract being $231,666. The Ministry contract per capita for Leeds Grenville
is $3.22 with Smiths Falls at $2.73. Recognizing this differential, there would be no
additional funding for Leeds Grenville should we wish to be inclusive of all municipalities
under its SBEC contract.
The Counties currently contributes $5,000 to the Smiths Falls SBEC that is not included
in these calculations.
STRATEGIC INITIATIVES
This report supports Section 1.6 – Encourage and Support Economic Development and
Tourism in the County. It is also a part of the 2026-2029 Leeds Grenville Economic
Development Strategic Areas of Focus under 2.0 - Initiate and facilitate business
development and investment attraction.
Page 2

footprint.

COMMUNICATIONS CONSIDERATIONS
Based on the option selection, staff will communicate the Counties decision with the
MEDJCT and the Town of Smiths Falls. Should option 2 be selected and the Ministry’s
approval occurs, a further communication strategy would be developed to ensure
businesses are made aware of these new geographic boundaries.
BACKGROUND
The Leeds Grenville Economic Development Department deliveries a Small Business
program that is funded by MEDJCT as part of an SBEC contract.
In June of 2024, Council requested staff investigate making the delivery of the SBEC
whole in Leeds Grenville, as the municipalities of Westport, Rideau Lakes, Merrickville-
Wolford and the Kitley portion of Elizabethtown-Kitley is delivered by the Town of
Smiths Falls SBEC contract.
In the fall of 2024, the Ministry decided to perform a program review as this had not
been done for many years. In the fall of 2025, the Ministry identified there would be no
geographic realignments, and any considerations would be handled on an individual
basis.
At the end of November 2025, an initial meeting occurred with the Town of Smiths Falls
to discuss the Counties request. Both parties acknowledge there is no Ministry formula
that determines how a SBEC is funded. It was agreed to utilize a standard municipal
approach to determine funding levels to ensure both parties felt there was equity based
on per capita by population.
Smiths Falls is not looking for a change in their SBEC contract as they believe it is
working the way it is but would not actively oppose.
Page 3
SMALL BUSINESS – CONSOLIDATION OF PROGRAM DELIVERY
COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE
The Leeds Grenville municipalities under the Smiths Falls contract represents 14% of the
overall population.
Both SBEC contracts are currently being drafted by MEDJCT for presentation and
approval as the current contract expired March 31, 2026.
DISCUSSION/ALTERNATIVES
Option 1
Continue to maintain its current geographic areas that have previously been part of the
United Counties of Leeds and Grenville SBEC contract.
No change in geographic boundaries would mean the two programs would be
promoted separately and run differently. The business ratio for microgrants would
remain the same.
A gap in communication would continue between the Smiths Falls SBEC and Counties
Economic Development and businesses served. This results in a reduced business
affiliation to Counties Economic Development and the additional programs offered.
The $5,000 budgeted for the Smiths Falls SBEC would continue to be funded by the
Counties.

SMALL BUSINESS – CONSOLIDATION OF PROGRAM DELIVERY

Notify the Town of Smiths Falls and express to MEDJCT, that the United Counties of Leeds
and Grenville would like to request all municipalities in the Counties be included as part of
its SBEC contract. These would include:
Township of Athens Township of Leeds and the Thousand Islands
Township of Augusta Village of Merrickville-Wolford*
City of Brockville Municipality of North Grenville
Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal Town of Prescott
Township of Elizabethtown-Kitley* Township of Rideau Lakes*
Township of Front of Yonge Village of Westport*
Town of Gananoque
* A portion of, or all the municipality was included under the Smiths Falls SBEC contract.
The inclusion of all municipalities in Leeds Grenville would be provided with the same
SBEC program delivery and associated promotions - such as Starter Company Plus and
Summer Company program launches and wrap-ups.
All businesses under one SBEC would have a continuum of support from ideation
through to succession by Counties Economic Development. They would be tracked with
a joint CRM system and registration to Counties business eNewsletter. Counties
Economic Development team members are cross trained to ensure there is no gap in
service delivery.
In addition, businesses would be better aligned for any further program enhancements
under the Economic Development strategic areas of focus, and its actions associated
such a youth entrepreneurship action plan and development a more robust business
mentorship / coaching program.
A Counties SBEC business outreach program would be expanded to ensure scheduled
business consultation dates are offered in various municipalities. The business ratio for

The $5,000 budgeted for the Smiths Falls SBEC would remain with Leeds Grenville to

In brief, this project involves two interrelated, but distinct work streams – construction

CONSTRUCTION ISSUES
As noted above, the project was originally forecast to receive a full construction
occupancy permit in Spring 2025. This permit relates to the actual completion of
construction and is issued by a municipal building official. It authorizes access to the
facility without use of personal protective equipment.
A building occupancy permit is different than the provincial commissioning (licensing)
approvals required to allow occupation of the building by the planned 192 residents,
staff and visitors. Building occupancy permits may also be conditional pending the
completion of outstanding deficiencies and final sign off by the building official.
In the case of the GTFH, the building official issued a conditional occupancy permit on
November 7, 2025, to provide staff access to the facility to start necessary training on
the new equipment and complete other commissioning work required by the Ministry of
Long-Term Care (MLTC). This provided staff and partners access to the entire complex
except the exterior patio where installation of the glass railing was delayed due to
delivery issues. Staff and contracted partners continue to work with the building official
to address outstanding deficiencies and secure a final unconditional building
construction occupancy permit.
Project Changes and Impact to Schedule
Over the course of the project, several modifications were incorporated into the design
and construction to better align the facility’s evolving operational and programming
requirements. While these adjustments were important to ensuring the long-term
functionality and quality of the home, they required additional coordination, design
refinement, procurement activities, and construction sequencing adjustments, which
collectively affected the overall timeline.
Examples of revisions that contributed to extended design development, longer
procurement lead times, and changes to construction sequencing include:

communications model that includes centralized grant development support.

processes.
• Working with staff and community partners to shape strong project proposals.

Between January 1 and June 30, 2026, four funding applications led by the Senior Advisor,

Partnership Program to support the Trail & Road Safety Community Partnership.
Through this project, the Northumberland and District ATV Riders Club, Ontario
Federation of ATV Clubs, and Northumberland County Public Works will promote safer
road use, improve off-road vehicle safety, and increase awareness of applicable Ministry
policies and legislation by installing 60 “ATV Crossing Ahead” warning signs at 30 trail
and County Road intersections and delivering a road safety awareness campaign.
• $1,500 from the Cameco Sponsorship Fund to support the delivery of the Golden
Plough Lodge’s Health and Wellness Festival. This event will bring together residents,
families, and staff for an engaging day focused on self-care, mental health awareness,
and overall well-being. Facilitated by the GPL Peer Support Team, the festival will reflect
a collaborative effort between Golden Plough Lodge and Cameco.

DISCUSSION
Background
On March 30, 2026, Canada and Ontario announced the Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build
(COPB), in support of shared goals, including building more homes faster to make housing
more affordable, getting shovels in the ground on key transit projects and supporting economic
development.
On June 1, 2026, the federal and provincial governments opened applications for the
Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) intended to reduce building costs and speed
up the construction of new homes. As part of the up to $8.8 billion partnership announced in
March, the DCRP will deliver federal and provincial funding over 10 years for housing-enabling
infrastructure projects, with funding prioritized for municipalities that reduce development
charges (DCs) for all residential types by at least 30% to 50% and maintain the reductions for at
least three years.
There will only be a single intake for this program. Key details on the program have been
provided below:
Program Outcomes
As described in the guideline “rising municipal DCs add to the cost of building homes and
therefore, are considered a major barrier to unlocking the housing supply. This program is
designed to address this barrier.”
There are two main outcomes of the program:

Key Requirements
 Municipalities that have an active DC by-law as of March 30, 2026, are eligible to
participate in this program.
 Must provide an agreement-in-principle at the time of application to reduce DCs for all
residential development by at least 30% to 50% for a three-year period.
 The DC reductions must be inclusive of area-specific DCs, but municipalities can choose
to reduce certain service categories more than others.
 Reductions in DC are based on rates in effect as of March 30, 2026. DC indexing would
not be completed during the three-year period of relief.
 DC reductions would take effect immediately upon entering into the Transfer Payment
Agreement (TPA) and would be retroactive to building permits obtained after March 30,
2026.
 Municipalities must make a commitment to fund at least 10% of the eligible (growth-
related) project costs from non-DC sources.
 Joint applications among municipalities are eligible as long as both municipalities meet
the eligibility requirements for the DCRP program.
 Eligible projects must be aligned with and support provincial land use planning priorities
and outcomes, as set out in provincial land use policy, municipal official plans and
zoning by-laws.
Application Requirements
The following information is required to be provided in the application:
 An estimate of the number of housing units that will benefit from reduced DCs and the
resulting amount of DC relief;
 A reasonable estimate of the number of housing units that would be enabled by the
proposed municipal infrastructure project(s);
 Proposed infrastructure projects for DCRP funding from within the municipal DC
background study and County’s approved capital plan;
 Commitment to funding at least 10% of eligible project costs; and
 Commitment to comply with the Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada’s Buy
Canadian Policy or Municipal Buy Ontario Procurement Directive, as set out in the TPA.
A municipality may submit more than one application individually or jointly with other
municipalities. Province encourages municipalities to limit the number of eligible projects to five
and to bundle, as appropriate. Project(s) and the requested funding amounts must be reflective
of the estimated amount of DC relief provided to builders and the proposed municipal
contribution for each project.
Evaluation of Application
Project decisions will be made by the province and the federal government. The province will
assess and prioritize applications based on:

Auto Mayors Motion
 WHEREAS the Auto Mayors work collaboratively at the provincial and federal orders of government to promote awareness, advocacy and strategic policy initiatives that strengthen the Canadian economy through advancements and investments in the automotive sector;
WHEREAS continued progress toward tariff-free access to the U.S. market and maintaining an integrated North American auto sector remain the auto sector’s top priority;
WHEREAS the Auto Mayors welcome ongoing collaboration with the Province and the Federal government on greenhouse gas regulations and electrification targets and policies that reflect current market demand, infrastructure readiness and alignment with the U.S.;
WHEREAS the Auto Mayors are ready to work with Federal partners on a coordinated approach to global competition that ensures Canada remains an attractive destination for investment;
WHEREAS strengthening domestic production requires aligning tariff remission frameworks with manufacturing levels and strengthening Buy Ontario procurement policies to ensure public sector fleet purchasing continues to support Ontario based manufacturers;
AND WHEREAS regular review and monitoring of industrial electricity rates, including how domestic rates compare to export rates, will help ensure Ontario manufacturers remain competitive and positioned for growth.

 The Development Charge Reduction Program presents a significant opportunity

while advancing critical infrastructure needed to support housing growth.
Background
The Development Charge Reduction Program (DCRP) is intended to help municipalities
reduce development charges (DCs) and build infrastructure that supports new housing.
Through the program, municipalities will need to reduce DCs by 30% to 50% or more for
3 years. The DCRP is part of the $8.8 billion Canada-Ontario Partnership to Build with
federal funding delivered through the Build Communities Strong Fund’s Provincial and
Territorial Stream.
On June 15, 2026, City Council approved a motion to reduce DCs by 50%, effective
March 30, 2026, and will maintain this reduction for all residential development types for
3 years.
As part of the June 15, 2026, approved City Council motion, it stated:
"4. The City Treasurer and the Commissioner of Infrastructure Planning and
Growth Management are authorized and directed to determine which housing-
enabling infrastructure projects will best support the creation of new housing and
thus be prioritized and to report back to Council on the projects selected for
inclusion in the application, and the rationale for their prioritization, at the first
regular meeting of Council following submission of the application."
On June 19, 2026, the City of Peterborough submitted two applications to the DCRP.
The first application included a total of 5 different Roads and Related projects, and the
second application included a series of Water and Wastewater projects intended to
service growth in the Coldsprings Planning Area. Details of each application and related
projects are further described below.
Application Criteria and Project Selection
A strong DCRP application demonstrates a clear connection between meaningful
residential development charge relief and the timely delivery of infrastructure required to
support housing growth. Competitive applications identify projects that directly enable a
significant number of housing units, are sufficiently advanced to proceed within the
program timelines, and are supported by municipal planning, development charge and
capital plans. Applications are further strengthened by a higher municipal contribution,

clear project scope and risks, and evidence that the municipality can finance, operate
and maintain the infrastructure over its lifecycle.
Key characteristics of a strong application include:
 A substantial, municipality-wide residential development charge reduction
maintained for three years.
 A clear and measurable housing benefit, including units receiving DC relief and
units enabled by each project.
 Priority investment in housing-enabling infrastructure such as roads, water,
wastewater, stormwater and transit.
 Strong project readiness, supported by completed planning, engineering,
approvals, land acquisition, dedicated reserves or tendering.
 Inclusion in the City’s Development Charge Background Study, capital plan and
future asset management planning.
 A clear scope, schedule, dependencies, risks and mitigation measures, with
completion by October 31, 2035.
 A credible financing plan, including the municipal contribution, upfront cash-flow
capacity and responsibility for cost overruns and lifecycle costs.
In consideration of the above guidance, staff included the following projects in the
DCRP applications:
Application 1
Chemong Road – Parkhill Road to North of Sunset Boulevard
The Chemong Road project is the City’s highest-priority submission for the funding
application due to the scale of planned residential growth, existing transportation and
safety deficiencies, and the project’s readiness to proceed. Chemong Road is identified
as a strategic growth area in the Official Plan, with approximately 5,372 residential units
approved or in progress, and 2,967 enabled by the project. The proposed improvements
include additional transportation capacity, a centre turn lane, active transportation and
transit infrastructure, and sanitary sewer upgrades required to support approximately
612 apartment units. The project would address an existing collision and level-of-service
concern while ensuring the corridor can accommodate planned development.
Alignment with program criteria:
 Directly supports a significant number of approved and planned housing units.
 Includes priority housing-enabling infrastructure: roads, active transportation,
transit-supportive facilities and wastewater servicing.
 Addresses a demonstrated capacity constraint that could limit future housing
development.

OF
THE CORPORATION OF THE COUNTY OF SIMCOE
A By-law to Govern the Calling, Place and Proceedings
of the Meetings of Council and Committees.
Whereas Section 238(2) of the Municipal Act, 2001, S.O. 2001, c. 25 (“Municipal Act”),
provides that every municipality shall pass a By-law governing the calling, place and
proceedings of meetings; and
Whereas by the adoption of Resolution 2025-271, the Council of the County of Simcoe
deems it expedient to enact a new updated Procedure By-law that reflects legislative
requirements, to govern the calling, place and proceedings of the meetings of Council
and Committees of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe;
Now therefore, the Council of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe hereby enacts
as follows:

SHORT TITLE
This By-law shall be cited as the Procedure By-law.
PART 1 - GENERAL
1.0 DEFINITIONS
For the purpose of this By-law:
"Business Sections" means the divisions within a regular Committee of the Whole
meeting each dedicated to specific subject matters within the scope and responsibility of
Council;
"Business Section Chair" means the person appointed by Council to preside during
their respective section at a regular Committee of the Whole meeting;
"Business Section Vice-Chair" means the person appointed by Council who would
preside over the proceedings of their respective section at a regular Committee of the
Whole meeting in the absence of the Chair;
"Chair" means the person appointed by Council or a Committee to preside at a
meeting;
"Chief Administrative Officer" means the Chief Administrative Officer of the
Corporation of the County of Simcoe;
"Clerk" means the County Clerk of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe or their
designate;
“Closed Session” means a meeting or a part of a meeting which is not open to the
public in accordance with the Municipal Act;
"Committee" means any Committee of Council or similar body of which at least 50 per
cent of the members are also members of one or more councils or local boards, and
includes the Committee of the Whole, Special or Ad Hoc Committees, Advisory
Committees or a Task Force of Council;
"Committee of the Whole" means all members of Council and appointed members
sitting as a Committee for the purpose of conducting business in a less formal manner
in accordance with this By-Law;
"Confirmatory By-law" means a By-law passed for the purpose of giving general effect
to the decisions or proceedings of Council;
Page 4 of 57
"Consent Items" means items placed in a section of the agenda that is used to adopt
items with one motion. Consent items may be pulled from the list of consent items by
any member, for further discussion, debate or motion;
"Council" means the Council of the Corporation of the County of Simcoe;
"Delegation" means an address to Council or a Committee at the request of a person
or an organization wishing to speak;
"Deputy Warden" means the person elected by Council to fulfill the duties of Head of
Council in the Warden's absence, and to support the Warden under their guidance and
direction;
“Electronic Meeting” means a meeting held in whole or in part by videoconference, or
other form of electronic means;
"Head of Council" means the Warden for the County of Simcoe or any member acting
in the capacity of the Warden;
"Majority Vote" means an affirmative vote of more than one half of the members
present and eligible to vote;
"Meeting" means any regular, special, or other meeting of Council, or of a Local Board
or a Committee of either of them where, a quorum is present and where members
discuss or otherwise deal with any matter in a way that materially advances the
business or decision-making of the Council, Local Board or Committee;
"Member" means a member of Council, a member of Committee or an alternate
member of Council appointed by a lower-tier municipality under Section 268 of the
Municipal Act;
"Motion" means a proposal by a member presented in a meeting, in accordance with
the rules of procedure, to deal with a matter before Council or Committee;
"Presentation" means an address to Council or Committee that has the consent of the
Warden or Chair and was arranged at the request of Council, Committee or staff, and
may include the presenting of an award, certificate, cheque, etc.;
"Quorum" means the number of members required to be present at a meeting to
validate the transaction of business, that number being more than half of the members
of the Council or Committee who are eligible to vote;
Page 5 of 57
"Recess" means a short intermission in meeting proceedings which does not close the
meeting, and after which business will immediately be resumed at exactly the point in
proceedings where it was stopped;
"Recorded Vote" means a written record of the name and vote of every member
present, voting on any matter or question at a Council meeting;
"Resolution" means the decision of Council on any motion;
"Two-thirds Majority Vote" means an affirmative vote of at least two-thirds of the
members present and eligible to vote at a meeting. Weighted vote shall not apply to
decisions where this By-law requires a two-thirds majority vote;
"Vice-Chair" means the person appointed by Council or Committee who would preside
over the proceedings of a Committee meeting in the absence of the Chair;
"Weighted Vote" refers to a vote where the number of votes allocated to members of
Council is prescribed by County By-law and is a written record of the name and vote of
every member present, voting on any matter or question. A weighted vote shall only
occur in a meeting of Council upon request and must be requested only prior to a matter
or question being put.
2.0 APPLICATION/INTERPRETATION
2.1 Application
The rules of procedure contained in this By-law, or any standing or special rules of
order adopted by the Corporation of the County of Simcoe shall be observed in all
proceedings of Council and, with necessary modifications, its Committees and
Boards. Failure to strictly adhere to the rules of procedure contained in this By-law
shall not invalidate the action(s) of Council or a Committee acting in good faith.
2.2 Statutes Affecting By-law
Whenever any reference is made in this By-law to a statute of the Legislature of the
Province of Ontario, such reference shall be deemed to include all subsequent
amendments to such statute and all successor legislation to such statute.
2.3 Matters Not Specifically Provided for in this By-law
Matters not specifically provided for in this By-law shall be decided by the Warden or
Chair, in accordance with as far as practicable, parliamentary procedures as
generally outlined in "Robert's Rules of Order''. The Clerk may be called upon to
provide advice regarding procedural matters. Following receipt of any advice from
the Clerk, the Warden or Chair shall announce their ruling.
Page 6 of 57
2.4 Notice Required for Amendment or Repeal of By-law
This By-law, or any part thereof, shall not be amended or repealed at any meeting of
Council unless notice of the proposed amendment or repeal has been given at a
previous meeting of Council. The requirement to give this notice shall not be waived.
2.5 Suspension of the Rules of this By-Law
Except for statutory provisions or unless otherwise provided for within this By-law,
any provision of this By-law may be suspended in whole or in part by Council on
obtaining not less than two-thirds majority vote and weighted vote shall not apply.
2.6 Statutory Requirements
Notwithstanding anything in this By-law, where Council or a Committee convenes for
the purpose of holding a hearing as required by any statute or By-law, the provisions
of the statute and the Statutory Powers Procedure Act, as applicable, shall govern
the proceedings. If there is found to be any conflict between this By-law and any
statute or By-law, the provisions of the statute or By-law shall prevail.
2.7 Schedules
Schedules 1, 2 and 3 to this By-law shall form part of this By-law.
2.8 Severability
If any section or part of this By-law is found by any court of competent jurisdiction to
be invalid, such section or part shall be deemed to be severable and shall not affect
the validity or enforceability of any other provisions of this By-law or the By-law as a
whole.
PART 2 - DUTIES/RESPONSIBILITIES AND POWERS
3.0 DUTIES AND RESPONSIBILITIES OF COUNCIL
3.1 Role of Council
In accordance with the Municipal Act, it is the role of Council:
a) to represent the citizens of Simcoe County and to consider the well-being and
interests of the County;
b) to develop and evaluate the policies and programs of the County;
c) to determine which services the County provides;
d) to ensure that administrative policies, practices and procedures and controllership
policies, practices and procedures are in place to implement the decisions of
County Council;
e) to ensure the accountability and transparency of the operations of the County,
including the activities of the senior management of the County; and
f) to maintain the financial integrity of the County; and
g) to carry out the duties of the County Council under the Municipal Act or any other
Act.
Page 7 of 57
4.0 CONDUCT OF MEMBERS
4.1 Respectful Conduct
Members in attendance at meetings shall conduct themselves with decorum in
accordance with the provisions of this By-law and in a manner that demonstrates
professionalism and fosters respect and recognition for the formal nature of such
proceedings.
4.2 Right to Participate
Members shall have the right to full participation in the proceedings of Council
unless prohibited by law or as otherwise prescribed in this By-law.
4.3 Restrictions
Unless otherwise prescribed in the Municipal Act, no member shall:
a) be absent from the meetings of Council for three successive months without
authorization by way of resolution of Council;
b) speak disrespectfully of the Reigning Sovereign, or of any member of the Royal
Family, the Governor General, the Lieutenant Governor of any Province, any
member municipality, any other Council member or any official or employee of
the County;
c) use indecent, offensive or insulting language in or against Council or any
member;
d) engage in private conversation while in a Council meeting or use electronic
devices including cellular phones, portable devices and computers for the
purposes of facilitating or engaging in private discussion with regard to any
matter on the agenda and/or any matter under debate at a meeting, except for
the purpose of communicating a proposed motion to the Clerk;
e) use electronic devices including cellular phones, portable devices and computers
in a manner which interrupts or is disruptive to the proceedings of the Council;
f) make noise or disturbance while a vote is being taken and until the result of the
vote is announced;

the public (closed session), and where the matter remains confidential, disclose

SECTION MENU
City Council meets regularly to discuss and make decisions on matters affecting the community.
Regular Council meetings are usually held on the third Tuesday of each month at 6:00 p.m. These meetings are live-streamed on the City’s Facebook and YouTube channels, allowing residents to watch from home.
Committee of the Whole meetings are generally held on the first Tuesday of each month at 3:00 p.m.
From time to time, special Council meetings may be scheduled as needed.
Meetings are held in the City Hall Council Chambers, located at 325 Farr Drive, Haileybury, unless another location is announced in advance.

Participate in a Council Meeting
Delegations provide members of the public with an opportunity to make a presentation to Council of up to 10 minutes.
Delegations at Regular Council meetings must relate to matters within the jurisdiction and authority of local government.
Delegations at Committee of the Whole meetings must relate to an item included on the published agenda.
Requests to appear as a delegation must be submitted to the Clerk’s Department by completing a Delegation Request Form or by emailing clerk@temiskamingshores.ca, no later than 4:30 p.m. on the Wednesday prior to the meeting. Submission of a request does not guarantee approval.
If a delegation request is approved, a written copy of the presentation must be provided to the Clerk by 4:30 p.m. on the Thursday prior to the meeting.
For additional information, please refer to the Delegation Protocol.
